title: Pope Leo XIV casts ballot in US midterms, becomes first pontiff to vote in a US general election
text: Pope Leo XIV/Image: AP Pope Leo XIV has voted in the 2026 US midterm elections, becoming the first sitting pope to cast a ballot in a US general election, the Vatican confirmed on Friday. The Chicago-born pontiff submitted a mail-in ballot in his home state of Illinois ahead of the November elections. The Holy See press office said Leo, formerly known as Robert Prevost, had exercised his voting rights whenever he was eligible as a US citizen. "The Holy Father expresses his belief in the right and the duty of citizens to participate in democratic processes," the Vatican statement said. The confirmation followed a report by the Chicago Sun-Times, which cited the chief of staff at the Will County clerk's office as saying that Leo had requested a mail-in ballot on October 3. He is registered at an address in New Lenox, Illinois. It remains unclear how the pontiff returned his ballot. His brother, John Prevost, was in Rome this week accompanying parishioners from St Jude's, an Augustinian-run church in New Lenox where the pope attends Mass. Leo also addressed the parish in 2024, when he was still a cardinal. The Vatican said Leo had also voted while living in Peru whenever he was eligible. His participation in the US midterms reflects his stated belief that citizens should take part in democratic elections. Records from the Illinois State Board of Elections cited by the AP show that Prevost requested ballots in five primary elections since 2000. He selected Democratic ballots in 2008 and 2010, followed by Republican ballots in 2012, 2014 and 2016. Illinois voters must declare a party preference when requesting a ballot in a primary election, which determines each party's candidates for the general election. However, voters are not required to declare a party preference when voting in general elections. The records also show that Prevost submitted ballots in every US general election since 2000 except those held in 2020 and 2022. They do not identify which candidates he supported in any election. His voting history spans two Illinois counties. While registered in Cook County, which is heavily Democratic, he requested Democratic primary ballots. After moving to Will County, a more conservative suburban area, he selected Republican ballots in three consecutive primary elections. You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. title: US charges 48 non-citizens over election-related crimes in Pennsylvania, California, Florida, New York and Nevada; two Indians among those accused of illegal voting and false citizenship claims
text: US Justice Department announces charges against 48 non-citizens in election-related cases across five states. (Photo: Office of Public Affairs) The US Department of Justice has announced charges against 48 non-US citizens in connection with alleged election-related offences across several states, including Pennsylvania, California, Florida, New York and Nevada. The cases involve allegations of illegal voting in federal elections, fraudulent voter registration and falsely claiming US citizenship to register or cast ballots. In a press release issued on October 26, 2026, the department detailed cases filed across multiple federal judicial districts. Several defendants are also accused of making false statements during naturalisation proceedings, including allegedly concealing previous voter registration or voting activity. The department said the cases involve both misdemeanour and felony charges, depending on the alleged offences. Two Indian nationals among those charged Two Indian nationals have been named in the announcement. Amandeep Kaur, 30, a lawful permanent resident who is seeking US citizenship, has been accused of registering to vote in December 2022 and voting in the November 2024 US election. The case has been filed in the Central District of California. Watch BREAKING: Horror BLOODBATH In Pennsylvania; Children, Pregnant Women Killed In Mass Shooting Kamlesh Navnitlal Shah, 67, a lawful permanent resident, has been charged in the Eastern District of California with voting by a non-citizen. According to the Justice Department, Shah allegedly registered to vote on the day of the November 2024 general election and cast a ballot that day. He has been charged by information. Both individuals face allegations that have yet to be proven in court. Pennsylvania cases involve nine defendants In Pennsylvania, nine non-citizens have been charged across two federal judicial districts with allegedly voting in elections involving federal offices. In the Eastern District, the defendants include Alfredo Santiesteban, 73, a Cuban national described as an illegal alien; Artur Kopacz, 50, a Polish national; Osmal Loy, 70, a Cuban national; and Yehuda Peer, 30, an Israeli national. The latter three are identified as lawful permanent residents. Prosecutors allege that the four voted in the 2022 or 2024 general elections. In the Middle District, the defendants include Kenyan nationals Nina Nyawara, 21, and Joyce Donovan, 38; Russian national Inna Henry, 52; Dutch national Joyce Pitts, 80; and Greek national Nourten Kuruju, 64. All are described as lawful permanent residents. The allegations concern voting in federal elections held in 2022 or 2024. California cases include allegations of voter fraud and naturalisation fraud The cases involve alleged voter registration fraud and false claims of US citizenship. (Photo: Office of Public Affairs) California accounts for several of the cases detailed by the department, with allegations ranging from illegal voting to false statements in citizenship applications. In the Central District of California, 13 defendants face felony charges, including allegations involving naturalisation applications. They include Belizean national Omar Alexander Munoz, 72, who allegedly registered to vote in 2019 while claiming to be a US citizen and voted in elections in 2020, twice in 2022 and in 2024. He is also accused of making a false statement in his naturalisation application. Other defendants in the district include Salvadoran national Ana Dominguez, 60; Guatemalan national Axel Giovani Prera Garcia, 46; Mexican nationals Flavio Alejandro Zuniga, 43, Ernest Gutierrez Ruvalcaba, 57, Jesus Narez-Madrigal, 52, Jose Antonio Banuelos-Diaz, 42, and Sulema de Leon, 35; Cambodian national Butleng Taing, 43; Honduran national Carlos Antonio Galeas, 54; Pakistani national Muhammad Khan, 50; and Canadian national Rouzbeh Seyamaknejad, 63. The allegations vary and include fraudulent registration, illegal voting and false statements in naturalisation paperwork. In the Eastern District of California, six defendants have been charged with voting by a non-citizen in a federal election. They include Mexican nationals Maricela Nazarin Gonzalez, 43, Camino Giles Jimenez, 51, and Juan Antonio Rivas Garcia, 46; Guatemalan national Rony de Jesus Sicaja, 38; Filipino national Giezell Viduya Adawag, 41; and Indian national Kamlesh Navnitlal Shah, 67. The Justice Department said the offence of voting by a non-citizen in a federal election carries a statutory maximum sentence of one year in federal prison. In the Northern District of California, five defendants face allegations involving illegal voting and false statements during naturalisation proceedings. They are Mexican national Veronica Bullene, 43; Georgian national David Shapiro, 41; Myanmar national Moe Thida Lwin, 57; Tongan national Manakotau Mataele Finau, 61; and Ecuadoran national Maribel del Carmen Garces Barriga, 62. The Southern District of California has four defendants facing allegations of falsely claiming US citizenship to vote, unlawful attempts to obtain naturalisation and false statements under oath. They include Filipino nationals Jose Probitsado Amaro, 51, and Pamele Arbues Line, 56; Canadian national Jennifer Jung, 31; and Guatemalan national Erick Ronaldo Soto Mendizabal, 64. Six defendants charged in Florida In the Middle District of Florida, six defendants have been charged with election-related offences. They include Cuban nationals Jamie Orlando Sosa Sardina, 60, and Luis Manuel Perez, 72; Ecuadorian national Martha Haydee Desantis, 81; Canadian nationals Lise Marie Johnson, 69, and Diane Wendy Curley, 55; and Brazilian national Pedro Igor A. Franco, 37. According to the department, Sardina, Desantis and Johnson face allegations of falsely claiming US citizenship to vote and voting illegally. The remaining defendants have been accused of voting by non-citizens. The alleged conduct includes voting in the 2022 and 2024 federal general elections. New York and Nevada cases In New York, German national Marva Cook, 66, a lawful permanent resident, has been charged in the Northern District with voting by a non-citizen. In the Eastern District of New York, three lawful permanent residents - Irish national Eoin Cranney, 35; Guyanese national Ronald Sheldon Baird, 47; and Jamaican national Karlene Daniels Samuels, 55 - have been charged with voting by non-citizens in federal elections. Prosecutors allege that all three submitted fraudulent voter registration applications and voted in the 2024 general election. The department also said the defendants made admissions about their non-citizen status and voting activity during voluntary interviews with federal agents. In Nevada, Filipino national Jullie Ann Sumalinog Moore, 44, a lawful permanent resident, has been charged with voting by a non-citizen in an election involving federal offices, including the presidency and seats in Congress. Charges do not establish guilt The cases involve allegations of illegal voting, fraudulent voter registration, false claims of US citizenship and misrepresentations in naturalisation proceedings. The charges differ according to the conduct prosecutors allege in each case. The Justice Department clarified that complaints, indictments and information contain allegations rather than findings of guilt. All defendants are presumed innocent unless and until they are proven guilty beyond a reasonable doubt in court. You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

title: 'Finally an Indian I'd vote for':  Ann Coulter, who once said she would never vote for Vivek Ramaswamy because he is of Indian origin, now supports Saritha Komatireddy
text: Ann Coulter who said she would never vote for Vivek Ramaswamy because of his Indian origin says she supports Saritha Komatireddy. Conservative commentator Ann Coulter has publicly expressed support for Indian-American Republican candidate Saritha Komatireddy in the New York attorney general race, saying she wants to vote for her while questioning why she is polling at just 5%. "Finally an Indian I'd vote for and SHE'S AT 5%??? What kind of country is this?" Coulter wrote in a post on X (formerly Twitter) on November 2, reacting to the betting odds for the New York attorney general election. Watch WATCH: Vivek Ramaswamy Nearly Drops Military Kid At Trumpâs Ohio Rally; Then Nasty Kamala Dig Komatireddy is the Republican and Conservative Party candidate challenging incumbent Democratic Attorney General Letitia James in the November 3 midterm elections. Coulter's remarks have attracted attention because of her previous comments about another Indian-American Republican politician, Vivek Ramaswamy. During an appearance on Ramaswamy's podcast in May 2024, Coulter told him she would not have voted for him in the presidential election because he was Indian. "I still would not have voted for you, because you're an Indian," she told Ramaswamy. The former Republican presidential candidate later acknowledged her remarks in a post on X, saying Coulter had told him directly that she could not vote for him because he was Indian, even though she agreed with him on several issues. Coulter's latest comment about Komatireddy has therefore drawn attention as she publicly expressed a willingness to vote for an Indian-American candidate. Who is Saritha Komatireddy? Saritha Komatireddy is a former federal prosecutor, a lecturer at Columbia Law School and a former chief of staff of the US Drug Enforcement Administration (DEA). She served as an assistant US attorney in the Eastern District of New York, where she held several leadership positions involving national security, cybercrime, narcotics and money laundering cases. She also served as the DEA's chief of staff from 2023 to 2024. A Harvard College and Harvard Law School graduate, Komatireddy was also nominated by President Donald Trump in 2020 to serve as a federal judge in the Eastern District of New York. Her nomination was not confirmed by the Senate. She is now a partner at the law firm Holtzman Vogel and teaches at Columbia Law School. Komatireddy is challenging Letitia James, who has served as New York attorney general since 2019. What is Komatireddy promising? Public safety is a central theme of Komatireddy's campaign. She has called for tougher action against repeat offenders, changes to New York's bail policies and stronger prosecution of crime. She has also made government fraud and corruption investigations part of her campaign platform. In interviews, Komatireddy has criticised James's approach to public safety and argued that the attorney general's office should do more to tackle crime and fraud. Why did Coulter mention the 5% figure? Coulter's post referred to betting-market odds for the New York attorney general contest. A market-tracking report on November 2 put Komatireddy at around 5%, compared with approximately 95% for James. The figures represent market-implied probabilities, not the percentage of voters supporting either candidate. They should not be confused with opinion-poll results. New Yorkers will vote on November 3 to decide whether James will secure another term or be replaced by Komatireddy. You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

title: Another 'exploding pager' plot? Israel eyes strike on Tehranâs top military bosses
text: Netanyahu holds up pager at UN, recalls Israelâs Hezbollah attack Israel is considering a covert operation modelled on its 2024 exploding-pager attacks against Hezbollah to target Iran's top military and security leadership, potentially eliminating key commanders and disrupting the country's wartime command structure, amid growing uncertainty over the possibility of renewed US-Israeli strikes against Tehran. "According to a report published by the New York Post, former Mossad deputy head of global operations Oded Ailam said Israel could consider a pager-style operation targeting Iran's military establishment, describing the option as 'fully on the table'." Watch Netanyahu's TIME RUNNING OUT? Arab Parties Signal Major Move To Topple Israeli PM After Deadlock He identified four senior figures as the people exercising real power in Tehran, including Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) chief Ahmad Vahidi, Basij commander Hossein Taeb, armed forces chief of staff Ali Abdollahi and security official Mohsen Rezaei. Ailam argued that Iran's military establishment has emerged as the principal centre of power, with the country's political leadership struggling to maintain control over strategic decisions. He suggested that disagreements between military hardliners and political officials have also complicated Tehran's negotiations with Washington. The proposed operation draws parallels with Israel's September 2024 covert campaign against Hezbollah, widely referred to as Operation Grim Beeper, in which thousands of pagers and walkie-talkies used by the Iran-backed militant group exploded across Lebanon in two successive waves. The first wave began on September 17, 2024, when thousands of pagers used by Hezbollah operatives exploded almost simultaneously across Lebanon, particularly in Beirut's southern suburbs, the Bekaa Valley and southern Lebanon. The following day, September 18, a second wave targeted handheld walkie-talkies used by the group, triggering explosions in several locations, including during funerals. The two attacks killed at least 39 people and injured more than 3,400, according to Reuters. According to Reuters, Hezbollah had ordered approximately 5,000 AR-924 pagers, which were allegedly modified before reaching the group. Explosives were concealed inside the devices, allowing Israeli intelligence to turn ordinary communication equipment into remotely activated weapons. In December 2024, two former Israeli intelligence officers, speaking anonymously to CBS News' 60 Minutes, disclosed further details about the operation. They said the planning had begun nearly a decade earlier with booby-trapped walkie-talkies, while the pager component was developed from 2022 onwards. The report comes amid growing indications that Washington and Tel Aviv are preparing for a possible resumption of military operations against Iran after the November 3 US midterm elections. A third American aircraft carrier, the USS Theodore Roosevelt, is heading towards the Middle East, where it is expected to join the USS George Washington and USS George HW Bush, already deployed in the region. US President Donald Trump told Kansas City radio station KCMO on Friday that the war was "going to get wrapped up soon", without providing details about how or when the conflict would end, according to the report. Retired US Army General Jack Keane argued that any renewed American and Israeli military campaign should target Iran's military leadership alongside its nuclear programme, domestic energy infrastructure and ballistic missile and drone facilities. title: TOI Bharat Abroad: US midterms - red, blue & a little desi too
text: India has wrapped up its election-season drama for the year, and the spotlight now shifts from the worldâs biggest democracy to the worldâs oldest. It's America's turn to count the votes, count the dollars and count on candidates to make their case. Indian-Americans are in the race, South Asian voters may be rethinking their loyalties, and Elon Musk is spending big. The US midterms are shaping up to be quite a ballot show. So, without further ado, letâs go! THE BIG STORY The desi ballot: From Capitol Hill to cowboy country The countdown to November 3 is on, and Indian-American candidates are fighting for a bigger place in the American political landscape. Some are defending seats they already hold, others are chasing their first election victory, and a handful are aiming for positions that could take them well beyond Congress. The big picture Four Indian-origin Democrats, Ro Khanna, Pramila Jayapal, Ami Bera and Suhas Subramanyam, are seeking re-election to the US House of Representatives. Republican Vivek Ramaswamy is running for governor of Ohio, while physician-turned-politician Amish Shah is trying to win an open congressional seat in Arizona. The field extends well beyond these familiar names. Pia Dandiya is contesting Florida's 22nd Congressional District, Republican Saritha Komatireddy is challenging New York Attorney General Letitia James, and Indian-origin candidates are competing for state-level offices across the country. Two House contests offer a particularly unusual twist: Indian-origin candidates are facing one another from opposing parties. In California's 17th Congressional District, Khanna faces Republican Ritesh Tandon. In Washington's 7th District, Jayapal is defending her seat against Republican Nirav Sheth. The Ohio governor's race is drawing national attention. Polling snapshots show a contest between Ramaswamy and Democratic candidate Amy Acton, a physician and former state health official. A RealClearPolling average dated October 19 put Acton at 48.7% and Ramaswamy at 44.3%, while a Fox News poll conducted from October 15 to 19 showed a narrower 50%-48% margin. The difference between the polls is a reminder that surveys are snapshots, not verdicts. Why it matters The midterms will decide control of Congress for the final two years of Donald Trump's presidency. All 435 House seats and 35 Senate seats are being contested, alongside gubernatorial and other state-level races. A change in congressional control could reshape the administration's legislative prospects and its ability to secure support for its policies. For Indian-Americans, the stakes go beyond the fate of individual candidates. Their growing presence in public office is bringing the community into debates on immigration, technology, healthcare, jobs, housing and US foreign policy, including relations with India. But there is no single Indian-American political agenda. The candidates span the ideological spectrum and offer sharply different ideas about government, immigration and the economy. Their electoral fortunes will depend on their own campaigns, local concerns and the national political climate, not simply on their heritage. The results will provide a measure of how far Indian-origin candidates have progressed from being a relatively small presence in American politics to competing for influence across Congress, state legislatures and governors' offices. The question is whether that growing visibility can translate into more seats and greater political influence. Read full story NRI WATCH A voter rethink: Survey points to a shift among South Asians Could some South Asian Americans who backed Donald Trump in 2024 be having second thoughts? A new survey suggests that a portion of those voters are considering a different choice in the November 3 midterms. The survey by advocacy group Indian American Impact found that at least 25% of South Asian Americans who voted for Trump in the 2024 presidential election now intend to support Democratic candidates. The findings are based on 800 registered South Asian voters, 87% of whom were Indian-American. The issues weighing on respondents include the cost of living, cited by 65%, healthcare at 53%, jobs and wages at 33%, and education at 28%. The survey also found that 67% of South Asian respondents who voted for Trump in 2024 still planned to back Republican candidates, underlining that the community's preferences remain mixed. The numbers offer a snapshot, not a prediction of how the entire community will vote. Nor do they establish that every respondent who plans to change their vote will do so on polling day. Still, the findings suggest that economic pressures, immigration and perceptions of discrimination could influence voting decisions. With several races expected to be closely fought, the question is whether these stated intentions translate into turnout and make a difference at the ballot box. Read full story OFFBEAT The money race: Musk's $445 million midterm bet Campaigns run on candidates and their messages, but the American midterms also come with an eye-watering price tag. Elon Musk has contributed more than $445 million to political groups during the current election cycle, emerging as one of the biggest donors to political action committees in US history, according to a report. Federal Election Commission filings show that Musk contributed $77 million to America PAC in the first two weeks of October. Since relaunching the group in July, he has given it $355 million, averaging $3.6 million a day, Bloomberg reported. The spending comes as both sides pour money into races that could determine control of Congress. Through October 14, Republican committees, congressional super PACs and Trump's MAGA Inc. had raised a combined $2.1 billion, compared with $1.4 billion raised by corresponding Democratic committees, according to the report. The figures illustrate how wealthy donors and outside political groups have become major forces in American campaigning. Their money can fund advertising, voter outreach and efforts to shape the debate, although donations alone cannot determine how people vote. Musk's involvement also puts the spotlight on the wider question of political influence: how much sway can a wealthy individual exercise over an election, and how does that spending translate into votes? The answer will not come from the fundraising totals alone. With polling day approaching, the final results will show how money, candidate appeal, local issues and turnout combine at the ballot box. title: 1 in 4 South Asian Americans who backed Trump in 2024 now plan to vote Democrat in midterms: Survey
text: Trump may be losing some South Asian voters ahead of US midterms At least 25% of South Asian Americans who voted for US President Donald Trump in the 2024 presidential election plan to back Democratic candidates in the November 3 midterm elections, according to a survey by advocacy group Indian American Impact. The survey identified the cost of living (65%), healthcare (53%), jobs and wages (33%), and education (28%) as the key issues influencing voters ahead of the midterms. Watch 'Veto, Veto, Veto...': Trump Hints At Massive 'Unrest' If Democrats Win Midterms Of the 800 registered South Asian voters surveyed, 87% were Indian-Americans, while the remaining 13% were from Pakistani, Bangladeshi, Sri Lankan, Nepali, Bhutanese, Maldivian, Afghani, Khmer and Burmese communities. Among respondents who voted for Kamala Harris in the 2024 presidential election, 96% said they planned to vote for a Democratic candidate in the upcoming polls. The survey found that while 67% of South Asian Americans who voted for Trump continued to support Republicans, 25% planned to vote for Democrats. The findings come as early voting has begun in several states, including Texas, where Democratic nominee James Talarico is locked in a tight race against Republican Ken Paxton, who has Trump's backing. Vasant Bhatt, a 21-year-old second-generation Indian-American who interned on Senator Ted Cruz's election campaign in 2024, said in a social media post that he had voted for Talarico. "I just cast my ballot for James Talarico. As a second-generation Indian American, I am thoroughly disgusted by the xenophobia, racial resentment, and increasingly brazen attacks on my identity," Bhatt wrote. The survey also pointed to widespread concerns about discrimination. As many as 90% of registered voters said they had experienced discrimination or knew someone who had, while 48% said they had personally faced it. âIt comes as no surprise that a quarter of Trumpâs 2024 voters in our community plan to vote Democratic. This community can make the margin, and we are working to reach every voter who can,â Chintan Patel, executive director of Indian American Impact, said in a statement. The survey found that 16% of respondents had not voted in any general election since 2020. It also highlighted a broader sense of disillusionment with elected representatives. While 78% of respondents believed their vote could bring about change, 79% felt elected officials quickly lost touch with ordinary people. Another 67% said public officials did not care about the views of people like them, while 43% felt they had no say in government decisions. The findings underscore the potential electoral influence of South Asian American voters, particularly in closely contested states. Michigan has around 187,000 South Asian residents. Nearly 30,000 registered South Asian voters did not vote in 2022, exceeding the roughly 19,000-vote margin that decided the state's 2024 Senate race. Texas, meanwhile, has more than 700,000 South Asian residents, with nearly 100,000 registered South Asian voters having sat out the 2022 elections. The Indian-American community also has a significant presence in California, Texas, New Jersey, New York, Washington, Illinois, Pennsylvania and Georgia. In battleground states such as Georgia, Pennsylvania, Michigan and North Carolina, where electoral contests can be decided by narrow margins, even a shift of one or two percentage points in voter support could influence the outcome. title: GVMC records 56.3% turnout, with core city areas lagging behind peripheral zones in voter participation
text: Visakhapatnam : The Greater Visakhapatnam Municipal Corporation (GVMC) election recorded a voter turnout of 56.32%, significantly lower than the 59.41% polled in 2021 and the 64% to 80% recorded across assembly constituencies within GVMC limits in the 2024 general elections. The turnout, nearly 15 percentage points below the 2024 assembly election levels in some areas, has triggered speculation among political parties over its possible impact on the results, which will be declared on Tuesday. While low polling has been a recurring feature of municipal elections in Visakhapatnam, parties had expected a better response, given growing political awareness and increased access to information through technology. The core city areas once again recorded lower polling than the peripheral zones, following a pattern similar to the 2024 assembly elections. Zone-wise turnout ranged from 49.71% to 66.27%. Bheemili topped the list with 66.27%, followed by Anakapalli (65.6%), Aganampudi (62.08%) and Gajuwaka (60.9%). West zone recorded 58.97%, while Pendurthi and Madhurawada registered 55.12% and 55.07%, respectively. East and South zones polled 54.21% and 52.61%, respectively. North zone recorded the lowest turnout at 49.71%. A similar pattern was evident in the 2024 assembly elections, when the four core city constituencies recorded relatively low polling. Vizag South registered 63.42%, the lowest, followed by North (64.63%), East (68.5%) and West (69.78%). All four constituencies fell short of the stateâs overall assembly election turnout of 80.66%. Among the seven assembly constituencies in Visakhapatnam district, only Pendurthi and Bheemili crossed the 70% mark, recording 74% and 76%, respectively. Anakapalli registered nearly 80%. The subdued turnout has left both major political parties assessing its possible implications for the mayoral contest and corporator results. The TDP is confident of securing the mayorâs post and a majority of the corporator seats. The YSRCP, meanwhile, is banking on cross-voting to win the mayoral election, while hoping to secure 40 to 50 of the 120 corporator seats. YSRCP leaders believe the candidature of MLC and party state womenâs wing president Varudu Kalyani has helped the party attract urban, educated voters and professionals. They expect this support to translate into a narrow victory in the mayoral contest. The TDP, on the other hand, is banking on its mayoral candidate, young corporator Mukka Sravani, arguing that her five years of work among the public will give the party an advantage. Political analysts attribute the low turnout to a combination of urban voter apathy, lacklustre campaigning and the absence of a strong political wave or compelling local issues. The delayed finalisation of candidates and release of manifestos also left parties with limited time to reach out to voters. Cyclone Arnab further disrupted normal life and electioneering during the crucial final days of campaigning, potentially affecting voter mobilisation. Another factor cited by observers is the cityâs growing migrant population. Many of those who have moved to Visakhapatnam in recent years may not yet have developed strong political connections with local leaders or the same level of engagement with civic affairs as long-time residents. Low-key contests in several wards and inadequate voter outreach may have further contributed to the subdued response. title: US midterms 2026: Early voting surpasses 50.5 million, Texas sees significant voter turnout increase
text: Over 50.5 million early votes cast by Saturday morning/Image: Reuters More than 50.5 million Americans have voted early ahead of the 2026 US midterm elections, nearly five million more than the total recorded during the 2022 midterms. The increase comes as both parties face closely contested races that could determine control of Congress for the final two years of President Donald Trump's second term. Data from the University of Florida's Election Lab showed that early voting had surpassed 50.5 million by Saturday morning, ahead of Tuesday's election. Among states that track voters' party affiliations, registered Democrats accounted for 10.7 million early ballots, compared with 7.8 million from registered Republicans. These figures reflect the political registration of voters who have cast ballots and do not indicate which candidates they have supported. Watch HUGE! Iran War Escalation Confirmed After Trump Defeat? Insider Discloses America's Gulf Plan The higher number of Democratic voters comes as Republicans face competitive contests in states that have traditionally favoured the party. Dissatisfaction with Trump's presidency and concerns about the cost of living have also become prominent issues in the campaign. Republicans currently hold a 53-47 majority in the Senate and are seeking to retain control of the chamber. Democrats are targeting traditionally Republican-leaning states, including Texas, Alaska and Kansas, where competitive races could help them secure a majority. Texas has become a major focus of the contest, with more than seven million people having already voted early, as per the University data. This is around 1.5 million more than the number recorded in the state during the 2022 midterms. The increase is also evident in Harris County, which includes Houston. By Wednesday, 862,700 people had cast early ballots there, compared with 564,500 at the same point in the 2022 election, the Associated Press analysis has found. Harris County has consistently backed Democratic candidates in recent elections. In 2024, Kamala Harris defeated Trump in the county by nearly six percentage points in the presidential election. Democratic Senate candidate Colin Allred also won the county by roughly 11 percentage points over Republican incumbent Ted Cruz. This year's Texas Senate contest has drawn national attention, with Republican Attorney General Ken Paxton facing Democratic candidate James Talarico. Republican Governor Greg Abbott is also seeking re-election against Democrat Gina Hinojosa. Early voting has also increased in other states with competitive Senate races. South Carolina, which Trump won by nearly 18 percentage points in the 2024 presidential election, has recorded an 83% rise in early voting compared with the 2022 midterms, as per AP analysis. In Kansas, where Republicans face another closely contested Senate race, early voting is up 34%. Maine has recorded a 44% increase, while Michigan has seen a rise of 32%, the AP reported. The midterm elections will determine the composition of the House of Representatives and Senate for the remaining two years of Trump's term. Rising prices of food, petrol and other essentials, the war involving Iran and concerns about government corruption have featured in the political debate ahead of the vote. Trump has held rallies across several states to support Republican candidates, including in areas that have traditionally been considered safe for the party. During his campaign appearances, he has repeatedly commented on candidates' physical appearance and dismissed concerns about rising petrol prices, pointing instead to the profits of fossil fuel companies. Speaking at a rally in Florida on Friday night, Trump acknowledged the demands of his campaign schedule. âI thought this was it,â he said. âI thought I could relax. title: US midterm elections: What a Democratic win could mean for India's trade
text: US midterms may raise shutdown, keep tariff uncertainty high The US is preparing for its November 3 midterm elections, but the results will be closely watched in India too, particularly for their possible impact on trade ties and business conditions. The outcome could bring fresh uncertainty around US trade policies, with tariffs, government spending and the risk of a government shutdown among the key issues. For India, a change in the political balance in Washington could mean greater scrutiny of President Donald Trump's policies, but businesses may not get an immediate relief from the existing tariff framework. A major shift in Trump's policy direction remains unlikely, according to a report by ICICI Bank. The report estimates that Democrats have a 63 per cent probability of gaining control of both chambers of Congress. Their chances of winning the House of Representatives stand at 90.9 per cent, while the probability of securing the Senate is 64 per cent. A Democratic sweep could bring the Trump administration's policies on tariffs, immigration and government spending under greater scrutiny. However, a change in congressional control may not necessarily lead to an immediate change in the policies currently in place. Tariff uncertainty to continue - Hereâs why A change in congressional control may bring more debate around US trade policies, but businesses should not expect the current tariff framework to disappear overnight. "The more immediate effects of Democratic control would likely be increased oversight, legislative disputes and greater uncertainty for businesses, rather than an automatic dismantling of the current tariff framework," the report said. Democrats could push for a review of certain tariffs or attempt to restrict the President's powers to impose them. However, any significant change could face hurdles, as the US President retains the power to veto legislation and has certain independent powers to impose tariffs. For India, this means that uncertainty around the US trade and tariff approach could remain even if Democrats make gains in Congress. A change in the political balance alone may not bring an immediate shift in the administration's policy direction. AI, data centres unlikely to face a major investment shift The report does not expect the midterm election results to significantly alter investments in artificial intelligence (AI) and data centres in the US. âThe toss-up states where Republicans can lose in the midterm collectively account for only ~15% of total data center capacity in the USâ, the report said. This limits the extent to which a change in political control could affect the sector's investment landscape. However, data centres could face greater scrutiny over their resource consumption and environmental impact. Democrats have raised concerns about the high electricity and water requirements of these facilities. An average data centre with a capacity of 100 megawatts consumes around 2 million litres of water daily and uses more electricity than 75,000 homes, according to the report. The sector could also face closer examination over its environmental impact and effect on employment. The report has also flagged the possibility of a fresh dispute over the US debt ceiling in mid-2027. The debt ceiling is the legal limit on how much the federal government can borrow. US government debt stood at around $40 trillion in late 2026, against a borrowing limit of $41.1 trillion. You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

title: Kamala Harris returns to campaign trail for US midterms amid speculation over 2028 presidential bid
text: Former US vice president Kamala Harris. Former US vice president Kamala Harris has returned to the campaign trail to support Democrats in closely contested races ahead of the November 3 midterm elections, as speculation grows over whether she will make another bid for the White House in 2028. According to news agency Reuters, Harris, the Democratic Party's 2024 presidential nominee, is campaigning in Georgia, Mississippi, Nevada, New Hampshire and Wisconsin. She has made relatively few public appearances this year but is now stepping up efforts to help Democrats challenge Republican control of Congress. Harris began her campaign tour in Las Vegas on Tuesday, criticising President Donald Trump and his administration over what she described as its cruelty and incompetence. Speaking alongside Nevada gubernatorial candidate Aaron Ford, she addressed members of the Culinary Workers Union. "We got a serious fight in front of us," Harris said, accusing the Trump administration of being corrupt, callous and incompetent. Ford, Nevada's first Black attorney general, is seeking to become the state's governor. Harris said his election would make him the first Black governor west of the Mississippi River. Harris continued her campaign appearances in Mississippi, where she rallied supporters of Democratic Senate candidate Scott Colom in Columbus. Colom is attempting to become the first Democrat elected to the US Senate from Mississippi since 1982. He is facing Republican incumbent Cindy Hyde-Smith in a closely contested race, Reuters reported. Addressing supporters, Harris encouraged young people not to let others' doubts limit their ambitions, drawing cheers from the crowd. Harris' popularity remains divided along party lines Harris' return to the campaign trail comes as both parties seek to mobilise voters ahead of the midterms. Trump has also been travelling across the country to campaign for Republican candidates facing competitive races. However, Harris continues to face challenges in winning support beyond the Democratic base. A Reuters/Ipsos poll conducted in June found that 39 per cent of Americans viewed her favourably. Her approval was significantly higher among Democrats, at 82 per cent, compared with 7 per cent among Republicans and 33 per cent among independents. Elaine Kamarck, a senior fellow at the Brookings Institution and a member of the Democratic National Committee, said parties typically turn to their most prominent figures towards the end of an election campaign. "At the end of a campaign, you bring out your heavy hitters," Kamarck was quoted as saying by Reuters, adding that this was the reason Harris and Trump were campaigning for their respective parties. Will Harris run for president again in 2028? Harris could emerge as one of the leading contenders if she decides to seek the Democratic presidential nomination in 2028. However, her political record includes two unsuccessful presidential campaigns. She lost to Trump in the 2024 election, while her first presidential campaign ended before the Democratic primaries began in 2020. A potential 2028 bid would also bring renewed scrutiny of the events surrounding the 2024 election, when then-president Joe Biden abandoned his re-election campaign amid concerns about his age and mental fitness, leaving Harris to take his place as the Democratic nominee. Harris later criticised Biden's decision to seek a second term as "reckless" in her memoir, 107 Days, named after the length of the presidential campaign she inherited. She has also become more vocal about the Biden administration's approach to Israel's war in Gaza. This month, Harris criticised the Israeli government's "horrific conduct" and said the US should have acted sooner and more forcefully. Harris says 2026 midterms come first Harris has not ruled out another presidential run, but she has repeatedly emphasised the importance of the upcoming midterm elections. During an appearance on the video podcast Baby, This Is Keke Palmer this month, actor Keke Palmer asked Harris whether she would run for president again. "Oh, girl, come on!" Harris replied, laughing. "I haven't decided yet." She then stressed that the immediate priority was the midterm elections. "2028 don't matter if we don't do 2026 right," Harris said. Her return to the campaign trail is likely to keep her in the political spotlight as Democrats seek to regain congressional ground and potential candidates begin positioning themselves for the next presidential election. title: US midterms 2026: How 9/11 shaped Saritha Komatireddyâs legal career as she runs for New York attorney general
text: Saritha Komatireddy is among the Indian-origin candidates contesting the US midterm elections on November 3. A former assistant attorney in the Eastern District of New York, she is the Republican nominee for New York attorney general and will challenge two-time incumbent Letitia James, the Democratic Party nominee. Among her prominent backers is US President Donald Trump, who nominated Komatireddy for a federal judgeship in the Eastern District of New York in May 2020, during his first term in office. Family life Komatireddyâs parents immigrated to the United States from what is now Telangana, in southern India, during the 1980s. Born in Brooklyn, New York, she spent part of her childhood in Missouri. In an interview with The Wall Street Journal, Komatireddy spoke about her father's humble beginnings in India and his decision to immigrate to the United States. âMy dad is from a small village in India that had no running water, and he left India when it was a socialist country. He came here for the same reason many New Yorkersâ families come here: work hard, dream big and have a shot at achieving your dreams," she said. How 9/11 changed her life According to Komatireddy, the September 11, 2001, terrorist attacks in New York City shaped her decision to pursue a career in law, with a focus on prosecuting terrorists and protecting national security. âMy first week in college, terrorists attacked New York. 9/11 changed my life. I chose law school to prosecute terrorists, to protect New York and America,â she said in her campaign video. Komatireddy graduated from both Harvard College and Harvard Law School. She began her legal career as a law clerk to Brett Kavanaugh, who was then a judge on the US Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia Circuit and now serves as an associate justice of the US Supreme Court. Professional career According to her campaign website, Komatireddy spent more than a decade prosecuting cases involving leaders of Al-Qaeda, ISIS and Mexican drug cartels. As a federal prosecutor in the Eastern District of New York, she handled high-profile cases involving international terrorism, cybercrime, narcotics trafficking, money laundering, fraud and foreign public corruption. From 2023 to 2024, she served as chief of staff of the Drug Enforcement Administration (DEA) under then-President Joe Biden. Komatireddy, a mother of four, is a partner at the law firm Holtzman Vogel and teaches at Columbia University. title: Fake US voters? China-linked accounts flood X with divisive posts ahead of midterms
text: China-linked accounts pose as US voters on X A China-linked influence operation known as Spamouflage is active ahead of the US midterm elections, with accounts allegedly posing as American voters and circulating divisive political content on X. The findings were reported by New York-based social media intelligence firm Graphika, which tracks online influence networks. In a blog post published on Friday, Graphika said it had identified a network of accounts linked to the long-running operation that were posting content targeting US politics, social issues and the electoral process. The activity, it said, closely resembled tactics documented ahead of the 2024 US presidential election. âThe accounts post content questioning election integrity and the legitimacy of US democracy,â Graphika said in its blog. The findings come amid longstanding warnings from US intelligence and national security officials about foreign influence operations targeting American voters. Russia, China and Iran have previously been identified as countries running online campaigns aimed at shaping political narratives and influencing public opinion. Watch Trumpâs Cheesecake Factory Controversy EXPLODES as Kimmel Launches Fresh Attack However, analysts, quoted by news agency AP, have said China's approach has largely focused on undermining public confidence in US democratic institutions rather than supporting one presidential candidate over another. China has rejected allegations of election interference. Liu Chang, spokesperson for the Chinese Embassy in Washington, said Beijing âhas never and will never interfere in the US elections." Despite the concerns raised by Graphika, some researchers have questioned the network's ability to influence mainstream political opinion. Darren Linvill, who co-directs Clemson University's Watt Family Innovation Center Media Forensics Hub and has tracked Spamouflage activity, said the operation was unlikely to sway political discussions. âThere is no chance it tips the balance in any real political conversation,â Linvill told AP. âSpamouflage is famously bad at mimicking real Americans," he added. âIt's outside their wheelhouse.â Linvill said the network's impact was more evident in its efforts to suppress information and target individuals, particularly members of the Chinese diaspora. The accounts linked to the operation âvery frequently attack and harass members of the Chinese diaspora communityâ, he said, describing the activity as part of a wider effort by Beijing to silence views it opposes. Graphika also identified specific accounts that appeared to have changed their identities or content strategies to target US political audiences. The firm also flagged four accounts with a history of Spamouflage activity that have since adopted MAGA-style personas, amplifying content associated with the political movement. Another account, which has more than 2,00,000 followers and presents itself as a Philippine culture blog, was found posting pro-China material alongside divisive content focused on US politics. Graphika said it could not establish whether the account had been hijacked, sold or otherwise transferred to a different operator, leaving questions about who currently controls it. title: US Midterm Polls: Democrats sniff opportunity, Trump fights to avoid a lame-duck presidency
text: Democrats sniff opportunity, Trump fights to avoid a lame-duck presidency As Americans head into the final stretch of campaigning for the Nov 3 US midterm polls, both Democratic and Republican parties are set to field their big guns â and go on an ad-blitz â across key battleground states. Weighing on votersâ minds are issues like the rising cost of living, Trumpâs war against Iran that has seen fuel prices skyrocket, healthcare and housing. Hereâs a quick primer on whatâs at stake in the polls, why it could be hugely consequential for the Trump presidency, and how it may shape US foreign policy. Betting on the House: All 435 seats in Congressâs House of Representatives are up for grabs. Republicans hold a slim majority of 218 to Democratsâ 214 in the House. But this is widely expected to flip. That hinges on about 50 competitive races. Pollsters say Democrats could end up with a majority of as many as 15 seats. Senatorial action: But itâs the Senate races that will determine whether Trumpâs agenda over the next two years sinks or floats. The chamber has only 100 seats, but senators have staggered six-year terms. That means only 35 seats are up for grabs this time, of which about 10 are really competitive and likely to flip. If Democrats snag them up, they will overturn Republicansâ current majority of 53 to 45. Which is precisely why Republicans are pulling out all stops to boost their candidates in key races. If Dems get House, GOP holds Senate: A likely scenario, although Republicans have been shaken up by reported close contests in red states like Texas and Kansas. Plus, Trumpâs approval rating is down â a record low for him at 31% in the latest poll. So, Republicans are divided over associating themselves with Trumpâs policies. For some, getting the Presidentâs endorsement may actually spell doom in tight races. Midterm in numbers But if Republicans do manage to hold onto their majority in Senate, Trump would still have room to manoeuvre and, more importantly, bat down political challenges emanating from a Democrats-dominated House. If Dems win both houses: Thatâs the nightmare scenario Trump and GOP are trying to avoid. If Democrats control both the House and Senate, they effectively gain control of the legislative agenda. Sure, Democrats would still have to contend with Trumpâs veto power â he could use that to block any Democrats-led legislation. And overturning a presidential veto requires two-thirds majority in both houses â a rarity. But Democrats could still prove a point by forcing Trump to exercise his veto. That in turn could have political implications for presidential polls in 2028, putting Republicans looking for a post-Trump future in a tight spot. Also, unlike the House where a simple majority passes legislation, for bills to pass Senate they require a supermajority of 60 votes. Still, this is a scenario that GOP would like to avoid at all costs. Key races: Naturally, most of them focus on Senate seats. In North Carolina , Democratic candidate Roy Cooper is leading in the polls over Republican candidate Michael Whatley. This is a seat GOP appears to be giving up on, holding back on ad spends in the final two weeks. Texas is turning out to be a humdinger. Polls show a tight race between Democrat James Talarico and Republican Ken Paxton. Talarico is pegged to be slightly ahead at this point. And if he pulls it off on election day, Dems would end their 32-year losing streak in the state. But Republicans are pouring big money into this race, and are slated to outspend Democrats by three times, with overall GOP ad spend on this race set to cross $380mn. Kansas , likewise, is witnessing a neck-to-neck race where Democrat Adam Hamilton is squaring off against GOP senator Roger Marshall. Recent polls showed thereâs practically nothing to separate the two candidates. If Democrats win here, it would be historic â the state hasnât elected a Democratic senator in 94 years. The race in Michigan is grabbing a lot of eyeballs, thanks to Democratic candidate Abdul El-Sayed who is going up against Republican Mike Rogers. Trump himself has taken potshots at El-Sayed, calling him a Muslim radical, while other Republican leaders have tried to associate him with the Muslim Brotherhood. If El-Sayed wins, he would be the first Muslim senator in US history. Impact on US foreign policy: If Democrats win back both houses, it would certainly reduce space for Trump to act unilaterally on the foreign policy front. However, there are many ways in which Trump could work around any restrictions. For example, his war against Iran has skirted around the 60-day window for congressional approval through White Houseâs clever classification of the military action as aimed at âprotecting American peopleâ. Trump has also argued that since the war has started and stopped several times, the 60-day window for approval has renewed each time. However, if Democrats control Congress, they could curtail any funding for that war. Conversely, they could also try to fast track funding support for Ukraine. But Trump could veto that or simply not act. So, it could be a stalemate between Trump and a Democrats-controlled Congress. A third impeachment: A nuclear option, but not beyond the realm of possibility if Democrats win Congress. More likely though would be Democrats taking control of several committees, launching investigations against Trump officials or Trump family members, and blocking Trumpâs appointments to key govt positions and roles, essentially leading to a lame-duck presidency. title: Two Indians among 28 green card holders charged with election fraud in California
text: 1. Two Indians face US election fraud charges over 2024 voting (Representative image: Reuters photo) Two Indian nationals are among 28 green card holders charged with election-related offences in California, including fraudulent voter registration and voting in the November 2024 US elections, the US Department of Justice said on Monday. The accused Indians have been identified as Amandeep Kaur, 30, a resident of Rancho Palos Verdes, and Kamlesh Shah, 67, who lives in Sacramento. It was not immediately clear whether either of them was among the 11 people arrested during early morning raids across California under âOperation Protect the Voteâ. According to the Justice Department, Shah fraudulently registered to vote on the day of the November 2024 general election and cast his ballot the same day. Kaur, who is seeking US citizenship, allegedly registered to vote in December 2022 and voted in the November 2024 election. âAll 28 foreign nationals charged are lawful permanent residents (LPRs), or 'green card' holders. Although LPRs have legal immigration status in the United States, they are not US citizens and are not permitted to vote in US elections,â the Justice Department said. The charges include making false statements in naturalisation applications and fraudulent voter registration. Both offences are felonies that carry a maximum penalty of five years in federal prison. DOJ links accused to voter registration list Acting Deputy Attorney General Trent McCotter said all 28 defendants appeared on a list of more than 20,000 people the Justice Department had provided to California election officials the previous week. âEach of the 28 defendants charged today appears on the list of more than 20,000 likely noncitizen registrants we provided to California election officials last week,â McCotter told reporters in Los Angeles. The charges come amid an escalating dispute between the Trump administration and California officials over allegations of non-citizen voter registration. The Justice Department has also asked a federal court to prevent California and Los Angeles County from processing ballots returned by people on the list, arguing that votes cast illegally could undermine election integrity. California officials have opposed the demand, saying the federal government has not provided sufficient evidence to establish that those listed are non-citizens. They have also argued that withholding or refusing to count ballots could violate federal and state law and disenfranchise eligible voters. Trump administration steps up election investigations The Justice Department has intensified investigations into alleged election-related offences as early voting begins in several states. Before Mondayâs announcement, it had charged about 90 people with various forms of election misconduct this year, including 50 accused of voting as non-citizens. The department said on Monday that it had charged 113 non-citizens across 20 states with voting and registration offences over the preceding seven weeks. Election law experts have cautioned that such cases do not establish widespread non-citizen voting. They have also warned that aggressive efforts to scrutinise voter rolls could risk removing eligible voters or undermining public confidence in elections. California officials have questioned the Justice Departmentâs methodology for identifying the 20,000 people, while the federal government has argued that access to additional voter registration data would help verify their citizenship status. title: Trump's Justice dept steps into US midterm battles before votes are counted, breaks decades-old practice
text: US Justice Department. US President Donald Trump's Justice Department has stepped into election disputes ahead of Tuesday's US midterm elections, breaking with decades of practice aimed at keeping federal law enforcement agencies from appearing to favour a political party or candidate. The department has filed lawsuits challenging election procedures in California and Alaska, raising concerns among critics that its powers are being used to influence contests that could determine control of Congress and several governors' offices, Reuters reported. In California, the Justice Department sought to block mail-in ballots from around 20,000 voters it suspects may be non-US citizens and therefore ineligible to vote. It has also demanded election records as part of a related criminal investigation. California officials have rejected the move, saying the state has safeguards to prevent noncitizens from voting and arguing that the federal government lacks the authority to block the ballots. In Alaska, the department has stepped up a criminal investigation into whether a Senate candidate sharing the name of Republican incumbent Dan Sullivan entered the race to confuse voters. It also moved to prevent certification of the election result if Sullivan narrowly loses. However, a federal judge dismissed the department's lawsuit on Sunday, ruling against its attempt to intervene in the state's election process. The Justice Department has appealed the decision. According to Reuters, courts have now rejected the department's lawsuits involving both California and Alaska. The cases have highlighted the Trump administration's willingness to intervene in election disputes before ballots are counted and results are certified. Critics have warned that such moves could give Trump an opportunity to question the legitimacy of the midterm results. "It appears that the administration wants the department to have an impact that was previously prohibited," Mark Blumberg, who formerly led the Justice Department's election response to civil rights threats, was quoted as saying by Reuters. He has since founded the Rule of Law Project. Attorney General Todd Blanche has defended the department's actions, saying they are lawful and intended to protect election integrity. "The Department isn't helping any campaign. It's enforcing the law," Justice Department spokesperson Kiersten Pels said. Trump's claims of voter fraud Under the US Constitution, individual states are responsible for administering elections. However, Trump has repeatedly accused Democratic-led states of failing to prevent noncitizens from voting, although voting by non-US citizens is already prohibited under federal law. Trump has also continued to make false claims that widespread voter fraud cost him the 2020 presidential election. Independent investigations and state audits have found that voter fraud is rare. During his first term, Justice Department officials resisted pressure to intervene in efforts to challenge Trump's 2020 election defeat. Outside groups aligned with the Republican leader subsequently filed more than 60 lawsuits disputing the results, but none succeeded. Lis Frost, a voting rights lawyer with Elias Law Group, which frequently represents Democrats in court, said the situation had changed. "The right-wing fringe outside groups are not going to have to do that this year because the DOJ is clearly standing ready and willing to do it," Frost told Reuters. Traditionally, the Justice Department's election-related interventions have focused on enforcing federal laws that protect the voting rights of racial minorities and other vulnerable groups. Alaska election becomes legal battleground Alaska has emerged as a major focus of the dispute following a New York Times report that Democratic candidate Mary Peltola's campaign was involved in recruiting retired teacher Daniel J Sullivan to challenge Republican Senator Dan Sullivan. The Justice Department's lawsuit, which Trump said he had directed the department to file, sought to halt certification of the results and order an investigation if the victory margin indicated that voter confusion could have affected the outcome. However, US District Judge Sharon Gleason in Anchorage dismissed the case on Sunday, saying Alaska could not conduct such an investigation while maintaining the secrecy of ballots. Legal experts had questioned whether the Justice Department had the authority to pursue the case, warning that the move could create the impression that the federal government was favouring the Republican incumbent. Peter Keisler, who served as acting attorney general under former Republican President George W Bush, said the department needed to maintain political neutrality to retain public trust. "For the department to be trusted in its law enforcement decisions it has to ensure that people understand it does not take sides in political partisan disputes," Keisler told Reuters. He added that the Alaska case had not only created the appearance of political interference but also represented an evident instance of taking sides. Blanche has defended the lawsuit, alleging that Daniel J Sullivan was involved in an attempt to mislead voters. The candidate has denied trying to confuse voters, while Peltola's campaign said it had "no involvement with either Sullivan campaign". Responding to criticism, a Justice Department official said during a press briefing on Thursday that the department filed lawsuits to enforce federal law. Trump allies gain greater control over election investigations The Justice Department has traditionally exercised caution in election-related investigations because federal intervention can create uncertainty and potentially be used by political candidates to challenge results. Its Public Integrity Section, which has career officials specialising in election law, previously advised investigators and prosecutors to wait until election results were certified before taking action, according to former department officials cited by Reuters. However, the Trump administration has reduced the size of the unit and suspended a requirement that federal prosecutors consult it during investigations into election-related corruption. Justice Department officials have argued that individual US attorney's offices are better placed to determine whether criminal charges should be pursued. According to three people familiar with internal discussions, agents and prosecutors have instead been told that political appointees of the Trump administration will decide unresolved disputes. The Deputy Attorney General's Office is also expected to mediate disagreements between investigators and prosecutors, a role former Justice Department officials said it has rarely played in election investigations. Pels defended the arrangement, saying resolving disputes that cannot be settled at the local level was precisely the purpose of the office. You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. title: Economy, not ideology
text: When populists and autocrats lose elections, are voters rejecting their ideas or reacting to their economic problems? Research suggests that democracy is in danger. According to Swedenâs V-Dem Institute, the average person today has about the same democratic freedoms as in 1978. So, election results in Brazil and Serbia may look like victories for democracy. In Brazil, voters narrowly stopped Flavio Bolsonaro, who has shown strong authoritarian tendencies, from winning. They gave Lula another term instead. In Serbia, voters defeated strongman Aleksandar Vucic by a large margin. The result has attracted much attention because the winning side is a student protest movement supported by academics, doctors and others. Serbia has just 65 lakh people and a GDP of $112 billion. But these election results may not mean that democracy is making a comeback. As Harvard professor Steven Levitsky pointed out in 2024, voters may simply be unhappy with the people in power. In Brazil, even Lula lost the first round of voting before fighting back strongly. This trend has been clear since 2020, when Covid disrupted economies and governments adopted policies that made money easily available. The result was high inflation. Billionaires benefited, but the middle class and poorer people struggled. Levitsky noted that people had become deeply unhappy with their governments. In 41 of 55 elections and polls held between 2020 and 2024, the party in power lost. He said this was almost certainly linked to inflation caused by the pandemic. Were young Serbians, who protested against Vucic for two years, fighting for a political idea or for a better economic future? Britain offers another example. The Labour Party won a huge victory in the election, but became unpopular within months. Germanyâs Social Democrats are also struggling. In the US, voters first removed populist Donald Trump and elected Joe Biden, only to bring Trump back four years later. Now, with US midterm elections scheduled for November 3, voters may use their chance to weaken Trumpâs control of Congress. Why? He promised to tackle the rising cost of living, but his war on Iran has made peopleâs economic problems worse. Israel is another test for democracy, with elections taking place today. Opinion polls do not show Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu winning a clear victory. But whoever wins is unlikely to take a softer stand towards Palestinians. Young Israelis, including first-time voters, do not appear to feel much sympathy for people in Gaza either. What they are tired of is endless war, the mental strain it causes and corruption. Everywhere, voters are asking their leaders a simple question: âWhat have you done for us and our future?â Leaders who are already in power are losing elections because they often have no convincing answer.
