title: Indian-American candidates in 2026 US midterms: Key races, profiles, latest polling & what's at stake
text: From left: Ami Bera, Pramila Jayapal, Ro Khanna, Suhas Subramanyam and Vivek Ramaswamy. The 2026 US midterm elections are shaping up to be a significant test of Indian-American political representation. Four Indian-origin Democrats â Ro Khanna, Pramila Jayapal, Ami Bera and Suhas Subramanyam â are seeking re-election to the House of Representatives. Meanwhile, Vivek Ramaswamy is locked in a high-octane race for governor of Ohio, and physician-turned-politician Amish Shah is attempting to capture an open Arizona congressional seat. Read also | US midterm elections 2026: Why it's a do-or-die fight for Trump & the Democracts - explained in 10 charts The contests extend beyond Congress. Indian-American candidates are competing for attorney-general positions, mayoralties and seats in state legislatures across the country. The elections on November 3 will take place against the backdrop of a closely divided Congress and a national debate over the economy, immigration, healthcare, technology and Trump's policies. The outcomes could determine not only which party controls Capitol Hill but also how much influence Indian-American lawmakers exercise in Washington and state governments. Indian-Americans in key congressional races 1. Ro Khanna Ro Khanna, one of the most prominent Indian-American Democrats in Congress at the moment, is seeking a sixth term from Californiaâs 17th Congressional District, which covers much of Silicon Valley, including parts of Santa Clara and Alameda counties. He faces Republican Ritesh Tandon in the midterms, after comfortably finishing first in Californiaâs June 2 nonpartisan primary with 62.3% of the vote. Tandon advanced with 14.8%. The district, home to major technology companies and a large population of technology workers, has consistently favoured Democrats. First elected to the House in 2016, Khanna has established himself as a progressive voice on economic policy, technology, foreign affairs and the role of American power overseas. Khanna has been a vocal critic of President Donald Trump, particularly over his economic policies Born in Philadelphia to Indian immigrant parents, he studied economics at the University of Chicago and earned a law degree from Yale University. Before entering Congress, he taught economics at Stanford University, practised law and served as deputy assistant secretary of commerce under President Barack Obama. He now sits on the House Armed Services Committee and has been an influential voice on issues ranging from artificial intelligence and semiconductor manufacturing to US competition with China. Read also | US midterms 2026: Meet Ro Khanna, Indian-American Congressman behind Epstein files push Khanna has been a vocal critic of President Donald Trump, particularly over his economic policies, immigration crackdown and approach to democratic institutions. He has challenged the administrationâs priorities on taxation and economic inequality, arguing that government policy should benefit working families rather than disproportionately favour wealthy individuals and corporations. His opposition to Trump also extends to the presidentâs use of executive power and his approach to foreign policy, where Khanna has advocated greater congressional oversight of military action and a stronger emphasis on diplomacy. At the same time, Khanna has sought to distinguish himself from the Democratic establishment by championing a more populist economic agenda, including investment in manufacturing, clean energy, education and healthcare. His views on technology, economic inequality and Americaâs global role frequently place him at the centre of the partyâs policy debate. 2. Pramila Jayapal Pramila Jayapal is seeking re-election from Washingtonâs 7th Congressional District, which includes much of Seattle and surrounding communities. She faces Republican Nirav Sheth in the midterms after dominating the stateâs nonpartisan primary, securing 84.4% of the vote against Shethâs 9.8%. The result underlined her strong standing in a heavily Democratic district, where she has built a substantial political base through her advocacy on immigration, healthcare and economic inequality. Elected to Congress in 2016, Jayapal made history as the first South Asian American woman elected to the House of Representatives. Pramila Jayapal serves on House committees that give her influence over debates on immigration. Born in India, she moved to the United States at 16 to attend Georgetown University and later earned an MBA from Northwestern University. Before entering electoral politics, she founded OneAmerica, a Washington-based immigrant-rights organisation, and became a prominent campaigner for immigration reform and civil liberties. Her experience as an activist has shaped her legislative priorities, particularly on deportations, detention, family separation and pathways to legal status. Jayapal has championed Medicare for All, stronger labour protections, affordable housing, climate action and expanded access to education. She has also held leadership positions in the Congressional Progressive Caucus and serves on the House Judiciary, Foreign Affairs and Budget committees, giving her influence over debates on immigration enforcement, federal spending and American foreign policy. Read also | US midterms 2026: From immigration reform to $15 minimum wage, all about Pramila Jayapal A vocal critic of President Donald Trump, Jayapal has repeatedly challenged his administrationâs immigration crackdown, deportation policies and restrictions on legal immigration. She has argued that the administrationâs approach threatens civil liberties and undermines protections for immigrant communities. Her opposition also extends to Trumpâs economic agenda and broader use of executive power, with Jayapal advocating stronger social protections and greater accountability for the administration. Her politics frequently put her to the left of the Democratic leadership, although she has worked within the party to advance progressive priorities. 3. Ami Bera Ami Bera, one of the longest-serving Indian-American members of Congress, is seeking another term in Californiaâs 3rd Congressional District, which covers Sacramento County and surrounding communities. He faces Republican Robb Tucker in the November 3 midterm elections. In the stateâs nonpartisan primary, Bera secured 34.3% of the vote against Tucker's 29.9%. His re-election bid comes as Democrats seek to regain control of the House, with the Sacramento region offering a test of whether his established local support can withstand the broader national political climate. Bera has supported stronger US engagement with India. First elected in 2012, Bera has represented the Sacramento area in Congress since January 2013. The son of Indian immigrants, he grew up in California and earned his medical degree from the University of California, Irvine. Before entering politics, he worked as a physician and served as Sacramento Countyâs chief medical officer. His background has helped shape his political identity as a pragmatic Democrat who emphasises healthcare, public services and evidence-based policymaking rather than the more sweeping economic agenda associated with the partyâs progressive wing. Read also | US midterms 2026: Who is Ami Bera, Indian-American Democrat seeking re-election from California's newly redrawn district Healthcare remains a central part of Beraâs political profile. He has advocated improving access to medical care, reducing prescription drug costs and strengthening Medicare, while also focusing on education, infrastructure, veteransâ services and economic development. His approach generally favours targeted reforms and bipartisan cooperation, positioning him closer to the Democratic Partyâs moderate wing on several policy questions. Foreign affairs, however, have become one of his defining areas of influence. Bera has served on the House Foreign Affairs Committee and the House Permanent Select Committee on Intelligence, with a particular interest in the Indo-Pacific. He has supported stronger US engagement with India and closer cooperation with regional partners, while emphasising the strategic challenge posed by China. His work has given him a prominent role in debates over US-India relations, regional security, intelligence oversight and the future of American engagement in Asia. 4. Suhas Subramanyam Suhas Subramanyam is seeking a second term in the US House of Representatives from Virginiaâs 10th Congressional District, which includes Loudoun County and parts of the surrounding Northern Virginia suburbs. He faces Republican Dave Beckwith and independent candidate Ahsen Mujeeb Malik in the midterms. The district, home to technology professionals, federal employees and government contractors, has generally favoured Democrats, but the Trump administrationâs cuts to the federal workforce and changes to government spending have made these issues particularly consequential for local voters. Suhas Subramanyam served as a technology policy adviser in the Obama White House. Subramanyam entered Congress in January 2025 after defeating Republican Mike Clancy in the 2024 election. His victory made him one of the newest Indian-American members of the House. Born in Houston to Indian immigrant parents, he studied at Tulane University and earned a law degree from Northwestern University. Before entering electoral politics, he worked with technology startups and served as a technology policy adviser in the Obama White House. He was elected to Virginiaâs House of Delegates in 2019, becoming the first South Asian American elected to the state legislature, and later served in the Virginia Senate before moving to Congress. His political profile combines technology policy, economic affordability and a focus on practical local concerns. During his time in the Virginia legislature, he worked on issues including utility bills, prescription drug costs, education and gun safety. In Congress, he has emphasised support for small businesses, infrastructure investment, healthcare access and protecting federal workers. His background in technology has also shaped his attention to the rapid expansion of data centres in Northern Virginia, where new developments promise investment and jobs but raise concerns about electricity demand, water consumption, land use and higher infrastructure costs. Read also | US midterms 2026: Meet Suhas Subramanyam, Indian-origin Democrat who served as advisor to Barack Obama Subramanyam has been critical of Trumpâs policies on federal employment and government restructuring, arguing that abrupt cuts and uncertainty can harm public services and communities that depend on government jobs. His district is particularly exposed to such changes because of its concentration of federal agencies, contractors and defence-related businesses. He has also advocated reproductive healthcare protections, stronger gun-safety measures and policies aimed at lowering household expenses. New entrants Amish Shah is running as the Democratic nominee in Arizona's 1st Congressional District. He previously contested the seat in 2024, losing to Republican David Schweikert. Schweikert is now running for governor, leaving the congressional seat open. Shah won the July 21, 2026, Democratic primary with 39.4% of the vote, defeating Marlene GalÃ¡n-Woods, who received 34.4%. He faces Republican Jay Feely, a former NFL kicker, in November. The district is competitive, making this one of the more consequential races involving an Indian-origin congressional candidate. A FirstStrategic poll conducted on October 1 found Shah at 44.4% and Feely at 41.6% among registered voters, with a margin of error of 5.4 percentage points. A forecast updated October 23 projects Shah at 63% to win. Read also | US midterms 2026: Meet Amish Shah, the doctor seeking a second shot at Congress Pia Dandiya is the Democratic nominee in Florida's 22nd Congressional District, an open seat where she faces Republican Casey Askar. Dandiya won the August 18 Democratic primary with 68.6% of the vote, defeating Kaysia Earley. Askar won the Republican primary with 30.9% in a crowded field. Read also | US midterms 2026: Meet Pia Dandiya, Indian-origin Democrat running for Floridaâs open 22nd House seat Ritesh Tandon is the Republican nominee challenging Khanna in California's 17th Congressional District. He advanced through the June 2 top-two primary with 19,793 votes, or 14.8%, finishing behind Khanna. The district is heavily Democratic, and current forecasts show Khanna with a substantial projected advantage. Nirav Sheth is the Republican challenger to Jayapal in Washington's 7th Congressional District. He secured second place in the state's nonpartisan primary, receiving 21,282 votes, or 9.8%. Jayapal won 84.4%. Sheth's advance means the November ballot will feature two races where Indian-origin candidates are facing off from opposing parties. Indian-American politicians not on the ballot Raja Krishnamoorthi lost the Democratic primary for the Illinois Senate seat and will not be the party's nominee in the November Senate election. His absence removes a high-profile Indian-American candidate from one of the year's most prominent Senate contests. Shri Thanedar lost the Democratic primary for Michigan's 13th Congressional District and is not the Democratic nominee in the November race. Gubernatorial race attracting national attention: Vivek Ramaswamy Vivek Ramaswamy, the Indian-American entrepreneur who emerged as a prominent voice in the Republican Party during the 2024 presidential race, is seeking to become governor of Ohio, the state where he was born and raised. The Republican nominee faces Democrat Amy Acton, a physician and former director of the Ohio Department of Health. The contest has become a closely watched test of Ramaswamy's transition from conservative political outsider to candidate for executive office. Born in Cincinnati to Indian immigrant parents, Ramaswamy studied biology at Harvard University and law at Yale. He made his fortune in biotechnology and investment management, founding Roivant Sciences in 2014. His 2021 book, Woke, Inc. , established his political identity as a critic of corporate diversity initiatives, environmental, social and governance investing and what he considers excessive ideological influence over business. Ramaswamy's political relationship with Trump remains a defining feature of his campaign During the 2024 Republican presidential primary, he advocated cutting government bureaucracy, restricting federal spending and challenging established political institutions. Although he withdrew from the race and endorsed Donald Trump, his combative campaign style helped establish him as a nationally recognised conservative figure. Trump subsequently selected Ramaswamy to co-lead the Department of Government Efficiency initiative alongside Elon Musk, although he left before the initiative's major restructuring efforts as he turned to the Ohio governor's race. His gubernatorial platform centres on reducing government costs, deregulation, education reform and expanding economic opportunity. His political relationship with Trump remains a defining feature of his campaign, even as he seeks to establish an independent record as a candidate for state leadership. The campaign has recently been embroiled in controversy over an advertisement featuring Acton's estranged mother criticising her daughter. Read also | US midterms 2026: Meet Vivek Ramaswamy, Trump-backed Republican seeking the Ohio governorship The ad drew bipartisan condemnation, including from DeWine, who urged Ramaswamy to withdraw it. Trump, however, defended the advertisement and encouraged Ramaswamy to continue running it, while Vice-President JD Vance also criticised Republicans who opposed it. The dispute has sharpened questions about the role of personal attacks in the campaign and whether the controversy could affect Ramaswamy's standing with voters. Polling has shown Acton ahead, although the size of her lead varies. The RealClearPolling average for October 19 put Acton at 48.7% and Ramaswamy at 44.3%, while a Fox News poll conducted October 15â19 found a narrower 50-48 margin. Other statewide contests Nirav Shah , a physician and public-health administrator, is the Democratic nominee for governor of Maine. He previously served as director of the Maine Center for Disease Control and Prevention from 2019 to 2023 and as principal deputy director of the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention from 2023 to 2025. Shah won Maine's June 9 Democratic gubernatorial primary with 26.9% of the vote. Aruna Miller , Maryland's lieutenant governor, is seeking to continue in office on the Democratic ticket led by Governor Wes Moore. Born in India, Miller immigrated to the US as a child and built a career as a transportation engineer before entering politics. Her career includes service in Maryland's House of Delegates and election as lieutenant governor in 2022. Miller's political position differs from that of a standalone gubernatorial candidate: the lieutenant governor runs on a joint ticket with the governor. Her electoral prospects therefore depend on the performance of the ticket as a whole as well as her own profile. Read also | US midterms 2026: Indian-American Democrat Aruna Miller seeks re-election as Maryland Lt Governor alongside Wes Moore Saritha Komatireddy , a Republican lawyer and former federal prosecutor, is the Republican nominee for New York attorney general. She is challenging Democratic incumbent Letitia James. Her campaign offers Republicans an opportunity to contest an office that has become nationally prominent because of high-profile investigations and litigation involving major businesses and political figures. Read also | US midterms 2026: How 9/11 shaped Saritha Komatireddyâs legal career as she runs for New York attorney general Josh Kaul , Wisconsin's Democratic attorney general, is seeking re-election. Nithya Raman: Running for Los Angeles mayor Raman is a Los Angeles City Council member and urban planner seeking to unseat Mayor Karen Bass. Her campaign focuses on housing, homelessness, city services and the cost of living. She has become a prominent figure in the city's progressive political movement. Raman advanced to the November 3 mayoral runoff after the June 2 primary. Certified results gave incumbent Bass 34.3%, Raman 29.0% and Spencer Pratt 25.5%. Raman's advance to the runoff turned the race into a direct contest between two Democrats. Read also | US midterms 2026: Indian-born Nithya Raman challenges LA mayor Karen Bass A McLaughlin & Associates/California Post poll conducted October 15â18 put Raman ahead by 7.9 percentage points. An Impact Research poll conducted October 2â7 put her ahead by 10 points, while a UC Berkeley Institute of Governmental Studies/Los Angeles Times poll from September 15â20 showed an 11-point lead. Raman's candidacy is significant beyond her own electoral prospects: a victory would make her the first South Asian woman to serve as Los Angeles mayor. Her campaign will test whether her progressive coalition can expand sufficiently to defeat an incumbent in a city facing persistent housing and homelessness challenges. What's at stake for Indian-Americans For the Indian-American community, the November 3 midterms are about more than individual victories. They are a test of how far a once-underrepresented community has come in American politics â and whether its growing presence can translate into greater influence in Congress, state governments and the national debate. The stakes are particularly high for the so-called âSamosa Caucusâ, the informal label for Indian-American lawmakers in the US Congress. November 3 mideterms will shape the scale and reach of Indian-American representation in American public life. Ro Khanna, Pramila Jayapal, Ami Bera and Suhas Subramanyam are fighting to retain their House seats, while challengers such as Amish Shah and Dandiya are seeking to expand the communityâs footprint on Capitol Hill. Their outcomes will help determine whether Indian-origin representation in Congress consolidates, grows or faces a setback at a time when immigration, technology, healthcare, economic opportunity and Americaâs role in the world are fiercely contested. The stakes extend beyond Washington. Vivek Ramaswamyâs bid for governor of Ohio could take an Indian-American politician from national prominence to one of the countryâs most powerful state offices. Nirav Shahâs campaign in Maine adds another dimension to the contest for statewide leadership. Success in races such as these would signal that Indian-origin candidates are competing not just in safe districts or within established political networks, but for executive power and leadership across the political map. Yet there is no single Indian-American political story. The candidates span the ideological spectrum â from progressive Democrats to more centrist lawmakers and conservative Republicans â and are campaigning on sharply different visions of government. Their fortunes will reflect not only the strength of their personal brands and local coalitions, but also how voters respond to their parties, their policies and the national political climate. Representation, in other words, does not automatically translate into a common agenda. Ultimately, November 3 will test whether Indian-American candidates can turn growing political visibility into electoral power. The results will shape not only the careers of individual candidates, but also the scale and reach of Indian-American representation in American public life â and the influence the next generation may be able to wield in setting the countryâs political priorities. title: US midterms: Five flashpoints election officials are watching as America votes
text: File photo: US midterm elections 2026 As Americans prepare to vote in the November 3 midterm elections, state and local officials are bracing for possible disruptions ranging from federal intervention at polling places to challenges over voter eligibility and the handling of ballots. The concerns follow a series of unprecedented moves by Trumpâs administration to increase federal control over elections, including demands for unredacted voter rolls, efforts to restrict mail-in voting and investigations targeting people suspected of voting as noncitizens. Courts have blocked several of these initiatives, but election officials and voting rights experts say the administrationâs actions have added uncertainty ahead of polling day. In a report published on Monday, investigative newsroom ProPublica identified five areas that voting experts and election officials are watching: possible federal interference, challenges to alleged noncitizen voters, problems with voting procedures, election security and disputes over results after voting ends. The administration has not explicitly ruled out sending federal agents to polling places or seizing ballots and voting machines. Election officials, however, say they have been preparing for such possibilities while stressing that there is no evidence of a planned federal operation that would prevent voters from casting their ballots. Could federal agents intervene at polling places? An incident in Floridaâs Leon County last month heightened concerns over federal law enforcement at polling sites. Mark Earley, the countyâs supervisor of elections, told ProPublica he was âfuriousâ when two marked US Customs and Border Protection vehicles appeared outside the countyâs busiest early-voting location, despite repeated assurances that federal agents would stay away. Earley alerted the FBI, but later learnt the agents had stopped to vote while travelling out of state. He said their use of official vehicles showed âpretty bad judgmentâ. Washington Attorney General Nick Brown told ProPublica that state officials and voting rights groups had rehearsed responses to possible federal attempts to seize ballots or voting equipment. âWeâve seen the tension and chaos thatâs in the air,â he said, calling the federal government âthe biggest challenge to smooth elections right nowâ. The Justice Department said its election monitors would follow the law, though officials in Wyoming raised concerns after monitors questioned poll workers about their training and sought to inspect voting systems. Could noncitizen voter investigations affect eligible voters? The Trump administrationâs efforts to identify suspected noncitizen voters have raised fears that eligible US citizens could be wrongly removed from voter rolls or discouraged from voting, according to voting rights groups cited by ProPublica. The Justice Department has sued California over more than 20,000 people it considers âlikelyâ to be noncitizens, seeking to prevent their ballots from being counted. California called the allegation âspeciousâ, while a Los Angeles County analysis found that many people on the list were not registered there or had never voted; some had said they were born in the US. Courts rejected the departmentâs bid to block the ballots and later restrained its demand for records from California officials, describing it as an âintimidation planâ. The department also threatened legal action against Washington state over a list of 400 suspected noncitizens. Secretary of state Steve Hobbs called the list unreliable, saying it included citizens, unregistered people and duplicate entries. Sam Trepel of the States United Democracy Center described the departmentâs actions as a âdisturbing use of prosecutorial authorityâ. Voting rights advocates warn that the investigations could deter eligible citizens from voting. The Department of Homeland Security said it was not planning operations targeting polling places, adding that ICE would only make arrests there in response to safety threats. A spokesperson said the DHS and Justice Department remained focused on identifying and prosecuting noncitizens who vote in US elections. Could changes to voting rules and systems cause problems? Changes to voting laws and administrative systems have raised concerns about ballot rejections and hurdles for voters. In North Carolina, new rules require mail-in voters to provide identification and seal two envelopes, with Democracy Docket reporting a sharp rise in rejections over incorrectly sealed inner envelopes. Texas and other states have reduced or relocated polling sites. Tarrant County, for instance, cut its polling locations by nearly a third, potentially increasing queues and confusion, ProPublica reported. Texas also faced registration-system errors that delayed hundreds of thousands of applications, though county officials said the backlogs had been addressed. Meanwhile, election experts told ProPublica that isolated complaints about touch-screen voting machines do not indicate tampering. Manufacturer ES&S said it had received no widespread reports of problems, while experts said attempts to alter machine programming would be detected during pre-election testing. How vulnerable are election systems to cyber and physical attacks? Security concerns have grown after suspicious packages and false bomb threats targeted election offices. Last month, officials in several states, including Arizona, received envelopes containing white powder, later found to be non-toxic in Arizona. During the 2024 election, false bomb threats believed to have originated abroad forced evacuations at vote-counting sites, with a CISA-funded message board helping officials respond after the FBI deemed them non-credible. ProPublica reported that Trumpâs dismantling of CISA has left state and local officials with less federal support, prompting nonprofits and states to take on a larger role in election security. Brennan Center for Justiceâs Derek Tisler said states lack the capacity to manage these threats alone. Could the results face legal challenges after voting? Election lawyers fear the administrationâs actions before the midterms could be followed by legal challenges after voting. The Justice Department sued Alaska to block certification of its Senate result if Republican incumbent Dan Sullivan loses, arguing that a second candidate with the same name could confuse voters. A federal judge dismissed the case on Sunday, but the administration is expected to appeal. Trump said he ordered the lawsuit, while The New York Times reported that aides to Democratic nominee Mary Peltola had helped organise the second candidateâs run. The intervention is unusual because federal law bars government interference in an active election, with challenges typically brought by losing candidates in state courts after voting. Washington Attorney General Nick Brown told ProPublica the case amounted to federal interference in the electoral process. Officials are also preparing for local boards to refuse certification over fraud allegations, while some lawyers fear Trump could pressure Congress to block newly elected Democrats from taking their seats. Legal experts cited by ProPublica said an incoming Democratic majority and the courts could resist such an effort, though it might cause temporary delays. Officials prepare for worst-case scenarios Across the country, state and local election officials have spent months training poll workers, coordinating with law enforcement and preparing legal responses in case federal agents or private groups attempt to disrupt voting. Election officials have also warned that threats and allegations of fraud could increase the risk of intimidation and violence against poll workers. Matt Crane, executive director of the Colorado County Clerks Association, told CNN that officials were under pressure because even a minor mistake could be amplified into a national disinformation campaign. Arizona Secretary of State Adrian Fontes said the administrationâs threats could themselves intimidate voters, but stressed that officials had not seen evidence of a planned disruption that would prevent people from voting. He said preparations were precautionary and should not deter people from going to the polls. Election officials have spent months preparing to run the 2026 vote, but the scale of those preparations reflects concerns that the challenges may extend beyond Election Day and into the counting and certification of results. title: EPS demands reopening of Amma Clinics
text: Chennai: AIADMK general secretary Edappadi K Palaniswami has demanded that chief minister C Joseph Vijay reopen Amma Clinics to shield people from exorbitant prices fixed by drug companies. He also chaired a district secretariesâ meeting in Chennai where rebel leaders S P Velumani and Natham Viswanathan were absent. Former police officer S Velladurai joined the party on the sidelines of the district secretariesâ meeting, triggering speculation that he might be fielded as the partyâs bypoll candidate in Ambasamudram. Velladurai, who retired from service in 2024, had turned a supporter of V K Sasikala . He was fielded as a candidate of All India Puratchi Thalaivar Makkal Munnetra Kazhagam headed by her in the 2026 assembly election in Nanguneri assembly constituency. However, he was defeated. With Sasikala herself distancing herself from AIPTMMK, Velladurai has opted to join AIADMK. âChief minister C Joseph Vijay cannot be compared to MGR (the late CM M G Ramachandran). MGR was a mountain, but the CM now is just a mound,â he told reporters. AIADMK functionaries said the subject of bypolls did come up during the district secretariesâ meeting, but candidates were not discussed. âLet the announcement of elections come, we shall speak about it after that,â Palaniswami told reporters after the meeting when asked whether AIADMK was prepared for the bypolls. Earlier in the day, he cited a report on rising drug prices and flayed TVK govt for not reopening Amma Clinics. Palaniswami said the state govt was keen on increasing liquor prices but the same attention was not given to pharmacies. title: Sadou Asom Karmachari Parishad to oppose Natâl Pension System
text: Guwahati: The Sadou Asom Karmachari Parishad (SAKP) will prioritise opposing the National Pension System , newly elected general secretary Pranab Bhuyan said on Sunday. Bhuyan made the announcement as the newly elected 199-member executive committee took charge at the Sadou Asom Karmachari Parishadâs central Shaheed Divas observance at Karmachari Bhavan in Sixmile-Panjabari. Kumud Kumar Kotoky was elected president, while Bhuyan became general secretary after the outgoing committee was dissolved. âOur priority will be to raise a strong voice against the National Pension System and take up issues affecting the interests and welfare of govt employees,â Bhuyan said. The programme paid tribute to Dilip Chakraborty, who died on Nov 1, 1980, following police atrocities during the Assam Movement. The council marked the 46th anniversary of his death and remembered his contribution to the movement. âChakrabortyâs sacrifice will remain an eternal inspiration for us,â Kotoky said. The observance began with the hoisting of the council flag, followed by the lighting of earthen lamps, floral tributes and traditional Diha Naam. Former office-bearers recalled the councilâs role during major political developments in Assam. Former senior bureaucrat and engineer Pradyut Kumar Choudhury, along with Nagen Kalita, Basanta Kalita and Charan Deka, attended the swearing-in ceremony. title: 'Maximum deterrence': Mojtaba Khamenei meets top generals, issues warning to US
text: The meeting marked the first publicly disclosed gathering between Khamenei and all three senior military commanders since the war began Iran's Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei has instructed the country's armed forces to deliver an immediate and forceful response to any renewed US or Israeli attack, warning that Tehran would decide when and under what conditions hostilities would end. In a meeting with the country's top three military commanders, Khamenei called for maximum combat readiness and said any threat must be met with an effective response, without geographical limitations, according to a statement from his office reported by Axios and Iranian state media outlet Tehran Times. Watch US Mainland Next Target? Mojtaba Unveils 'No Geographic Limits' Missile Threat; Trump In Shock "If the enemies once again launch military or terrorist attacks, it will be the Islamic Republic of Iran's Armed Forces and the Iranian nation that determine when and under what conditions those hostilities will end," Khamenei said. The meeting marked the first publicly disclosed gathering between Khamenei and all three senior military commanders since the war began, Axios reported. The development comes amid heightened tensions between Washington and Tehran, even as diplomatic efforts continue to prevent a fresh outbreak of hostilities. Khamenei also directed the military leadership to update its target database to bring all physical and non-physical assets belonging to what Tehran describes as the "US-Zionist enemy" within the reach of Iranian forces. He called for strengthening military intelligence, expanding indigenous defence capabilities and incorporating emerging technologies into the country's security infrastructure. The commanders, including Armed Forces Chief of Staff Major General Ali Abdollahi, Army Commander Major General Amir Hatami and Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps chief Major General Ahmad Vahidi, briefed Khamenei on military preparedness along the Persian Gulf coastline, the Strait of Hormuz, the Gulf of Oman and Iran's northwestern and southeastern borders. They also reported a several-fold increase in the production of ammunition, reconnaissance equipment and support and combat weapons, according to Tehran Times. The warning was reinforced by Iran's top security official Mohsen Rezaei, who threatened "devastating blows" against any aggressor, saying Tehran would use "new weaponry" if attacked. In a post on X, Rezaei said diplomacy remained possible if Washington fulfilled Iran's seven conditions for negotiations. The demands include lifting US sanctions, reducing American military presence in the region, releasing frozen Iranian assets, restoring oil waivers and recognising a new shipping route through the Strait of Hormuz agreed upon by Iran and Oman. Tehran has also demanded an end to hostilities across the region, including Israeli attacks on Lebanon. The latest warnings come as Washington and Tehran exchange proposals through Qatari mediators. US Vice-President JD Vance reportedly sent a framework for negotiations to Iran, with Tehran describing Washington's attempt to open dialogue as a positive step. However, US President Donald Trump has continued to warn that Washington could strike Iran's remaining nuclear facilities. While saying discussions were going well, he also described Tehran as "not very reliable". You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

title: Trump gives reporter fitness lecture as MAGA loses shape
text: The exchange was not merely an illustration of a President with an unusually short fuse that has been sizzling lately; it was also a revealing snapshot of a leader entering the final stretch of an election campaign with considerably more anxiety than his public bravado suggests. (Photo: AP) TOI Correspondent from Washington: Four days before a midterm election that could leave him politically out of shape, US President Donald Trump decided to conduct a fitness assessment --- of a Reuters journalist. Faced with an innocuous question about why he was cancelling campaign rallies in Kansas and Iowa, the MAGA boss erupted into an unsolicited lecture on the journalist's weight, appearance, and general state of health, betraying frayed nerves that do not augur well for his party. âYou are a sick guy! Reuters is terrible, by the way. Look at this guy... he's way out of shape... You are disgusting! Put yourself in shape! You look like hell!â Trump exploded at the reporter, pushing back at any suggestion that he was tired or backing out of rallies because of heckling and poor attendance. He said he felt great and the reason he was not going to those states was because Republican candidates were doing very well and his energies were better devoted elsewhere. The exchange was not merely an illustration of a President with an unusually short fuse that has been sizzling lately; it was also a revealing snapshot of a leader entering the final stretch of an election campaign with considerably more anxiety than his public bravado suggests. Polls show Democratic candidates leading, tied, or narrowing margins in the most unexpected places, including ruby red states Trump won by 10 to 20 points in the 2024 Presidential elections. For instance, in Kansas, a state that has not elected a Democrat Senator since 1932, polls put Democrat Adam Hamilton ahead of incumbent Roger Marshall 49-45. Texas, which last elected a Democrat Senator in 1988 and which Trump carried comfortably in 2024, has become a genuine Senate battleground, with Democrat James Talarico -- who incidentally was ladling out dosas on Thursday in an effort to court Indian-American votes --- ahead of Republican Ken Paxton. South Carolina, where Republican Darline Graham is hoping to succeed her late brother Lindsay Graham as senator, has also tightened considerably. Even more unnerving for Republicans are the warning signs from states that have traditionally been considered political fortresses, including Louisiana and Mississippi, which last elected a Democratic senator in 1982. If Dems win all these races, they would be on track to reverse the Republicansâ 53-47 control of the Senate, A Democratic takeover of both chambers would leave Trump facing not merely hostile congressional hearings but chambers capable of blocking appointments, frustrating legislation, and investigating an administration dogged by allegations of cronyism and self-enrichment. Republicans, naturally, have a theory about why the polls are wrong: the hidden Trump voter. They argue that there are millions of Trump supporters who refuse to participate in polls, conceal their preferences or simply do not admit to pollsters that they intend to vote Republican. They will emerge, the theory goes, on Election Day and deliver the customary surprise. But hoping for invisible voters is not quite the same as having visible enthusiasm. In fact, some of the most visible activity at recent Trump rallies has been distinctly uncomfortable for the president and his MAGA faithful. Hecklers have interrupted Trump's speeches at rallies and his surrogates have been pranked on several occasions. At an Ohio rally, a comedian who goes by the name Robby Roadsteamer managed to interrupt Trump with a reference to Jeffrey Epstein, before being escorted out amid chants of "USA!USA!" a standard MAGA response. The president's explanation was that such protesters were paid by radical left political enemies. Roadstreamer meanwhile took credit for Trump's subsequent cancellation of the Kansas and Iowa appearances, announcing online: âTrump cancelled the rest of his rallies! You're welcome, America.â Trump allies, including Vivek Ramaswamy and Fox News, have also been punked by pranksters, who present themselves as MAGA loyalists before turning on them on camera. Trump's own response to the heckling and harsh scrutiny by the mainstream media has been to crank the personal insults up another notch, with consequent blowback that is raising political temperature all around. When he suggested that Democratic Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed should have to pass through a metal detector before entering the Senate (suggesting he is a jihadist who cannot be trusted), the Michigan Democrat clapped back: âI'll go through a metal detector if you'll sit for a lie detectorâ -- to answer questions about his ties to Epstein. Trump has also repeatedly disparaged Texas' Democratic candidate James Talarico as "Tala-freako" -- part of his chronic habit of name-calling. There is a broader political backdrop to the president's increasingly irritable demeanour. His administration is facing mounting accusations of corruption, grift, and self-dealing, while its aggressive efforts to influence election processes have raised questions about whether Trump is prepared to accept an adverse outcome in the election. title: US Supreme Court rejects Trump's push to isolate 20,000 California ballots over citizenship claims
text: Trump administration argued that setting aside the disputed ballots was a limited measure that would allow officials to verify voter eligibility without preventing legitimate votes from eventually being counted. The US Supreme Court on Monday rejected the Trump administrationâs emergency request to set aside around 20,000 ballots in California over claims that the voters may not be US citizens. The decision came a day before the final day of voting in the crucial midterm elections, dealing another legal setback to US President Donald Trumpâs efforts to intervene in the electoral process. The court refused to intervene in the dispute involving voters flagged by the federal government as likely noncitizens on Californiaâs voter rolls. It did not explain its decision. No justice publicly dissented. The rejection came without the court asking California officials to respond to the administrationâs appeal. California governor Gavin Newsom welcomed the decision, saying on X, âThe Court rejected Trumpâs emergency request without even asking the other side to respond. Democracy won.â The ruling marks another setback for the administration, which has faced repeated defeats in its efforts to have the disputed ballots kept separate until the votersâ citizenship status is verified. California Attorney General Rob Bonta said courts had rejected the administrationâs attempts to interfere in the stateâs elections four times, including at the district court, the Ninth Circuit Court of Appeals and the Supreme Court. âCourts have now rejected the Trump Administrationâs attempts to interfere in Californiaâs elections not once, not twice, not three times, but four times â from the district court to the Ninth Circuit to the U.S. Supreme Court,â Bonta said. âThis latest decision should put an end to the Administrationâs attempt to disrupt Californiaâs elections through emergency court orders," he added. Voting by noncitizens rare in US The Trump administration has made identifying suspected noncitizen voters a priority this year, despite such cases being rare in the US. It argued that setting aside the disputed ballots was a limited measure that would allow officials to verify voter eligibility without preventing legitimate votes from eventually being counted. However, California officials questioned the reliability of the federal government's list, saying it contained errors and could lead to eligible voters being disenfranchised. The administration's request also faced criticism over its timing, with election officials pointing out that it came only weeks before voting concluded. The Justice Department has acknowledged that its list was not entirely reliable. During a hearing on whether to lift an order preventing the administration from threatening to prosecute election workers who allowed potentially ineligible voters to cast ballots, US District Court Judge Trina Thompson questioned the accuracy of the federal data. âWould you agree there's a high error rate?â the San Francisco-based judge asked Justice Department attorney Kenneth Kao. âThat's a fair statement,â Kao said. âThat's why we ask for the registrars' aid in verifying these are all valid voters.â However, Bill Essayli, the federal prosecutor overseeing the Justice Department's Los Angeles office, expressed confidence that the people on the list were not eligible to vote. âThis isnât speculation. This isnât a theory,â Essayli said at a news conference, while later acknowledging that the list could contain errors. Lower courts also reject administration's request The Supreme Court's decision followed a series of rulings in favour of California. A district court had earlier rejected the Justice Department's request, warning that separating the ballots could disrupt the election and undermine public confidence in the democratic process. US District Judge David O. Carter said such a move could âwreak havocâ on the midterm elections. âIf the Executive can discount votes and threaten an ongoing election due to unproven allegations, then our democracy is in danger,â Carter wrote. A 2-1 appeals court panel subsequently upheld his order. One judge appointed by Trump and another appointed by former President Joe Biden voted in favour of California. The third judge, also appointed by Trump, dissented, arguing that the state's refusal to separate the ballots encouraged the âviolation of federal lawâ. In a separate development on Monday, US District Judge James Boasberg ruled against the administration's attempts to make last-minute demands of California election officials, saying they likely violated the Constitution. âThe Executive Branch has likely violated the Constitutionâs Elections Clause, which commits authority over election rules to the states and Congress alone,â Boasberg wrote. However, in a separate ruling later on Monday, Boasberg declined to issue another order restraining the administration. He said the Democratic groups that had filed the lawsuit lacked legal standing and that the issue had already been addressed by states and courts. Millions of California ballots already returned California has been conducting voting by mail since early October. The state sends ballots to all its approximately 23 million registered voters. More than 6 million ballots had already been returned, according to Associated Press election data. State election officials had argued that identifying and separating the disputed ballots at this stage would be logistically impossible. The Supreme Court had also rejected Trump's attempt to restrict mail-in voting across the country in September, although it has sided with his administration in several other emergency appeals. Reacting to Monday's decision, Kristen Clarke, general counsel of the NAACP, criticised the administration's efforts. âThe DOJâs baseless challenge was yet another attempt at federal overreach and voter suppression,â she said. âWe will not stand for the Trump Administrationâs bullying campaign, and we will continue to use every tool at our disposal to ensure the American peopleâs voices are not silenced.â You use AI every day. title: 2 yrs, 122 days of protests later, PU still awaits Senate
text: Two years, 122 days of stir later, PU still awaits Senate Chandigarh: Nearly two years after Panjab Universityâs previous Senate completed its tenure, 122 days of protests over its governing structure and a year-long standoff later, the university still awaits the formal constitution of its new 91-member Senate. The electoral process concluded on Oct 4, but Nov 1, the traditional date for commencement of the Senateâs four-year tenure, has passed without the 47 elected fellows being formally notified or the 36 members to be nominated by Vice-President CP Radhakrishnan, the university Chancellor, being announced. The previous Senateâs four-year tenure ended on Oct 31, 2024, without fresh elections being held. The absence of an elected House triggered a 96-day agitation by students under the Panjab University Bachao Morcha. The issue took another turn in Oct 2025 when the Centre proposed restructuring the Senate and Syndicate by reducing the Senateâs size and changing its composition. The move triggered widespread opposition on campus and another 26-day protest. The Centre eventually withdrew the changes on Nov 7, 2025, and the Vice-President approved the election schedule on Nov 27, ending the immediate deadlock over holding the polls. The Senate comprises 91 members, including 47 elected fellows, 36 nominated by the Chancellor, two members nominated by the Punjab legislative assembly and six ex-officio members. While results for the elected constituencies have been declared, their formal approval and notification by the Chancellor are awaited. The list of 36 nominated members is also pending. Prof Rajat Sandhir, elected from the Combined Faculties constituency, said there should be no further delay in constituting the Senate. âThe notification should be issued immediately so that Panjab University has its governing body in place. The Senate is the universityâs highest statutory authority and important decisions concerning the institution need to be deliberated upon and taken through this body. There is no reason for the process to be held up any further,â he said. Simranjit Singh Dhillon, elected from the Registered Graduates constituency, said the delay was unjustified, particularly after the university had already remained without an elected Senate for nearly two years. âIt is absolutely unjustified that such delays continue even after the election process has been completed. The university has already lost considerable time without an elected Senate. Any further delay does not send the right signal. The notification should come without any more waiting,â he said. Jodh Singh, also elected from the Registered Graduates constituency, said the Senate should be constituted and convened before the Vice-Presidentâs proposed visit to the university in Dec. âThe Senate should be in place before the Vice-Presidentâs visit. Important decisions taken by the present and previous vice-chancellors during the period when the elected Senate was absent should be placed before the House for discussion and appropriate consideration. The university cannot continue functioning indefinitely without its elected governing body,â he said. In the absence of the Senate, important university decisions have been handled through committees and other administrative mechanisms rather than an elected House. Once the Senate is notified, the university will also be able to initiate the process of constituting the Syndicate, its executive body, through elections among senators. The elected representatives are now seeking early notification of both categories of members so that the new House can be convened and resume its statutory functions. title: US midterms 2026: Meet Vivek Ramaswamy, Trump-backed Republican seeking the Ohio governorship
text: Ramaswamy has recently faced bipartisan criticism over a campaign advertisement. President Donald Trump-backed Indian-American Republican Vivek Ramaswamy rose to prominence during the 2024 US presidential race, positioning himself as a bold, unconventional candidate. He challenged Trump for the Republican nomination before suspending his campaign in January 2024 and endorsing him. Ramaswamy remains a prominent figure in business and politics and is now the Republican candidate for Ohio governor. He will face Democratic nominee Amy Acton in the November 3 2026, general election. The 40-year-old biotech entrepreneur has recently faced bipartisan criticism over a campaign advertisement featuring Acton's estranged mother, Donna Arthur, who calls her daughter a liar. Ramaswamy has defended the advertisement, saying it is about alleged dishonesty rather than Acton's childhood abuse. Watch 'HE NEEDS A METAL DETECTOR!' Trump Targets El-Sayed At Michigan Rally, Calls Him 'Jihadist' Who is Vivek Ramaswamy? Born on August 9, 1985, in Cincinnati, Ohio, Vivek Ramaswamy is the son of Indian immigrants from Kerala who moved to the US in the 1970s. His mother was a geriatric psychiatrist, while his father worked as an engineer and patent lawyer at General Electric. Ramaswamy grew up with his younger brother, Shankar, and graduated as the valedictorian of his Jesuit high school. He was also a nationally ranked junior tennis player and an accomplished pianist. Ramaswamy graduated summa cum laude from Harvard University in 2007 with a degree in biology. He later worked in life sciences investing before earning a law degree from Yale Law School in 2013. He met his future wife, Apoorva Tewari, a medical student who later became a throat surgeon, while studying at Yale. In 2014, at the age of 29, Ramaswamy founded Roivant Sciences, a biopharmaceutical company focused on developing medicines. His business ventures helped him build substantial wealth and establish himself in the biotechnology industry. He later gained national attention for his criticism of environmental, social and governance (ESG) investing, arguing that companies should focus on business performance rather than social and political causes. His views, frequent media appearances and book Woke, Inc. helped raise his profile in conservative political circles. Ramaswamy's presidential bid and ties with Trump Ramaswamy announced his candidacy for Ohio governor in February 2025 and received Trump's endorsement. His campaign has focused on economic opportunity, tax cuts and education reform. Among his proposals are eliminating Ohio's state income tax, reducing property taxes and raising academic standards in public schools. He has also pledged to engage with voters across all 88 counties in the state. Ramaswamy won the Republican primary in May 2026 and will face Acton, a physician and former director of the Ohio Department of Health, in the general election. Why is Ramaswamy facing backlash over his campaign ad? The controversy centres on an advertisement featuring Acton's estranged mother, Donna Arthur, who accuses her daughter of lying and questions her account of her childhood. Acton has spoken publicly about experiencing homelessness and abuse as a child. Her stepfather was indicted on charges of raping her when she was 12, after her biological father reported the allegations. Acton and her brother were removed from their mother's custody. Her stepfather pleaded not guilty and later died. Ramaswamy defended the advertisement at a campaign stop in northeast Ohio, saying it had nothing to do with childhood abuse. âThe irony is theyâre lying about an ad that is about lying,â he said, the Associated Press reported. âTheyâre changing the subject because they donât want to answer for their own failures." Acton condemned the advertisement, telling Spectrum News, âI wonât normalize somebody who has said that my childhood is just something Iâm complaining about.â The advertisement has drawn criticism from Republicans and Democrats. Ohio Governor Mike DeWine called for it to be taken down, saying, âItâs wrong to run this ad.â Trump, however, backed the campaign's approach, describing the advertisement as âhitting pay dirtâ. Vice-President JD Vance also defended Ramaswamy, criticising Republicans who objected to the ad. The controversy has brought renewed national attention to the Ohio governor's race ahead of the November 3 election. You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

title: US Midterm Election Day forecast: Storm threatens to dampen voter turnout in key states
text: Storm threatens to dampen US Election Day turnout in key states Rain could affect voter turnout in parts of the central United States on midterm election day, as a storm threatens to bring wet and windy weather to several states with key races. More than 35 million people have already voted early, but those heading to polling stations on Tuesday may face rain depending on the stormâs path. Multiple studies cited by CNN have found that rain and bad weather tend to keep voters away from polling stations, while sunshine has the opposite effect. The extent of the impact will depend on which areas receive rainfall. The storm could bring rain from parts of the Great Lakes and Upper Midwest to the western Gulf Coast. However, its exact path remains uncertain, with some areas potentially staying dry while others could experience steady rain or passing showers. Gusty winds are possible across the Midwest and Plains, while strong thunderstorms could develop along the stormâs southern side. Much of the East Coast and the western United States is expected to remain dry. However, coastal areas of the Mid-Atlantic and Southeast could see light showers. Most of the eastern half of the country is forecast to experience temperatures 5 to 15 degrees Fahrenheit above average. The Southwest is expected to see slightly cooler-than-average temperatures. The forecasts could change as meteorologists gain more confidence in the stormâs path by the weekend. State-wise Election Day weather forecast Georgia and North Carolina: Both states are likely to remain dry. Highs in Georgia are expected to reach the 70s and low 80s, while North Carolina could see temperatures in the 70s. Iowa and Kansas: Iowa is likely to receive rain for at least part of Tuesday, although showers could move out by early morning. Highs are forecast to reach the 50s and low 60s. In Kansas, rain is likely in some areas, but its location and amount remain uncertain. Temperatures could range from the 50s to the 60s. Michigan: Forecast models differ considerably, with some predicting widespread rain and others suggesting only light showers in western Michigan or the Upper Peninsula. Highs could range from the 40s and 50s in the Upper Peninsula to the 60s in southern Lower Michigan. Ohio: Most forecast models keep rain west of the state, although wet weather remains possible. Highs are expected to reach the 60s. Maine and New Hampshire: Both states are likely to remain dry. Maine could see highs in the 40s and lower 50s, while New Hampshire is forecast to experience temperatures in the 40s and 50s. Texas: The eastern half of the state, particularly areas along and east of Interstate 35, has the highest chance of rain. Thunderstorms are also possible. Highs could reach the 80s near the coast and the 60s in the Panhandle. The stormâs final path will determine which states face rain, strong winds and possible thunderstorms on Election Day. title: First Mahatma Gandhi statue in North Dakota unveiled at Bismarck's Peace Park
text: First Mahatma Gandhi statue in North Dakota unveiled at Bismarck's Peace Park. The first life-size statue of Mahatma Gandhi in North Dakota was unveiled at Peace Park in downtown Bismarck, the state's capital, in a ceremony attended by the state's first lady Kjersti Armstrong and agriculture commissioner Doug Goehring. The statue was installed with the assistance of the Consulate General of India in Seattle, with technical support from the Indian American community in North Dakota and the North Dakota Trade Office, the consulate said in a press release. The unveiling ceremony began with the national anthems of India and the United States, followed by musical renditions of Gandhi's favourite hymns by school students from North Dakota. Officials from the Bismarck Parks and Recreation District and members of the Indian American community also attended the event. The unveiling took place during the month of Gandhi Jayanti , observed worldwide on October 2 as the International Day of Non-Violence. It also marked the year of Gandhi's 157th birth anniversary. Addressing the gathering, North Dakota agriculture commissioner Doug Goehring highlighted the growing friendship between India and North Dakota. He said Gandhi's message resonated not only with India and the rest of the world but also with people in North Dakota. Goehring described the statue as a symbol of peace and non-violence and recalled Gandhi's timeless message. North Dakota first lady Kjersti Armstrong expressed her admiration for Gandhi, saying it was an honour to celebrate his legacy, which she described as being more important today than it had been in a very long time. Peace Park adds Gandhi statue to public art installations Located at 400 East Front Avenue in downtown Bismarck, Peace Park was developed shortly after the September 11, 2001, attacks. It is also home to a Peace Pole installed by the Gandhi Peace Network of North Dakota, along with other bronze sculptural artefacts. The Gandhi statue joins these installations, adding to the public art heritage of North Dakota's capital city. The consulate described Gandhi's life and message as universal symbols of peace and non-violence. The installation also comes amid growing engagement between India and North Dakota since the establishment of the Consulate General of India in Seattle. According to the consulate, visits by the Consul General to North Dakota in 2024 and 2026 included meetings with the governor, the mayor of Bismarck and leaders from the agriculture, business and education sectors. The consulate has also organised cultural and consular outreach programmes in Fargo, including the International Day of Yoga 2026 and a consular camp in February 2026. Senior delegates from the North Dakota Trade Office also visited India earlier this year as part of ongoing exchanges between the two sides. Fifth Gandhi monument under Seattle consulate's jurisdiction The Bismarck installation is the latest addition to the Consulate General of India's initiative to establish Gandhi monuments across the US Pacific North and Midwest. Watch Mahatma Gandhi Statue Restored: From Attack to Renewal on International Day of Non-Violence Earlier statues were installed at the base of the Space Needle in Seattle in October 2024, at the State Capitol in Lincoln, Nebraska, in December 2024, and at the Mansfield Center at the University of Montana in Missoula in March 2026. Along with the statue installed at Bellevue Public Library in October 2009, the Bismarck monument is the fifth Mahatma Gandhi statue within the jurisdiction of the Consulate General of India in Seattle, the press release said. title: Andhra Pradesh urban polls set to become first mid-term test for NDA govt
text: Around one crore voters are eligible to cast their votes in 100 urban local bodies going to polls on Sunday. The electorate accounts for nearly a quarter of the stateâs voters and spans around 60 assembly constituencies, making the outcome politically significant for both the ruling alliance and the opposition Vijayawada : The urban local body elections scheduled for Sunday are set to be the first major political test for the ruling NDA coalition since it came to power with a near sweep in the 2024 assembly elections. More than a civic contest, the polls are being viewed as a mid-term assessment of the Chandrababu Naidu-led NDA govtâs performance over the last two-and-a-half years and an opportunity for the opposition YSRCP to gauge its prospects of a political resurgence. The NDAâs landslide victory in the 2024 elections, when it won 164 of the 175 assembly seats and reduced the YSRCP to just 11 seats, fundamentally altered Andhra Pradesh âs political landscape. The municipal elections will be the first occasion on which the ruling coalition seeks a fresh mandate from voters after assuming office. The significance of the exercise extends beyond the urban local bodies, and rural local body elections are scheduled to follow next. This effectively brings the entire electorate of the state back to the polling booth. Political parties therefore view the municipal polls as an early indicator of public mood ahead of a larger electoral cycle. Around one crore voters are eligible to cast their votes in 100 urban local bodies going to polls on Sunday. The electorate accounts for nearly a quarter of the stateâs voters and spans around 60 assembly constituencies, making the outcome politically significant for both the ruling alliance and the opposition. Although municipal elections are traditionally fought on civic issues such as roads, drainage, sanitation, drinking water and urban infrastructure, the campaign in Andhra Pradesh has largely revolved around broader political narratives. In several towns and cities, parties framed the election as a contest between the NDA govtâs performance and the YSRCPâs bid for a comeback rather than a debate on local governance. The intensity of the campaign, particularly in parts of Rayalaseema, has reflected the high political stakes involved. Reports of clashes and confrontations during the filing of nominations and campaigning underscored the extent to which the elections have transcended civic issues and assumed the character of a larger political battle. For the NDA, retaining dominance in urban local bodies is crucial. A favourable verdict would be seen as public endorsement of govtâs performance and a validation of the coalitionâs governance agenda. The results will also be closely scrutinised for evidence of how effectively votes are being transferred among the alliance partners â TDP, Jana Sena and BJP â at the grassroots level. The elections are equally important for the YSRCP, which is attempting to recover from its worst electoral defeat. Despite the collapse in seat share in the 2024 assembly polls, the party retained roughly 40% of the vote share statewide. YSRCP leaders believe the municipal elections could provide an opportunity to demonstrate that the party continues to enjoy substantial voter support despite its diminished legislative presence. title: US midterms: At Florida rally, Trump vows action against Cuba after Iran war
text: US President Donald Trump. US President Donald Trump has said he will turn his attention to Cuba once the war with Iran is settled, using a campaign rally in Florida to signal further pressure on the communist-run island ahead of the November 3 midterm elections. Speaking for around 90 minutes in Fort Myers on Friday, Trump suggested that US military forces returning from the Iran conflict could stop near Cuba. His remarks came as his administration continues to tighten pressure on the Cuban government. âWe'll have one of them stop about 50 yards off the coast. They'll raise up their hands, and then we're going to send Marco Rubio in to finish up the deal,â Trump said, referring to the US secretary of state, who has played a key role in shaping Washington's Cuba policy. Trump's comments come as the Iran war continues without a clear end in sight. He reiterated that further military action against Iran could be possible as his administration grapples with rising oil prices, which have put Republicans on the defensive ahead of the midterm elections. Trump steps up pressure on Cuba Trump has increasingly made Cuba a target of his foreign policy in his second term, seeking fundamental changes to the country's government. His administration has imposed an oil blockade that has added to the island's economic difficulties, including fuel shortages and power blackouts worsened by ageing infrastructure. In September, Trump called Cuba a âfailed stateâ during his address to the United Nations General Assembly and declared that âFreedom will be coming to Cubaâ. The remarks prompted the Cuban delegation to walk out. On Friday, Secretary of State Marco Rubio also called for change on the island. In a post on X, he urged people seeking a different future for Cuba to work with the CIA, writing that those disappointed with the Cuban government should âcreate the change you desire through a discrete partnership with the CIAâ. He did not provide further details. Trump's latest remarks follow Washington's broader campaign to increase pressure on leftist governments in the region. Earlier this year, the US ousted Venezuela's leader, adding to concerns about the administration's approach towards governments opposed to Washington. UN human rights experts have criticised the US oil blockade against Cuba, describing it as a violation of international law. Rights advocates have also accused the Trump administration of adopting an imperialist approach to foreign policy. Florida rally targets voters ahead of midterms Trump's rally was aimed at boosting the electoral prospects of Florida Republican Representative Byron Donalds, who is running for governor against Democrat David Jolly. Florida is home to a significant Cuban American population, making its voters an important constituency in US elections. Trump won 68% of the Cuban American vote in Florida in the 2024 presidential election. Alongside his remarks on Cuba and Iran, Trump announced plans to spend $250 million to hire at least 5,000 nurses for elder care facilities across the US, appealing to the state's large population of older residents. The speech was the latest in a series of campaign rallies in Republican-friendly areas as the president seeks to support his party ahead of the November 3 congressional elections.
