title: Immigration, economy, US-India ties: What is weighing on Indian-American voters as US heads into midterms
text: Indian-Americans remain predominantly Democratic-leaning, but their voting preferences are more fluid than traditional descriptions of the diaspora might suggest. Indian-Americans may account for only around 1.5% of the US population, but their political preferences are attracting growing attention ahead of the November 3 midterm elections. A community that has traditionally been among the Democratic Partyâs most dependable constituencies is once again moving decisively towards Democrats after a period of growing Republican appeal. Immigration, the domestic economy, international economic policy and the state of US-India relations have all become sources of dissatisfaction with Trump. These concerns have coincided with a broader debate over the place of Indian-Americans in US society, making the political choices confronting the community particularly consequential. Immigration Immigration is one of the most politically sensitive issues for Indian-Americans, many of whom have personal, family or professional connections to the immigration system. Trump's approach to immigration has therefore become an important source of discontent, particularly as his administration's policies affect the broader environment in which immigrant communities live and work. The Carnegie survey found that 64% of Indian-Americans disapproved of Trump's handling of immigration. This dissatisfaction is particularly significant because immigration was one of the areas in which Trump had sought to build support among voters who were traditionally more inclined towards Democrats. The issue also carries a wider significance for Indian-Americans. Immigration policy is not simply about border enforcement or the treatment of undocumented migrants. It touches on questions of opportunity, family stability, professional mobility and the place of immigrant communities in American society. The survey's findings suggest that Trump's immigration agenda has failed to retain the support that Republicans had begun attracting within the Indian-American community. There is, however, an important political distinction. Disapproval of Trump's immigration policies does not automatically translate into unconditional support for Democrats. Indian-Americans may be unhappy with the Republican approach while continuing to have reservations about the Democratic Party's own immigration positions. The economy Economic performance is another major source of dissatisfaction with the Trump administration. For Indian-Americans, as for voters across the United States, the domestic economy is an important measure of presidential performance. The Carnegie survey found that 68% of Indian-Americans disapproved of Trump's handling of domestic economic policy. This assessment covered issues including inflation, taxes and government spending. Economic policy is not a niche concern affecting one section of the community. It is a broad measure of how voters assess the administration's ability to manage their everyday financial circumstances. The economy also complicates the Republican Party's efforts to retain the support it gained among Indian-Americans in 2024. Trump's appeal to some sections of the community was part of a wider shift that narrowed the Democrats' traditional advantage. But dissatisfaction with his administration's economic management has weakened the prospects of converting those gains into lasting political support. Trade and tariffs International economic policy is another area where Trump faces considerable opposition among Indian-Americans. The Carnegie survey found that 70% disapproved of his handling of international economic policy, including trade, tariffs and sanctions. This was the highest disapproval figure among the three broad policy areas examined in the survey. For a community with strong professional, commercial and family connections across national borders, international economic decisions can carry consequences beyond diplomatic disagreements. Trade policy, tariffs and sanctions form part of the wider economic relationship between the United States and the rest of the world. They also influence the environment in which businesses, professionals and international partnerships operate. The finding is particularly important because it suggests that dissatisfaction with Trump is not restricted to domestic economic management or immigration. His administration's approach to the global economy is also facing resistance within a community that has traditionally maintained strong international connections. Republican gains among Indian-Americans in 2024 demonstrated that the community was not immune to Trump's economic and political messaging. But the latest findings indicate that those gains have proved difficult to sustain. US-India relations The state of US-India relations is another issue shaping the political mood among Indian-Americans, although it is important not to overstate its electoral significance. For years, the strengthening of ties between Washington and New Delhi was viewed positively by many in the Indian-American community. The relationship had become an important part of the broader narrative of India's growing international influence and the diaspora's increasing political visibility in the United States. But Trump's second term has brought fresh uncertainty to the relationship. The Carnegie survey found that large majorities of Indian-Americans disapproved of Trump's handling of US-India relations, which had once been a relative strength for him. This is particularly notable because the community's assessment of the president's performance on India has deteriorated alongside its views on immigration and economic policy. However, there is an important caveat. The October 2026 survey does not provide a separate percentage ranking US-India relations among voters' most important election issues. It establishes dissatisfaction with the administration's handling of the relationship, not that foreign policy is necessarily a decisive factor in the congressional vote. The survey, however, notes that Indian-Americans may be concerned about the direction of bilateral ties, but their electoral decisions are not necessarily driven by what happens between Washington and New Delhi. Identity and belonging Beyond conventional policy questions, Indian-Americans are increasingly finding themselves at the centre of a debate about national identity and belonging. The Carnegie report points to an incident that brought these tensions into sharp focus ahead of the midterms. Republican candidate Bo French, running for state office in Texas, posted a photograph of University of Texas students of visibly South Asian origin celebrating their football team's success. His accompanying remark â questioning whether the university's graduation ceremony looked like the photograph â ignited a debate about the place of Indian-Americans in American society. The controversy showed how questions of immigration, identity and belonging can become intertwined. Indian-Americans number fewer than six million and constitute approximately 1.5% of the US population. Yet their growing presence in professional, academic and political life has made them increasingly visible in national debates. The Texas controversy also illustrates how political rhetoric about demographic change can affect communities that have traditionally been regarded as successful examples of immigrant integration. The Carnegie survey's October article does not quantify how much this particular controversy will influence voting decisions. Nevertheless, the debate provides an important backdrop to the midterm elections. For Indian-Americans, the political conversation is not confined to taxation, economic performance or immigration rules. It also concerns how comfortably they feel represented and accepted in the country they call home. The Republican problem Perhaps the most consequential finding of the Carnegie survey is not about any single policy issue but the extent to which Indian-American voters appear to be moving away from Republican candidates. For decades, Indian-Americans have been among the Democratic Party's most reliable constituencies. But the 2024 presidential election demonstrated that this loyalty was not permanent. In 2020, 68% of Indian-American citizens intended to vote for Joe Biden, compared with 22% who supported Trump. Four years later, 62% backed Kamala Harris while 30% favoured Trump. The Republican gains were significant, particularly because they suggested that Trump was making inroads into a community that had traditionally leaned heavily towards Democrats. But the latest Carnegie findings indicate that this momentum has not endured. In the October 2026 survey, 62% of Indian-American citizens said they intended to vote for the Democratic candidate in their congressional district. Only 19% favoured the Republican candidate. Another 12% remained undecided. The Democratic advantage was similarly pronounced in Senate contests. Among respondents in states holding Senate elections, 63% supported the Democratic candidate, compared with 21% backing Republicans. The figures represent a 43-percentage-point Democratic advantage in congressional voting intentions. This is considerably larger than the 32-point margin Harris enjoyed over Trump in 2024. However, the authors caution that the two figures are not directly comparable because one measures congressional voting intentions and the other presidential preferences. Read also | US midterm elections 2026: Why it's a do-or-die fight for Trump & the Democracts - explained in 10 charts The reversal is particularly visible among older Indian-American men, a group that had previously shown increasing openness to Republican candidates. Among men aged 40 and above, Republican support fell to 16% in October, compared with 32% who supported Trump in January 2026. Democratic support among this group rose from 53% to 68%. Younger men have also moved towards Democrats. Among those aged 18-39, 64% now favour Democratic congressional candidates, compared with 23% who support Republicans. Among women, the picture is somewhat more mixed. Younger women remain strongly Democratic, with 58% supporting Democratic congressional candidates and 21% backing Republicans. The findings suggest that the Republican gains among Indian Americans in 2024 have largely been reversed. A Democratic advantage There is, however, another important dimension to the findings: Indian-Americans may be voting Democratic without necessarily identifying themselves as Democrats. The October survey found that 46% of Indian-Americans identified with the Democratic Party, while 19% identified as Republicans and 26% as independents. These figures were virtually unchanged from January 2026. The contrast between party identification and voting intentions is striking. While 46% identify as Democrats, 62% intend to vote for Democratic congressional candidates. This suggests that the party is attracting support beyond its established base. But the motivations behind that support also reveal a degree of political dissatisfaction. Among Indian-Americans intending to vote for Democrats, 65% said their decision was primarily driven by support for the Democratic candidate or party. The remaining 35% said they were motivated primarily by opposition to the Republican candidate or party. Among Republican supporters, the pattern was different. As many as 83% said they were voting primarily to support their candidate or party, while only 17% were motivated by opposition to Democrats. This suggests that negative partisanship â voting against one party rather than necessarily embracing another â plays a more prominent role in Democratic voting intentions among Indian-Americans. For Democrats, this is both an opportunity and a warning. They appear to have recovered considerable electoral ground, but the numbers do not indicate a corresponding strengthening of partisan loyalty. Indian-origin candidates The Indian-American story in the 2026 elections is not just about how the community votes, but also about who is asking for its vote. A growing list of candidates of Indian origin is seeking office across the country, reflecting the community's expanding footprint in American politics. On the Democratic side, sitting Congressmen Ro Khanna, Ami Bera, Suhas Subramanyam and Congresswoman Pramila Jayapal are seeking another term in the House of Representatives. Republican Vivek Ramaswamy, meanwhile, is taking his political ambitions to Ohio, where he is running for governor after winning the party's nomination with Trump's backing. Read also | Indian-American candidates in 2026 US midterms: Key races, profiles, latest polling & what's at stake The contest extends well beyond Washington. Nithya Raman is in the race for Los Angeles mayor, while Pooja Sethi is contesting Texas House District 47, Sandeep Srivastava is running in Texas House District 66 and Pia Dandiya is seeking a seat in Florida's 22nd Congressional District. Their presence on the ballot shows how Indian-origin Americans are increasingly moving from political representation to positions of greater electoral influence. But they are hardly a unified political bloc: their party affiliations, ideologies and political ambitions vary widely. Indian ancestry may be a common thread, but it does not mean a common political playbook. As candidates of Indian origin seek office across the country and voters reassess their political loyalties, the community is increasingly becoming a constituency that neither party can afford to take for granted. title: Gyanesh has to go, PM & Shah next, says Rahul Gandhi at anti-CEC rally
text: Around 50,000 people turned up for INDIA blocâs rally in Delhi on Sunday, according to Delhi Police estimates NEW DELHI: In a Ramlila Maidan packed with protesters and ringing with anti-BJP and anti-CEC slogans Sunday, Congress MP Rahul Gandhi said the opposition will confront the top BJP duo of Narendra Modi and Amit Shah after Gyanesh Kumar's removal as chief election commissioner. The trio was losing sleep over the agitation, he claimed, and said the CEC's exit would be the first step in putting the country back on track. With opposition biggies Congress chief Mallikarjun Kharge, Sonia Gandhi, Akhilesh Yadav, Mamata Banerjee, Tejashwi Yadav, Dipankar Bhattacharya, MA Baby, Farooq Abdullah and Mehbooba Mufti on the dais, leader of opposition in Lok Sabha said the "voice of the people of India" is greater to him than religion, and he will brook no assault on it. Mocking BJP's catchphrase - "Modi kahin nahin jayega" - which was coined in response to Kharge's comment, Rahul said the PM won't be allowed to go anywhere. "You cannot flee... You will stay here and face action." 2024 polls illegal, says Rahul; Modi picking voters: Kharge With a âvote bachao, desh bachaoâ banner forming the backdrop of the dais, the speakers focused on âvote choriâ, repeating allegations about SIR and deletion of around 14 crore voters. Rahul accused the CEC, PM and Shah of suppressing the voice of people through âvote choriâ. While Mamata and Akhilesh said the West Bengal mandate to BJP was âstolenâ, Rahul mentioned the Maharashtra, Haryana, Chhattisgarh, MP and 2024 Lok Sabha polls. He said the 2024 polls were illegal, arguing the difference between NDA and opposition was merely 3%, while 15% of the 2024 voters have been deleted under SIR. âModi is selecting the voters,â Congress chief Kharge said. Led by Kharge, most INDIA bloc members stressed ejecting BJP from office was a must to save democracy, even leading the crowd in âBJP hatao, desh bachaoâ chants. Some reminded the crowd that Ramlila Maidan has been the harbinger of history and change in the past. SP chief Akhilesh called the historic venue the âHaldighati of democracyâ, referring to the battlefield in Rajasthan where Maharana Pratap faced off with the Mughals in 1576, remembered as a symbol of defiant resistance to a powerful empire. Addressing the crowd that had been growing since 9am and remained eager even as main INDIA bloc members came on the dais only by 3pm, Akhilesh, who occupied a key spot with UP polls looming, hit out at Modi, saying, âJo UP se aaye the, woh UP se hi jaayenge (those who came from UP, will go from UP)â. Watch âGyanesh Kumar Is Modiâs Puppetâ: Tejashwi Yadavâs âMahabharataâ Attack At Anti-SIR Rally âThe UP poll results will see off BJP from office in Lucknow and Delhi,â he said, also raising âchanda choriâ in Ayodhya in his speech. Akhilesh warned BJP was constantly trying to steal elections, even blaming SPâs 2022 assembly defeat on voter list manipulation. The SP chief said UP BJP has stated that 1.27 crore votes of Hindus have been deleted in UP. He said the statement seems designed to âput the blame for their upcoming defeat on someone elseâ â touching upon the much-talked about âDelhi vs Lucknowâ faultlines in BJP. Indulging the sloganeering crowd, Rahul said his predictions always come true, and he was now forecasting that CEC Kumar would go to jail. âVote choriâ is no smalltime shoplifting but a ârarest of rare caseâ which qualifies as âtreasonâ, Rahul said. âWithout Gyanesh, Modi would not be PM and Shah would not be HM. He also accused RSS of capturing all institutions, including judiciary and bureaucracy, while âtwo or three people like Ambani and Adani have cornered all the wealthâ. title: Jharkhand tennis association appeals against voting rights to Goa, Rajasthan
text: Pune: The Jharkhand Tennis Association (JTA) has filed an intervening application in the Delhi High Court against the All India Tennis Associationâs decision to promote Goa and Rajasthan from associate to affiliate membership with voting rights during the Annual General Meeting on September 30. The JTA said that it was not against conferring affiliate membership on Goa and Rajasthan itself, but objected to the manner in which was done and that the two state unitsâ voting rights must be suspended until the matter is adjudicated upon by the court. Chintan Parikh, the AITA interim president, however, said that denying the two associations their voting rights would have been âunfairâ. AITA, which is at present governed by an interim committee supervised by an Administrator appointed by the Delhi HC, is scheduled to hold its elections on November 27. In its appeal, the JTA has argued that the matter was not listed on the agenda for the AGM, which was originally supposed to be an Extraordinary General Meeting, and the promotion of Goa and Rajasthan added four votes â two votes for each association â to the electoral college. Given that the election process was already underway and that Parikh was a prospective candidate, the decision without prior notice raised concerns over fairness of the election process, the JTA said in its application. Parikh indeed announced on Sunday (November 1) his decision to contest for president in alliance with the legendary Leander Paes, who currently heads the Bengal association and will stand for vice president. Parikh said that Goa and Rajasthan had completed the mandatory two-year period of associateship to be eligible for affiliate membership and the decision to promote them was approved unanimously by the General Body. âRajasthan and Goa have completed their mandatory period of two years as associated Affiliates. They sent us an application to be come full state affiliates,â Parikh said in a statement to The Times of India. âThe matter was to go to AGM in November. Due to legal provision in the constitution, annual accounts need to be passed in AGM and that too before September 30th. Hence, we decided to convert the September meeting as AGM. âA communication was sent in advance about it to the members. In an EGM only the mentioned agenda can be discussed, while in the AGM any agenda with permission of the Chair can be discussed. Yes, we could have placed the matter in agenda but that does not change the legal position of the matters that can be discussed in AGM. âThere were 28 out of 30 states present. All of them unanimously approved the matter, because it was not a matter with any hidden agenda. âWhat is unanimously approved by the General Body, a lone state who was absent cannot and should not challenge, whether the matter was an agenda item or not. âThe spirit was not to deprive two states of their voting rights until 2030. This would have been very unfair,â he said. With regard to JTAâs specific claim that Parikhâs decision was âaimed at manipulating the elections by attempting to secure favourable votesâ from Goa and Rajasthan, Parikh said: âThey may vote for anybody. They are independent affiliates. They are given the voting power by the General Body and not by the President. It is a foolish hypothesis.â The matter is expected to be heard on November 6. title: Trump escalates attacks on Muslim Senate hopeful, drawing Arab American rebuke
text: US President Donald Trump (left) and Michigan Democratic Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed (right), who is seeking to become America's first Muslim Senator. President Trump intensified attacks on Michigan Democratic Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed at a rally in Port Huron Sunday, calling him a âjihadistâ who was âon the side of the terroristsâ and questioning his loyalty to US. The remarks drew condemnation from a former Trump ally in the Arab American community. Trump said El-Sayed, a former Detroit health official, would âhave to go through a metal detector before heâs allowed to go into Senateâ. He repeatedly invoked the 9/11 attacks and compared blocking El-Sayed from the Senate chamber with passengers fighting hijackers aboard United Flight 93. El-Sayed would become the first Muslim American senator if elected. He has denied any ties to extremist groups and called attacks on his loyalty âshamefulâ. At a Grand Rapids rally later Sunday, he responded to Trumpâs repeated mockery of his name: âI donât even care that he remembers my whole name because he can just go on and call me âsenatorâ after Nov,â El-Sayed said. âI will be Senator Muhammad to you, bro.â Watch Trumpâs âBlonde Beautyâ Moment Backfires? Critics Accuse POTUS Of 'Creepy' Crowd Talk Bishara Bahbah, a founder of Arab Americans for Trump, which helped lead Trumpâs outreach to Arab American voters in 2024, called the comments racist. âThe presidentâs statements are out of line,â he said. âThey are crossing a red line. They are racist.â The organisation has since been renamed Arab Americans for Peace. Bahbah said the remarks were unacceptable to Arab and Muslim communities, including Christian Arabs, and voters would remember them on Nov 3. Trump won Dearborn in 2024, becoming the first Republican presidential candidate since 2000 to carry the city, which has one of the countryâs largest concentrations of Arab Americans. Many voters had opposed the Biden administrationâs handling of the Gaza war. The race between El-Sayed and Republican Mike Rogers to succeed retiring Democratic Senator Gary Peters is among a handful that could determine control of the Senate. With Republicans under pressure over inflation, fuel prices and the Iran war, Trump has portrayed El-Sayed as a threat to US. Trump also declared he had come to Michigan âto keep a jihadist Muslim Brotherhood member from becoming a United States senatorâ. There is no evidence El-Sayed has any affiliation with the Muslim Brotherhood. Republicans have cited a 2012 social media post by his half-sister, Eman Abdelhadi, who wrote that âmy family has long been MBâ and described their motherâs involvement with the group in the early 1970s. El-Sayed was born in the US to Egyptian immigrant parents who divorced when he was young. He was raised by his father, not his biological mother. Rogers questioned El-Sayedâs loyalty during their final general-election debate, asking, âAre you for America, or are you for these terrorist groups overseas?â El-Sayed replied: âIâm proud of our Constitution that guarantees all of us the right to pray as we choose to pray.â Rogers repeated the Muslim Brotherhood allegation before Trumpâs appearance. Trump attacked El-Sayedâs links to streamer Hasan Piker, who appeared with him during the primary campaign. Piker has said âHamas is a thousand times betterâ than Israel, called some Orthodox Jews âinbredâ and said âAmerica deserved 9/11.â El-Sayed has also faced criticism over his rhetoric. After an attack on a Detroit-area synagogue, he said âhurt people hurt peopleâ. The attacker had lost four relatives in an Israeli airstrike on Lebanon a week earlier. El-Sayed later apologised, saying he had not intended to justify the attack. Senator Bernie Sanders, appearing with El-Sayed in Grand Rapids, accused Trump and his allies of using Islamophobia because they had ânothing to sayâ about healthcare, housing and income inequality. âAll they can do is foment hatred and divisiveness,â he said. title: $12 billion battle for US Congress: Musk, Soros and other billionaires pour in cash
text: The 2026 midterm elections in the U.S. are on track to raise a staggering $12 billion, marking the most expensive campaign in history. The 2026 US midterm election campaign is expected to become the most expensive in the country's history, with total spending projected to reach nearly $12 billion, according to Opensecrets, an independent organisation that monitors campaign finances. A significant share of the expenditure is being driven by outside political groups, particularly super political action committees (Super PACs), which are investing heavily in key electoral contests ahead of the November 3 election. Billionaire businessman Elon Musk has emerged as the biggest individual donor, contributing nearly half a billion dollars to support republican candidates. Much of his spending has focused on Texas, where several of his companies are headquartered. BBC Verify has examined the campaign finance figures to assess how much has been spent, who is funding the candidates and where the money is going. The president says he has held 31 rallies over 27 days, along with many tele-rallies, a term that's been used recently in US media to describe when a politician phones into a rally. How much money has been spent? US campaign finance regulations place limits on the amount individuals, political parties and traditional political action committees (PACs) can contribute directly to candidates. However, Super PACs can accept unlimited donations from individuals, corporations, labour unions and other political committees. Although they cannot donate directly to candidates, they can independently spend money to support or oppose them. The latest filings with the federal election commission (FEC), covering spending up to mid-October, show that more than $9.5 billion had already been spent during the current election cycle. PACs and Super PACs accounted for more than half of the expenditure, contributing approximately $5.5 billion. Their spending almost doubled over the preceding couple of months. Candidates, political parties and outside organisations are required to report their expenditure to the FEC. However, the complete figures will only become available after the elections. Based on spending patterns from previous election cycles, Opensecrets estimates that the final amount could reach $11.9 billion. This would represent an increase of around 30% compared with the 2022 midterm elections. Who are the biggest political donors? According to the liberal-leaning Brennan Center for Justice, the 40 largest donors had contributed a combined $2.4 billion by October 14, marking a record amount for this stage of a midterm election cycle. Michael Beckel, a US campaign finance expert, said the 2026 elections had broken spending records, with an increasing proportion of the money coming from wealthy individuals and organisations. Apart from individual contributions, organisations also provide substantial funding to PACs. Geosor Corp and the Fund for Policy Reform, both established by billionaire financier George Soros, have together donated $102 million to liberal groups. Former New York City mayor and businessman Michael Bloomberg has been another major democratic donor, contributing more than $60 million. On the Republican side, several wealthy contributors have made large donations. These include Jeff Yass, head of a major trading firm, and business supply company owners Richard and Elizabeth Uihlein, who have collectively contributed more than $100 million to Republican causes during the campaign, according to FEC records. Musk, however, remains the biggest individual contributor, having donated nearly $500 million as of October. A large portion of his contributions has gone to America PAC, a Super PAC he established in 2024, as well as the republican-aligned senate leadership fund. Much of the funding has been directed towards the Texas Senate contest, where republican candidate Ken Paxton is facing democrat James Talarico. America PAC has invested more than $45 million in the Texas race. It has also allocated approximately $10 million each to senate contests in Michigan and Ohio. The cryptocurrency industry has also emerged as a significant contributor this election cycle. Brendan J Glavin of Opensecrets said ripple and coinbase had together donated $63 million to Super PACs seeking to advance the interests of the crypto sector. Where is the campaign money being spent? Political campaigns and outside groups use their funds for a range of activities, including recruiting workers for grassroots voter outreach, organising rallies and other campaign events, and conducting internal opinion polls. However, advertising accounts for the largest share of campaign expenditure, particularly television commercials. According to advertising tracking firm AdImpact, $11.15 billion had been spent on political advertising by the end of October. Beckel said traditional broadcast television continued to receive the largest share of advertising expenditure, although spending on digital platforms was also increasing. AdImpact's tracking showed that the biggest advertising investments were concentrated in Senate contests in Michigan, Texas and Ohio, followed by Iowa and Maine. You use AI every day. title: HC admits BJP petition challenging Narla MLAâs election
text: Orissa high court Cuttack : Orissa high court has kept alive a legal challenge to the 2024 election of Narla MLA Manorama Mohanty of BJD, admitting a petition by BJP candidate Aniruddha Pradhan seeking to take over the election case withdrawn by former Congress candidate Bhakta Charan Das. Justice Sashikanta Mishra, while hearing Pradhanâs petition on Oct 30, treated service of notice on Mohanty as sufficient after she reportedly refused to accept it. âOffice note indicates that notice sent to the respondent (Manorama Mohanty) was refused. Hence, the same is treated as sufficient. List this matter on 11.11.2026,â the judge ordered. Pradhan, who finished third in the 2024 Assembly election from Narla, has sought permission to substitute himself as the petitioner in place of Das, who had challenged Mohantyâs election. The court had issued notice to the sitting BJD MLA on Aug 19. The BJP candidate has questioned the manner in which Das was allowed to withdraw his election petition, alleging that mandatory procedures under the Representation of the People Act, 1951, were not followed. He contended that no gazette notification, required under Sections 109(2), 110(3)(b) and 111 of the Act, was published following the withdrawal. Pradhan argued that the omission deprived him and other voters of an opportunity to object to the withdrawal or seek substitution. He relied on Section 110(3)(c), which allows a candidate who contested the election to seek substitution in place of a petitioner withdrawing an election challenge. He has also sought continuation of the original allegations against Mohanty, particularly that her nomination papers were improperly accepted because of alleged misinformation or suppression of material particulars about her educational qualification in the election affidavit. Pradhan claimed oral and documentary evidence had already been placed before the court and said the issue involved public interest. Das, who is also Odisha Pradesh Congress Committee president and a former MP, had lost the Narla election to Mohanty by 5,205 votes. His election petition had reached the evidence stage, with two witnesses examined, before he sought withdrawal on March 30 following instructions from the partyâs central leadership. Justice Mishra allowed the withdrawal the same day. title: Trump says Bolsonaro can remain in US indefinitely, calls Brazil election a 'disgrace'
text: Trump made the remarks while speaking to reporters at a Halloween party at his Mar-a-Lago club in Florida. US President Donald Trump has said Brazilian politician Flavio Bolsonaro can remain in the United States for as long as he wishes, signalling that tensions between Washington and Brasilia could continue despite recent diplomatic contact between the two countries. Trump made the remarks while speaking to reporters at a Halloween party at his Mar-a-Lago club in Florida on Saturday. He also questioned the outcome of Brazil's presidential election, in which Bolsonaro lost to incumbent Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva. Watch 'U.S. Role In Bolsonaro Escape?': Marco Rubio Cornered After Brazil Deals Election Blow To Trump "He can stay here as long as he wants," Trump was qutoed as saying by news agency Reuters. "In my opinion, the election was a disgrace." Bolsonaro left Brazil after his electoral defeat, despite having led in several opinion polls. His departure came after a Brazilian Supreme Court justice ordered his passport revoked. He is also facing two federal money-laundering investigations, while police in Brazil had considered him a flight risk. Bolsonaro's stay in US raises questions Bolsonaro entered the United States under humanitarian parole, Reuters had previously reported. The immigration status is generally granted for a limited period, typically one year. Trump's latest remarks suggest he is willing to let Bolsonaro remain in the country beyond that period. However, the US President said he had no plans to meet the Brazilian politician, who has described himself as Brazil's rightful leader. A US official and another person familiar with the matter told Reuters that Trump currently has no plans to support Bolsonaro's political ambitions, despite allowing him to enter the United States. US and Brazil maintain diplomatic contact The comments came as US Secretary of State Marco Rubio held talks with Brazilian Foreign Minister Mauro Vieira on the sidelines of a Group of 20 meeting in Atlanta on Saturday. Rubio said the two had spoken and were expected to meet again in France next month during a G7 foreign ministers' summit. Brazil is expected to attend the meeting as an observer. The diplomatic engagement had raised the possibility of improved relations between the two countries, even as Trump's comments on Bolsonaro pointed to continued political differences. Rubio also said the US government "was not involved directly in any of the moves" that led to Bolsonaro's departure from Brazil earlier this week. However, Reuters and other media organisations have reported that Jason Miller, a White House official, helped arrange the Brazilian politician's journey to the US. Political turmoil in Bolsonaro family Flavio Bolsonaro is the son of former Brazilian president Jair Bolsonaro, who is currently in prison in Brazil for plotting a coup after losing his re-election bid in 2022. Lula, who defeated Jair Bolsonaro in that election, also has a history of legal troubles. He spent 17 months in prison in 2018 and 2019 on corruption charges, which were later annulled. The developments come amid continuing political tensions in Brazil and uncertainty over how Flavio Bolsonaro's presence in the US could affect relations between the two countries. title: US midterm elections 2026: What they are, why they matter and when results will be out
text: US midterms voting to be conducted on November 3 The US midterm elections are nationwide elections held every two years, halfway through a president's four-year term. This year's elections will take place on Wednesday (early Thursday, as per Indian time) with voters choosing members of Congress as well as several state and local officials. Unlike presidential elections, midterms do not decide who occupies the White House. Instead, they determine which party controls Congress for the next two years, making them a crucial test of President Donald Trump's political standing and his ability to push through his agenda. What are the US midterm elections? The US Congress has two chambers, the House of Representatives and the Senate, and midterm elections determine the composition of both. All 435 seats in the House are contested every two years, as members serve two-year terms. In the Senate, where members serve six-year terms, roughly one-third of the 100 seats come up for election every two years. This time, 35 Senate seats, including two special-election contests, are at stake. Alongside congressional races, voters in several states will also elect governors and other state and local officials. Watch Indian-Americans Give Republicans A 4:1 Cash Edge With $15.8 Million Bet On Trump In U.S Midterms What is at stake in the 2026 midterms? Republicans currently hold narrow majorities in both chambers of Congress. The 435-member House has 218 Republicans, 214 Democrats, one independent who caucuses with Republicans and two vacant seats. A party needs 218 seats for a majority. Meanwhile, the Senate has 53 Republicans and 47 Democrats and allied independents, with 51 seats required for a majority. Democrats need a net gain of four seats in each chamber to take control of both. Chances of Democrats (prediction) The outcome could therefore hinge on a small number of closely contested races. Who might win? Why do the midterms matter for Trump? The party controlling Congress has considerable influence over the president's ability to govern. Congress passes legislation, approves government spending and oversees the executive branch. The Senate also confirms presidential nominees to key government positions, including federal judges and senior administration officials. If Democrats take control of either chamber, they could make it harder for Trump to pass legislation, influence budget negotiations and intensify congressional scrutiny of his administration through hearings and investigations. A Democratic majority in the House could also revive discussions of impeachment, although impeachment by itself would not remove the president from office. Removal requires a two-thirds vote in the Senate. Trump would remain president regardless of the election outcome. He would retain his executive powers and the ability to veto legislation, but a divided Congress could significantly constrain his domestic agenda. The stakes extend well beyond Capitol Hill What issues are shaping the vote? The cost of living, inflation, immigration and the economy are among the major concerns for voters. Foreign policy, including the war involving Iran, is also part of the political debate. Trump's approval ratings and public perceptions of his administration's performance are likely to influence the results. Midterm elections are often viewed as a referendum on the sitting president, with the party in the White House frequently losing congressional seats. Disputes over voting rules, election administration and the drawing of congressional district boundaries have also become contentious issues. When will voting take place and when will results come? Voting will take place on Tuesday, November 3, across the United States. Polling hours vary by state, and there is no single nationwide closing time. The first polling stations in parts of Indiana and Kentucky are scheduled to close at 6 pm Eastern Time, which is around 4.30 am on November 4 as per Indian Standard Time. Results are expected to emerge through the night, but close contests may take longer to resolve. Election officials must count outstanding ballots, verify results and, where necessary, conduct recounts or deal with legal challenges. News organisations may project winners before every ballot has been counted. Such projections are not official results. State election authorities certify the final results, a process that can take days or weeks. The House is where the battle for congressional control is expected to be particularly intense. Where can you check the results? US Election Assistance Commission (EAC): A federal agency that provides election information and links to official state election offices. USA.gov: The US government's official portal, which directs users to state websites for election results and voting information. Federal Election Commission (FEC): The federal agency responsible for campaign finance oversight. It provides information on federal elections but does not publish live results or certify current election outcomes. State election offices remain the primary source for official results, including vote counts, recounts and final certification. What happens if an election result is contested? A close result can lead to recounts, court challenges and disputes over ballot validity. State officials handle the initial counting and certification process, but the US Constitution gives the House and Senate the power to judge the elections, returns and qualifications of their own members. A candidate or sitting member can challenge a congressional election result. In the House, such disputes are referred to the House Administration Committee, while Senate challenges go to the Senate Rules Committee. The respective chamber ultimately decides whether a member should be seated. This power could become significant if a handful of unresolved races determine which party controls Congress. Any House contests still unresolved when the new Congress convenes in January would be considered by the incoming House. The process can become politically contentious, particularly when party control is at stake. A disputed result may also leave a seat vacant while legal or congressional proceedings continue. title: Indian-American Texas student says he's 'politically homeless' after facing backlash for voting for Democrat: 'My biggest concern is....'
text: 21-year-old Indian-American Vasant Bhatt says his future votes are likely to be for the Democrats. 21-year-old Vasant Bhatt announced on social media that despite identifying with conservative politics so far, he voted for Democrat James Talarico in the Texas election against Republican candidate Ken Paxton to reject anti-India hatred in his state and in the US. Though he is a second-generation Indian-American, he was asked to leave the US after his post went viral. The Political Science student of the University of Houston was removed from Campus Reform's correspondent program as an apparent fallout but he said he won't retract his beliefs and neither would he abandon his community. MAGA had a problem with Bhatt putting Indian first in his hyphenated Indian-American identity and still considering Indian-American as his community. title: US midterms 2026: Meet Suhas Subramanyam, Indian-origin Democrat who served as advisor to Barack Obama
text: Suhas Subramanyam of Virginia is among several Indian-origin candidates contesting the US midterm elections on November 3. The Democrat is seeking re-election from Virginiaâs 10th Congressional District, where he faces Republican challenger Dave Beckwith, a 30-year veteran of the US Air Force. A lawyer by profession, Subramanyam served as a White House policy advisor during Barack Obamaâs presidency. Family life Born in Virginia in 1979, Subramanyam is the son of Indian immigrants. His mother, a Bengaluru native, moved to the US to join his father, who grew up in Chennai and Secunderabad, and to pursue higher education. Subramanyam is married to Miranda Pena Subramanyam, and the couple have two daughters. The family lives in Loudoun County, Virginia. Education and pre-political career Subramanyam holds a bachelorâs degree from Tulane University and a Juris Doctor (J.D.) from Northwestern Universityâs Pritzker School of Law. Thereafter, he worked as White House technology policy advisor under Obama. After his stint at the White House, Subramanyam launched a small business in Loudoun County and volunteered as an emergency medical technician (EMT) and firefighter. Political career Subramanyam was first elected to the Virginia House of Delegates, where he served from 2019 to 2023, before joining the Virginia State Senate in 2023, serving until 2024. During his time in the state legislature, he passed legislation aimed at lowering tolls, utility bills and prescription drug costs. He also co-founded a caucus focused on bipartisanship and helped pass bipartisan bills on K-12 education, tax cuts and gun safety. Subramanyam was elected to represent Virginiaâs 10th Congressional District in 2024, succeeding retiring Democratic incumbent Jennifer Wexton. He defeated Republican candidate Mike Clancy, securing 215,131 votes against Clancyâs 196,343. Political position Subramanyam has accused US President Donald Trumpâs Republican administration of driving up costs and undermining healthcare and the federal workforce. He has also continued to raise issues affecting Indian professionals, including lengthy green card backlogs and structural challenges with the H-1B visa programme. After US law enforcement foiled an alleged plot to vandalise a Hindu temple in Illinois earlier this month, Subramanyam called on lawmakers from both parties to condemn what he described as rising anti-Indian hostility, hate speech and discrimination. âEvery American deserves to practice their faith without fear of violence. title: $445 million and counting: Elon Musk goes all in for Republicans ahead of US midterms
text: US President Donald Trump and Tesla and SpaceX CEO Elon Musk Elon Musk has contributed more than $445 million to political groups during the current US election cycle, emerging as one of the biggest-ever donors to super political action committees (super PACs), according to a report. Muskâs donations have helped widen the Republican Partyâs fundraising advantage ahead of the November midterm elections, which are projected to be the most expensive elections ever in the US. Watch 'New Round Of Heavy Strikes':Trumpâs Post-Midterm Iran Plan Revealed, Gulf Allies Put On ALERT Federal Election Commission (FEC) filings show Musk contributed $77 million to America PAC in the first two weeks of October. Since relaunching the political group in July, he has given it $355 million, averaging $3.6 million a day, Bloomberg reported. The Republican Party, its congressional super PACs and US president Donald Trumpâs MAGA Inc. had raised $2.1 billion through October 14, compared with $1.4 billion raised by corresponding Democratic committees. Muskâs political spending has supported Republican candidates across several contests, including the Texas Senate race involving Attorney General Ken Paxton and Democratic candidate James Talarico. His America PAC has also spent money on voter outreach through canvassing, digital media, text messages and printed material. Talaricoâs campaign has criticised the billionaireâs financial influence. An advertisement released by the campaign said: âHe knows that if his millions drag the most corrupt politician in Texas across the finish line, Ken Paxton will owe him everything. So letâs remind Elon: Texas is not for sale.â On Friday, Trump said on Truth Social he planned to spend $400 million to $500 million by election day, then less than two weeks away. Filings show $225 million of recent spending went through super PACs No Going Back and Safety & Affordability. Meanwhile, Reuters reported that Republican megadonors, including Stephen Wynn, Stephen Schwarzman and Diane Hendricks, contributed millions to Trump-aligned MAGA Inc., which had raised roughly $450 million this cycle and held $164 million in available cash. What are the US election contribution limits? US federal election law sets limits on how much individuals and political committees can contribute directly to candidates and certain political organisations. However, super PACs operate under different rules and can accept unlimited contributions. This distinction helps explain how Musk can give hundreds of millions of dollars to political groups despite restrictions on direct donations to candidates. According to the US Federal Election Commissionâs (FEC) limits for the 2025â2026 election cycle, individuals can contribute up to $3,500 per election to a federal candidate. The limit applies separately to each election, so the primary and general elections have separate limits. Individuals can contribute up to $5,000 per year to a conventional political action committee (PAC), $10,000 annually in combined contributions to state, district and local party committees, and $44,300 per year to each national party committee. They can also contribute up to $132,900 per year to each eligible additional national party account, earmarked for specific expenses such as presidential nominating conventions, election recounts and legal proceedings and party headquarters buildings, under the Federal Election Commissionâs 2025â2026 limits. Super PACs, formally known as independent-expenditure-only committees, can accept unlimited contributions from individuals, corporations, labour organisations and other political committees to fund independent political spending. However, they cannot contribute directly to federal candidates, and their spending must not be coordinated with candidatesâ campaigns. Why Muskâs donations matter Musk has substantial business interests in companies including Tesla and SpaceX, which are subject to federal regulation. Bloomberg reported that his political spending could also influence the balance of power in Congress, particularly if Democrats win control of the House of Representatives. You use AI every day. title: Blue wave meets red flag: On cusp of big win, Democrats face internal sabotage
text: Rep. Haley Stevens (AP Photo) TOI Correspondent From Washington: Just when Democrats in America were beginning to entertain thoughts of a blue wave, possibly even a blue tsunami, along came Haley Stevens to remind them that nobody is quite as capable of complicating Democratic fortunes as a Democrat. In an extraordinary convulsion barely 48 hours before Tuesday's midterm elections, the Democratic Michigan congresswoman, who lost a bitter party primary (inner party election) to progressive Abdul El-Sayed, crossed the political aisle to endorse his Republican opponent, Mike Rogers, in what would be called a last minute âdefectionâ in Indian political parlance. The immediate political damage is difficult to quantify, but the optics and the timing â coming just when many polls are showing a Republican rout â could hardly be worse for Democrats, who are trying to persuade voters that they are united and ready to take back control of Washington. Instead, one of their own has provided Republicans with a ready-made advertisement for Democratic disarray. MAGA boss Donald Trump immediately jumped on the break, praising her âbravery. â The Stevens-El-Sayed rupture had been simmering since a bitter August primary,, which El-Sayed won by less than one percent. It was not simply a case of a disappointed politician nursing wounded ambitions within the party; the two represent sharply different constituencies and political instincts, particularly over Israel and the Gaza war. Stevens, a staunch supporter of Israel, was bankrolled by the so-called âJewish lobby.â El-Sayed, a progressive son of Egyptian immigrants, campaigned on a more critical position towards Israeli policy and US military support for Israel. The primary exposed fault lines between pro-Israel Dems and the party's vocal progressive wing, and the schism is now threatening to play out nationally, undercutting polls pointing to a big win. Stevens initially endorsed El-Sayed after losing -- albeit without much enthusiasm -- but the truce was always more a marriage of political convenience than a true reconciliation. The trigger for the final explosion was an ad by El-Sayed supporters linking U.S financial support for Israel to the rising cost of groceries. Stevens considered the advertisement antisemitic and demanded that El-Sayed disavow it. He eventually rejected the ad's contents, but the dispute had gone personal by then, with El Sayed, likely emboldened by polls showing he was leading by 10+ points, torching a planned joint church appearance with Stevens and asking her to take a walk. She walked -- over to Republican candidate Mike Rogers. Such election-eve defections being rare in America, Democratic leaders were aghast, even as Trump and his flock welcomed her. Democratic Party boss and NY Senator Chuck Schumer, who had backed Stevens during the primary, called her decision a "despicable betrayal," while furious party flacks like James Carville used gross reproductive metaphors to warn her that Republicans would use her and discard. Democratic partisans are still hoping that a NYT/Siena poll showing the party leading in all seven crucial Senate -- five of them by +5 percent â--can withstand the last minute Stephens torpedo. The numbers are unbelievable for Dems, particularly in Kansas and Texas, where they have not won a Senate seat in decades. Even allowing for polling error, the geographical breadth of the Democratic advantage suggests a national political environment hostile to Republicans. Still, the Dem are nervous, and the feeling is not entirely irrational. The party has repeatedly discovered that the electorate it sees in surveys is not necessarily the one that turns up at polling stations. Donald Trump's political career has been built, in considerable measure, on voters who are difficult for traditional polling models to capture: less politically engaged people, rural and small-town voters, working-class whites, and those who are reluctant to identify openly with MAGA and some of its nativist and racist agenda. The 2016 election remains the defining example. Hillary Clinton's 97 percent winning certainty evaporated in the industrial Midwest and boondocks America, where Trump mobilised voters who had been insufficiently represented in polling samples and turnout assumptions. Even in 2024, Dems were surprised by the extent of Trump's support among working-class voters, including sections of the electorate that had previously been part of their coalition. This is the so-called hidden Trump voter: somebody who may not be particularly enthusiastic about the Republican Party, may not even like Trump personally, but will turn up to vote Republican when sufficiently motivated. There is another complication: Midterm elections generally have a different electorate from presidential contests. Older, more habitual voters tend to dominate, while younger and less politically engaged voters are more likely to stay home. That will favour Republicans if the Democratic advantage in current surveys â captured by a range of pollsters from Nate Silver to NYT, from Emerson College to Marist University â does not translate into actual turnout. Republicans, meanwhile, have their own problems. Trump's economic message of unprecedented prosperity is difficult to reconcile with voters worried about grocery bills, tariffs and household expenses. His rallies, which many now see as entertainment, may fill arenas but they do not necessarily fill ballot boxes. The most important question on Tuesday will therefore not be whether Democrats are ahead in the polls, which they are. It will be whether their lead survives the transition from the pollster's carefully constructed likely-voter sample to the rather less predictable business of actually voting. You use AI every day. title: Fired US general admits leaking classified Iran, Ukraine information to journalists: Report
text: File photo: Fired Lt Gen Brett Sylvia The US Army general fired by defence secretary Pete Hegseth admitted to leaking classified information about the wars in Iran and Ukraine to journalists over a period of roughly a year, according to an internal investigation report reviewed by Axios. Lt Gen Brett Sylvia, who headed the Joint Chiefs of Staffâs Strategy, Plans and Policy Directorate, known as the J5, acknowledged sharing classified information with two reporters from separate media outlets, according to the report. A US official told Axios that Sylvia made the admissions on video after failing multiple polygraph tests during the investigation. Sylvia was dismissed by Hegseth on Wednesday over what the Pentagon described as severe misconduct. The investigation, which has been referred to the Department of Justice for further action, remains ongoing. According to the report, the disclosures began as early as June 2025 and continued after the Pentagon tightened restrictions on media access. Sylvia allegedly communicated with reporters through the encrypted messaging application Signal and also met one journalist in person at a Silver Diner in Arlington, Virginia. The report said the diner meeting took place after the journalistâs access to the Pentagon had been revoked. During the meeting, Sylvia relied on notes he had made while reviewing a classified report to orally share information about US assistance to Ukraine. The journalist was working on a book and met Sylvia twice, the report said. Sylvia did not coordinate the meetings with the Pentagonâs public affairs office or seek clearance before sharing the information. Investigation points to deleted messages The investigation also raised questions about Sylviaâs handling of communications with one of the reporters. According to the report, he received a Signal message sometime in June or July that he believed concerned Iran. Sylvia said he could not recall its precise contents and claimed he had deleted the message, believing he had accidentally erased the entire conversation thread. This also removed Signal messages and calls that could otherwise have been recovered from his personal phone. US officials suspect Sylvia deliberately deleted the communications and presented the action as accidental. The report also said he admitted to being one of 20 officials cited in a media story critical of Pentagon leadership. Another US official told Axios that Acting Army Secretary Adam Telle and his office had lobbied the Joint Staff to issue a statement supporting Sylvia in an effort to limit the damage from any future allegations of leaks. The Joint Staff later withdrew the statement after someone in the Defence Department informed it of the reasons behind Sylviaâs dismissal. US president Donald Trump, asked about the firing on Thursday, said Sylvia had âbig problemsâ and that the administration was âvery much looking for leakersâ. Trump appeared to refer to Sylvia using female pronouns. Separately to the Axios report, a defence department official also confirmed to Al Jazeera that Sylvia was under investigation for leaking classified information concerning the Iran war, Russiaâs war against Ukraine and other matters. The official said he had failed three polygraph tests and accused him of putting national security at risk. The official also stressed that Sylvia was not a central planner for the Iran war, saying that responsibility rested with Centcom and its commander, Adm Brad Cooper. Hegsethâs wider crackdown on leaks Sylviaâs dismissal is the latest action in Hegsethâs campaign against unauthorised disclosures to the media. In July, the Pentagon announced a joint task force with the Justice Department to identify leakers and directed its Office of General Counsel to prioritise prosecutions over the unauthorised release of classified information. The Pentagon had also introduced restrictive rules governing journalistsâ access and reporting in October 2025, prompting several news organisations and defence reporters to surrender their press credentials. Sylvia is the second officer to be removed from the J5 position under Hegseth. His predecessor, Lt Gen Joseph McGee, was forced into retirement in October last year. No immediate replacement has been named for Sylvia, according to an official cited by The Associated Press. You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

title: Can the man Trump called a 'jihadist' become America's first Muslim senator?
text: US President Donald Trump (left) and Michigan Democratic Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed (right), who is seeking to become America's first Muslim Senator. NEW DELHI: With just over a week left for the US midterm elections, a Senate race in Michigan has drawn national attention. US President Donald Trump unleashed a series of attacks on Democratic Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed, calling him a "jihadist" and accusing him of having links to extremist groups. El-Sayed is seeking to become America's first Muslim senator in the November 3 midterm elections. At a campaign rally in Port Huron, Trump called El-Sayed a "jihadist" who was "on the side of the terrorists" and claimed he would "have to go through a metal detector before he's allowed to go into the Senate." Trump also referred to the September 11, 2001, terrorist attacks, comparing efforts to stop El-Sayed from entering the Senate with the passengers who fought back against hijackers aboard United Airlines Flight 93. Watch Trump Snaps Back At Russia Sanctions Critics, Defends Moscow Oil Relief Amid Backlash The president accused El-Sayed of having links to the Muslim Brotherhood and wanting to impose sharia law. However, no evidence has been presented linking El-Sayed to the organisation, and he has repeatedly denied the allegations. Who is Abdul El-Sayed? Born in the United States to Egyptian immigrant parents, El-Sayed is a physician and epidemiologist who previously served as Detroit's health director. He unsuccessfully contested Michigan's Democratic gubernatorial primary in 2018 before winning the party's Senate nomination in August 2026. His campaign focuses on healthcare, affordable housing and economic inequality. He has also criticised US military assistance to Israel. What has El-Sayed said? Responding to Trump at a rally in Grand Rapids on Sunday, El-Sayed accused the president of using his name and religion to distract voters from economic concerns. "They think that by pointing at my name and my faith, that somehow you're going to ignore the fact that you can't afford your gas or your groceries, can't see a doctor," he said. El-Sayed also responded to Trump's repeated use of his middle name. "I don't even care that he remembers my whole name because he can just go on and call me 'senator' after November," he said. "I will be Senator Muhammad to you, bro." His Republican opponent, Mike Rogers, has also questioned his loyalty to the United States. "Are you for America, or are you for these terrorist groups overseas?" Rogers asked during a debate. El-Sayed called the question "shameful", adding: "I'm proud of our Constitution that guarantees all of us the right to pray as we choose to pray." Trump's remarks also drew criticism from Bishara Bahbah, a founder of Arab Americans for Trump, a group that supported the president's outreach to Arab American voters in 2024. "The president's statements are out of line," Bahbah said. "They are crossing a red line. They are racist." Can El-Sayed win the Michigan Senate race? El-Sayed faces Republican Mike Rogers, a former congressman, in the November 3 election for the seat being vacated by Democratic Senator Gary Peters. The contest is closely fought. According to the RealClearPolling average of surveys conducted between September 24 and October 22, El-Sayed was ahead of Rogers by 47.9% to 46%, a difference of 1.9 percentage points. Former President Barack Obama campaigned for El-Sayed in Michigan on Saturday, while Senator Bernie Sanders has also backed his candidacy. Michigan is an important state in the battle for control of the US Senate. Republicans have not won a Senate election in the state for more than three decades. The state also has a large Arab American population, particularly in Dearborn, which Trump won in 2024 amid dissatisfaction with the Biden administration's handling of the Gaza war. If El-Sayed wins on November 3, he will become the first Muslim elected to the US Senate. You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

title: Hackers disrupt US election watchdogâs filing system days before midterm polls
text: The US Federal Election Commission (FEC) has temporarily shut down its electronic filing system following a suspected hacking attempt. The outage occurred on Monday night, 26 October 2026, just one week before the November 3 midterm elections The US Federal Election Commissionâs (FEC) electronic filing system was taken offline after an attempted cyberattack, disrupting campaign finance disclosures a week before the November 3 midterm elections, Reuters reported, citing an email sent to campaign compliance firms. The outage has prevented political organisations from submitting mandatory 24-hour and 48-hour spending reports, which provide details of campaign expenditure on specific races. The disruption comes as political groups and super PACs spend record amounts in the final days of the campaign. In a statement, the FEC said, "At this time, the FEC's electronic filing system is currently offline and our IT staff are actively working to restore service." An FEC electronic filings officer said in an email to campaign compliance firms on Monday night, "We have a bad actor attempting to breach FEC systems. As a result, weâve had to temporarily shut down our web-facing services," Reuters reported. The agency later said the issue had been identified and a fix was being implemented. However, its filing system remained offline, while users could still search the website for previously filed reports. Steven Mele, president and CEO of political finance compliance firm MBA Consulting Group, said he had never seen such an incident in 26 years. The FEC tracks campaign spending by candidates and political committees but does not administer elections. The disruption is therefore not expected to affect votersâ ability to cast their ballots. Campaign spending reaches record levels The outage comes as the November 3 midterm elections have become the most expensive US election in history, with around $11.21 billion spent on advertising and future reservations so far, according to political advertising tracker AdImpact. The figure surpasses the $11.2 billion spent across all races in the 2024 elections, including $3.2 billion on the presidential contest between Donald Trump and Kamala Harris. Super PACs, which can accept unlimited contributions from wealthy individuals and corporations and spend heavily on campaigns, are driving much of the expenditure. Dark money groups are also spending large sums in the final stretch. Brendan Glavin, research director at nonpartisan campaign watchdog OpenSecrets, said super PACs and dark money groups had spent an average of more than $50 million a day over the previous week. More than $250 million in spending was reported on October 20 alone, he said. "It's a big deal," Glavin said of the outage, which has left voters without timely access to the latest spending disclosures. "These are the key reports that tell us what is happening," he said. "In the last days of the election this is the only way for us to keep track of where the money's being spent" and who's spending it. Midterms to decide control of Congress The November 3 elections will determine whether Trumpâs Republican Party retains its majorities in Congress for the next two years. All 435 seats in the House of Representatives and around one-third of the Senate seats are being contested. The Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency and the FBI referred questions about the cyber incident to the FEC. The agency did not immediately respond to Reutersâ request for comment. The FECâs filing system had been down since around 10pm ET on Monday, according to a status notice posted on its website. A later update on Tuesday said the issue had been identified and a fix was being implemented, although the system remained offline. You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

title: 'Nobody told me..that's very confusing': Indian man Kamlesh Shah charged with election fraud in US says he didn't know he was not supposed to vote
text: Indian man Kamlesh Shah charged with voter fraud in California says nobody told him that he was not allowed to vote in US elections. 67-year-old Kamlesh Navnitlal Shah, a retired dentist from California, said he had no idea that he was not supposed to vote in the 2024 election, as he was a permanent resident but not a citizen. He has now been charged with fraudulently registering to vote in US elections. After his name came up in the list of foreign nationals who voted in the election in California, he said he was scared as he was not aware of the situation. Dr Shah said he met an accident five to six years ago and was in a coma for six months, and can hardly talk or walk. Apart from Shah, another Indian on the list is 30-year-old Amandeep Kaur, a resident of Rancho Palos Verdes. According to the law enforcement record, Kaur is seeking to become a US citizen, and fraudulently registered to vote in December 2022 and then voted in the November 2024 US election. Shah said he went to the community center "to vote with my blind roommate". He said his was asked to produce his ID. "I showed them the ID and my Social Security card. They did something...I don't remember...it was a long time ago. They gave me the paperwork to vote. I thought I was registering to vote. I didn't know about my pending citizenship. I thought I must be a citizen. I had no idea I wasn't," Shah said, adding that nobody told him that he was not a citizen and was not supposed to vote. What is 'Operation Protect the Vote'? The administration said Operation Protect the Vote is a coordinated effort among all four California-based US Attorney's offices to combat and root out fraud in US elections. 11 foreign nationals among 28 total charged were arrested for voter fraud. All these 28 foreign nationals have Green cards but they are not US citizens and no one except US citizens are allowed to vote in US elections. The criminal charges include making false statements in a naturalization application and some of the defendants also are charged with fraudulent voter registration. Both charges are felonies that carry a maximum penalty of five years in federal prison. On October 13, the federal government provided a list of these individuals to California to ensure that their vote-by-mail ballots were set aside until these individualsâ citizenship status could be confirmed. California declined to assist the federal government in setting aside their ballots, prompting a lawsuit by the United States that seeks a court order to prevent the unlawful dilution of American citizensâ votes and to uphold the integrity of our elections. âEvery illegal vote cancels out the vote of a lawful American citizen,â said Acting Deputy Attorney General Trent McCotter. âEach of the 28 defendants charged today appears on the list of more than 20,000 likely noncitizen registrants we provided to California election officials last week. California refused to look at that list. Today's charges show exactly what that refusal puts at risk. California must verify the citizenship of those more than 20,000 registrants before mail-in ballots are counted. â You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

title: Low-key campaign, voter apathy, political infighting pull down Visakhapatnam turnout
text: A woman shows her inked-finger after casting vote for GVMC polls in Visakhapatnam on Sunday. Pic-A Sarath Kumar Visakhapatnam : Urban voter apathy was once again evident in the GVMC election held on Sunday. O nly 51.47% of voters in Vizag exercised their franchise, according to official data available till 10 pm , the lowest turnout among the major urban local bodies of Andhra Pradesh that went to polls on Sunday. The slow pace of polling in Vizag was evident right from the morning. Only around 3.34% of voters had cast their votes by 9 am. The turnout rose to 26.5% by 1 pm, six hours after polling began at 7 am. The sluggish response continued through the day, pointing to a lack of enthusiasm among urban voters. Low voter turnout has been a recurring feature of elections to the Vizag municipal body. Of the six elections held before Sundayâs poll, turnout crossed 70% only once, in 1981. In all the other elections, it remained below the 60% mark. Sundayâs election followed the same pattern, with polling settling at around 51.5% . This is even lower than the over 59% recorded in the 2021 GVMC elections and far below the 64-76% turnout recorded across different Assembly segments of the city in the 2024 elections. When TOI visited several polling booths in the East, North and South zones, queues were thin right from the morning. This was in sharp contrast to the scenes witnessed during the 2024 elections. Political enthusiasm was largely missing on the streets, except for some activity around polling booths. Several factors appear to have contributed to the subdued voter response. As TOI reported earlier, campaigning for this municipal election was largely lacklustre in Visakhapatnam. Except for the last two days of campaigning on Oct 29 and 30, there was little visible political activity on the streets. Cyclone Arnab also disrupted normal life, public services and campaigning for nearly three days. Before the cyclone, political parties were grappling with internal issues over ticket allotments and rebel candidates. It took nearly a week for the parties to persuade disgruntled aspirants to withdraw from the contest. Even after these efforts, nearly 40 rebel candidates remained in the fray, affecting the election campaign in several wards. The limited campaigning, internal differences within political parties, and disruption caused by the cyclone appear to have together affected voter participation. The late release of manifestos by the main parties may have also contributed to the lack of public engagement. The TDP released its manifesto only on Oct 29, while the YSRCP announced its promises on Oct 30, leaving voters little time to assess their proposals for the city. Another possible factor is the perception among residents that the state and central govts play a bigger role in shaping major projects, infrastructure and policies for Visakhapatnam than the municipal corporation. This could have reduced the importance attached to the local body election by some sections of the electorate. A section of the cityâs educated and working population may also have limited direct engagement with local corporators and mayoral candidates. The presence of several migrant families, some of whom may not have strong connections with local political leaders, could be another factor behind the subdued participation. Speaking to TOI, M Ravi Kanth, who voted at a booth set up at Girijan Bhavan in MVP Colony, said the turnout appeared to be thin. âI came early, thinking I could finish voting before the queues became longer. However, I was surprised to find only a few people waiting. The manifestos and campaigning may not have reached the public. Even from my conversations with friends, the enthusiasm I noticed during the 2024 polls was largely missing this time,â said Ravi Kanth, a private employee. R Srinath, a young voter who was spotted at a polling booth in Peda Waltair, said the political parties had not made any significant announcements for the GVMC elections. âIt has been a complete dud, both in terms of campaigning and election promises,â he said. Apart from minor clashes in a few wards between workers of NDA parties and the YSRCP, polling passed off largely peacefully in Visakhapatnam. The YSRCP, however, alleged rigging in some wards.
