title: NDA leaders urge rebels to withdraw from AP local body polls
text: CM Chandrababu Naidu with deputy CM Pawan Kalyan during a joint press meet on Tuesday Vijayawada : The top leadership of the NDA alliance on Tuesday appealed to rebel candidates of the TDP , Jana Sena and BJP to respect the allianceâs seat-sharing arrangement and withdraw from the election fray. They appealed to their respective party workers to work for the victory of officially nominated candidates in the local body elections. Addressing a joint press conference, chief minister N Chandrababu Naidu , deputy chief minister K Pawan Kalyan , and BJP state president P V N Madhav said an elaborate exercise was undertaken to finalise seat-sharing and candidate selection at every level of the local body elections. Naidu said the coalition had carefully balanced alliance compulsions, local realities, social engineering and winnability before finalising candidates. He said the exercise was more complex than the one carried out during the 2024 assembly and Lok Sabha elections since seat-sharing had to be worked out down to the MPTC level. Pawan Kalyan said local body elections posed challenges different from those in general elections, as seat adjustments had to be made for thousands of positions. While acknowledging that several aspirants could not be accommodated despite their work for the parties, he assured them that the alliance leadership would do justice to such leaders and workers in future. The alliance leaders urged cadres to uphold the decisions taken by the three parties and campaign only for candidates officially allotted tickets under the coalition arrangement. Naidu said the alliance had taken decisions after extensive consultations and warned that action would be taken against those working against officially nominated candidates. Seeking public support for the coalition, Naidu said local bodies needed to be strengthened and promised greater financial support and development works if NDA-backed candidates were elected. Turning his attack on the YSRCP and its president, YS Jagan Mohan Reddy , Naidu accused the opposition of attempting to stall local body elections through litigation, violence and misinformation. He alleged that the party had filed dozens of court cases seeking to halt the electoral process and was unwilling to accept democratic outcomes. Describing Jaganâs politics as âhit-and-runâ, Naidu said the YSRCPâs ideology is revolving around âcriminalisation, litigation and fake propagandaâ, whereas the NDA stood for welfare, development, governance and public service. The chief minister also urged the YSRCP leadership to abandon violence and join the democratic mainstream. Drawing parallels with his earlier appeals to extremist groups to join the democratic process, Naidu said the opposition should participate in elections and seek votes from the people rather than resorting to confrontation. Escalating the attack further, Naidu referred to the internal disputes within Jaganâs family. He alleged that the Vivekananda Reddy murder case had created a crisis within the family and said disputes over assets had further deepened those divisions. âJaganâs struggle is for his palaces; our struggle is for the poor,â he said. Pawan Kalyan joined the attack by taking exception to remarks made by Jagan. âIf you show 2.0, we will show 10X,â he said, adding that nobody in the alliance was prepared to be intimidated. He said such language reflected weakness rather than strength and suggested that Jagan should heed Naiduâs advice and rejoin the democratic mainstream. Pawan said direct interaction with people would help the former chief minister understand public sentiment. He reiterated that the alliance would remain united despite the complexities of local body elections and would continue to work together for the stateâs development. BJP state president P V N Madhav appealed to voters to bless NDA candidates and said the coalition was delivering welfare, development and good governance with the support of the Centre under Prime Minister Narendra Modi. The NDA leaders maintained that despite intense competition for tickets, the coalition had made every effort to accommodate deserving aspirants and appealed to dissatisfied leaders to put the allianceâs larger objective ahead of individual aspirations. They urged voters to replicate the support extended to the NDA in the 2024 elections and ensure victory for coalition candidates in the local body polls. title: 'This is America! Not your communist dictatorship': US, Cuban envoys scream at each other at UN - watch
text: âThis is not your communist dictatorshipâ: US, Cuban envoys clash at UN A heated exchange broke out at the United Nations General Assembly after US Ambassador Mike Waltz told Cuban Foreign Minister Bruno RodrÃ­guez Parrilla to âback upâ when the Cuban diplomat approached the podium while Waltz was speaking. The confrontation took place during the General Assemblyâs annual debate on the decades-old US embargo on Cuba, ahead of a vote on a resolution calling for an end to the restrictions. âDo you understand who you're dealing with? This is America!â Waltz said during the exchange, accusing the Cuban government of enriching its leaders while its people faced hardship. As the Cuban delegation sought to interrupt his remarks, Waltz said, âI know you don't like to hear this,â before adding, âThis is America, my friend. This is the United Nations. This isn't your communist dictatorship. You cannot silence me.â RodrÃ­guez continued towards the podium as the president of the General Assembly attempted to restore order, reminding delegates that the Cuban delegation would have an opportunity to respond. âThis individual needs to back away from this podium,â Waltz said. âHe's not going to intimidate me in the United States of America.â âI'm the representative of the United States of America. Back up! Back up, Ambassador. Back away! This isn't Havana.â Waltz urged UN member states to reject the resolution seeking to end the US embargo. He blamed corruption and repression within Cuba for the hardships faced by its people and accused the countryâs communist government of enriching itself. After Cuba was given the floor, RodrÃ­guez accused Waltz of making false claims and asked the General Assembly president to call him to order. âMr. Waltz is lying yet again,â he said, arguing that the US ambassadorâs remarks were âbeneath the dignity of this forum and member statesâ and were insulting to Cubaâs government and people. In a subsequent post on X, Waltz accused Cubaâs âCommunist leadersâ of concealing their luxury real estate holdings, adding that he was presenting evidence that the delegation did not want discussed. The confrontation came amid renewed debate over Washingtonâs decades-old economic embargo on Cuba, which has remained a point of contention between the two countries. title: Economy, not ideology
text: . When populists and autocrats lose, is the vote on political theory or economic reality? Thereâs a view, supported by research, that democracy is in danger. Per Swedenâs V-Dem Institute, the average person has about the same democratic freedoms now as in 1978. So, itâs tempting to read election results from Brazil and Serbia as an endorsement of democracy. In Brazil, voters narrowly denied Flavio Bolsonaro, a candidate with undisguised authoritarian tendencies, and gave Lula another term. In Serbia, they roundly defeated strongman Aleksandar Vucic. The Serbian result has got outsized attention â itâs a country of just 65L people and $112bn GDP â because the winning side is a student protest movement, fronted by academics, doctors, etc. Yet, this may not be the democratic revival many are hoping for. Rather, as Harvard Prof Steven Levitsky pointed out in 2024, such results could chiefly be anti-incumbency. Even Lula in Brazil lost the first round to Bolsonaro, before staging a spirited fightback. The trend has been clear since 2020, when Covid, and economic disruption, led govts to adopt easy-money policies. The resultant inflation worked for billionaires, but left the middle class, and everyone below, worse off. Levitsky noted that citizen distrust and discontent were running high, and in 41 of 55 polls between 2020 and 2024, the incumbent lost: âalmost certainly a product of and part of Covid inflationâ. Were young Serbians, who campaigned against Vucic for two years, fighting for an ideology or their economic future? Weâve seen how Labour won a landslide in UK, only to become unpopular within months. In Germany, Social Democrats arenât in a happy place either. Or look at US, which ousted Trump, a populist, for Biden, only to vote him back four years later. And now, with US midterms scheduled for Nov 3, it looks like Americans will pounce on the chance to clip Trumpâs wings in Congress. Why? Because, far from addressing their cost-of-living crisis, as he promised, heâs worsened their economic pain with the war on Iran. Israel, another test case for democracy, votes today. And while polls donât show Netanyahu winning outright, whoever wins is unlikely to go soft on Palestinians. In fact, young Israelis, first-time voters, donât appear to have much sympathy for Gazans either. What they are weary of is endless war and psychological hardship. And corruption. People everywhere are asking elected leaders, âWhat have you done for us, for our future?â And incumbents are losing because they usually donât have a convincing answer. title: Trump says Brazil's defeated presidential candidate Bolsonaro can stay in US âas long as he wantsâ

title: US midterms 2026: Meet Amish Shah, the doctor seeking a second shot at Congress
text: Amish Shah , an emergency-room physician and former Arizona state legislator, is seeking a seat in the US House of Representatives for a second time, placing health-care costs, household affordability and access to federal benefits at the centre of his campaign. He focused on public health, education, small businesses and public safety. In 2024, he contested the congressional seat but lost to Schweikert in a closely fought election. He secured the Democratic nomination in July 2026 after defeating several challengers, including Marlene GalÃ¡n-Woods, who had received backing from the Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee. Shah's campaign promises to lower prescription-drug costs, protect Medicare and Social Security, defend abortion rights and address rising household expenses. title: US launches 'secret' strikes on Iranâs Qeshm Island amid Netanyahu push for post-midterm attacks
text: US launches 'secret' strikes on Iranâs Qeshm Island as peace talks teeter along The United States launched "secret" strikes on Iran's Qeshm Island, the Wall Street Journal reported on Monday, citing US officials, amid renewed tensions over the possibility of fresh military action against Tehran. The attack triggered a series of explosions on the island, located in the Strait of Hormuz, Iranian state media outlet IRNA reported. The strikes were part of a series of limited military operations carried out by Washington in recent weeks, the WSJ said, adding that the attacks had been deliberately kept secret and conducted on a smaller scale to avoid signalling an intention to resume its broader military campaign against Iran. Watch War Begins Even Before Midterms? U.S. Bombs Iranian Territory; Explosions Rock Qeshm Island The developments came as Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu reportedly pressed US President Donald Trump to consider fresh military action against Iran after Tuesday's US midterm elections. Trump and Netanyahu held a telephone conversation on Saturday to discuss Washington's negotiations with Tehran and the possibility of resuming military operations, Axios reported, citing one Israeli and one US source. Follow live updates: âHands stained with bloodâ - Iran warns employees of 3 firms over alleged Israeli military links According to the report, Netanyahu urged Trump to launch fresh strikes after the elections, while the US president wanted to allow diplomatic efforts to continue for now. An Israeli source described the conversation as "tough", while a US source called it "direct". Earlier on Monday, Trump cast doubt on whether he would follow through on his threat to resume military strikes against Iran, while indicating that a diplomatic agreement remained possible. Asked by reporters whether he was considering striking Iran after Tuesday's midterm elections, Trump replied, "No." US Vice President JD Vance on Monday expressed optimism that Washington and Tehran could still reach a deal to prevent President Donald Trump from ordering fresh strikes against Iran after the US midterm elections. Vance sent a letter to Iran's security chief Mohsen Rezaei last week, but the White House has shared few details about its contents. Trump said the letter focused on helping Iran with "medical supplies and various things". "We've had a number of good conversations with the Iranians," Vance told reporters, adding that he had spoken to Trump about the matter. "The president and I both feel pretty good about the prospects for potentially coming to a negotiated settlement. We're going to keep on working at it," he said. title: Can Trump defy history? The big battles shaping US midterms
text: A referendum on Trump? Why US midterms matter for his presidency The central question in the US midterm elections is whether MAGA supremo Donald Trump can retain control of Congress or whether voters will hand Democrats the opportunity to challenge his agenda during the final two years of his presidency. With Americans heading to the polls on Tuesday, all 435 seats in the House of Representatives and 35 of the 100 Senate seats are up for grabs. Republicans currently control both chambers, but Trump's falling approval ratings, rising living costs and the war with Iran have given Democrats fresh hope of making gains. According to a BBC report, the elections could determine how much freedom Trump has to push his policies through Congress and how effectively Democrats can challenge his administration. Why midterms matter for Trump The midterm elections are traditionally a test of the sitting president's popularity. The party in power often loses seats as voters use the elections to express dissatisfaction with the administration. Trump's approval ratings have added to Republican concerns. According to polling data cited by the BBC, his approval rating began his second term at just over 50% but subsequently fell into the 40s. It dropped below 40% after the US and Israel launched air strikes against Iran at the end of February and currently stands at around 38%. Historically, the president's party has lost an average of 27 House seats in midterm elections since 1934. It has gained seats in only three of the 23 elections held during that period, the BBC reported. Watch Vance Grilled On Cam: âWhy Are Trumpâs Approval Ratings âUnderwaterâ? VP Abruptly Ends Gaggle The political stakes are particularly high because Republicans have only narrow control of the House. A Democratic takeover of either chamber could make it harder for Trump to advance his legislative agenda. House battle: Republicans face a narrow majority The Republicans currently hold 218 seats in the 435-member House of Representatives, giving them a razor-thin majority. All 435 seats are being contested because House members serve two-year terms. Chart explaining the midterms in numbers However, not every constituency is expected to witness a close contest. According to the Cook Political Report, only 18 seats are considered toss-ups, meaning either party has a realistic chance of winning them. Of these, 14 are currently held by Republicans and four by Democrats. Democrats could also take control by winning seats in constituencies already classified as likely or leaning towards them. The narrow Republican majority means even a relatively small shift in voter support could change control of the House. Senate race: Democrats face a tougher challenge The battle for the Senate is more complicated for Democrats. Republicans currently hold 53 of the 100 seats, while Democrats have 45. Two independents also vote with the Democrats. Unlike the House, only about one-third of Senate seats are contested every two years because senators serve six-year terms. This time, 35 seats are up for election. The Senate race The Cook Political Report identifies seven Senate races as toss-ups, six of which are currently held by Republicans. Democrats would need to win four of these seats, along with four seats classified as likely or leaning Democratic, to reach the 51-seat majority. Among the closely watched contests is Michigan, where Democrat Abdul El-Sayed faces Republican Mike Rogers, a Trump ally and former FBI agent. Democrats are also targeting traditionally Republican states, including Alaska, Iowa and Ohio. Texas is another key battleground, where Democrat James Talarico is challenging Republican Ken Paxton. A Talarico victory would give Democrats their first Senate seat in the state since 1988, according to the BBC. Cost of living, healthcare and immigration dominate voter concerns The economy remains one of the biggest challenges for Republicans heading into the elections. Trump had promised to bring down inflation and make everyday life more affordable during his 2024 campaign, but rising costs have remained a major concern for American households. The war with Iran has added to the pressure. Trump had highlighted falling petrol prices in his State of the Union address on February 24, saying prices were below $2.30 per gallon in most states. However, the conflict with Iran began four days later, disrupting energy supplies from the Middle East and pushing petrol prices to around $4 per gallon. Issues in US elections The war has also become increasingly unpopular among Americans. A poll conducted in August found that 63% of respondents disapproved of Trump's handling of the conflict, the BBC reported. Healthcare and immigration are other major issues shaping the campaign. Democratic candidates have focused on the rising cost of health insurance and concerns over access to healthcare under Trump's policies. Republicans, meanwhile, have highlighted the administration's immigration measures, with Trump pointing to a sharp fall in illegal border crossings as evidence of their success. Can Trump overcome the political headwinds? Despite the challenges, Republicans have an advantage when it comes to campaign funding. According to figures cited by the BBC, the Republican National Committee and its allied groups had around $320 million in cash reserves in mid-October, compared with just under $230 million for Democrats. Trump's political fundraising group, MAGA Inc, had an additional $160 million or more at its disposal. Republicans have used their financial advantage to step up advertising ahead of the vote. More than $1 billion worth of political advertisements were aired in September, according to research firm AdImpact. Republicans outspent Democrats by around $200 million and had higher advertising expenditure in nearly all closely contested Senate races. The late campaign push is aimed at mobilising Republican voters and limiting potential losses in both chambers. While the overall political environment appears favourable to Democrats, Trump and his party have previously performed better than expected in elections despite unfavourable polling. What happens after the midterms? The outcome will shape the final two years of Trump's presidency. If Democrats take control of either chamber, they could use their position to challenge his policies, scrutinise his administration and make it harder for Republicans to pass legislation. If Republicans retain control of both chambers, Trump will have greater room to pursue his legislative priorities. The elections will also set the stage for the next presidential race in 2028. With Trump constitutionally barred from seeking a third term, political attention is likely to shift towards the next generation of leadership and what Democrats offer voters beyond opposition to the Republican president. title: Will the US elections make Trump stop the Iran war?
text: Donald Trump has hinted at a possible US attack on Iran as soon as Sunday while keeping open the possibility of a deal, amid conflicting reports over Tehran's position on the Strait of Hormuz and the US naval blockade. The US midterm elections could limit Trumpâs power to continue the war with Iran. This could help bring down oil prices around the world. The world is watching the upcoming US midterm elections closely. People want to know if the results will help end the war with Iran and bring down oil prices. Oil prices are very high because of the war started by US President Donald Trump against Iran. Indiaâs External Affairs Minister, S Jaishankar, has said that oil costing more than $100 per barrel should not be considered normal. The price of Brent crude oil, an important type of oil traded around the world, is about $115 per barrel. The Strait of Hormuz, a narrow sea passage through which many oil ships travel, is facing serious disruption, and ships are still being attacked. The best way to bring oil prices down is to end the war. But Trump may choose to increase the fighting instead. He has already sent a third aircraft carrier and 10,000 more soldiers to the region. If the war becomes more serious, it could hurt countries around the world, especially India, which buys a lot of oil from other countries. How Can the Elections Limit Trumpâs Power? The US midterm elections decide who controls Congress, the part of the government that makes laws. Congress has two parts: the House of Representatives and the Senate. If the Democratic Party wins control of either or both houses, it could make it harder for Trump to continue the war. Experts believe the Democrats have a good chance of winning the House of Representatives, though winning the Senate may be more difficult. If Democrats control the House, they could use their power over government spending to put pressure on Trump. For example, they could threaten to reduce money for the military unless he gets Congressâs permission to continue the war. US law says that a president cannot continue certain military actions for a long time without involving Congress. However, Trump has tried to avoid these restrictions. Even if Democrats win, Trump could still block some of their plans using his presidential veto. But many Republicans also oppose the war, and more Americans are becoming unhappy with it. This could make it harder for Trump to ignore calls for peace. Will Republicans Stand Up to Trump? Suppose Democrats win the elections, but Trump still refuses to stop the war. Then members of his own Republican Party may have to decide whether to challenge him. If the fighting becomes worse, oil prices could rise to $120 per barrel or even higher. Prices might then stay high throughout 2027, making life more expensive for people and businesses around the world. High oil prices could also hurt the Republicansâ chances in the 2028 presidential election. Trump cannot run for president again, but other Republicans, including JD Vance and Marco Rubio, may want to become the next president. The big question is this: If the Democrats win the midterms and Trump refuses to change course, will the Republicans finally stand up to him and push him to end the war? The election could become an important test of how much power Trump hasâand whether other politicians are willing to stop him from continuing a war that is hurting the world. title: Officer who presided over Gokul meet promoted
text: Kolhapur : Maharashtra govt has promoted deputy collector Mausami Chougule to the rank of additional collector and posted her as assistant commissioner (rehabilitation) at the Chhatrapati Sambhajinagar divisional commissionerate. However, she will continue in her present assignment until the completion of the Special Intensive Revision exercise, as she is currently on election duty. The promotion order also makes it clear that the elevation is temporary and subject to the outcome of petitions pending before the Bombay high court and Supreme Court over seniority disputes. Govt said the promotion has been granted under the provisions of the General Administration Departmentâs May 7, 2021 decision governing such cases. Chougule is currently serving as sub-divisional officer of Karvir division in Kolhapur district. She recently presided over the meeting convened to elect the chairperson of the Kolhapur District Cooperative Milk Producers Federation, popularly known as Gokul Dairy. The meeting was adjourned without electing a chairman after she cited lack of quorum. The chairpersonâs election has since become the focus of a political and legal tussle. The Satej Patil-led Samavichari Aghadi holds 13 elected directors, while the Mahayuti-backed panel has 12. The Mahayuti directors stayed away from the meeting, resulting in the quorum falling short. Under the federationâs bylaws, 14 directors must be present to conduct the meeting, while the chairperson can be elected by a simple majority. The decision to adjourn the meeting has been challenged in the Bombay high court. The matter is scheduled to come up for hearing on Monday. Chougule was unavailable for comment. However, officials said her transfer is part of a larger round of promotions involving several deputy collectors. âShe currently holds the post of sub-divisional officer. If the HC directs that the adjourned Gokul meeting be reconvened, she can still preside over it,â a senior official said on condition of anonymity. Meanwhile, speaking to reporters in New Delhi on Sunday, Satej Patil said Nov 3 is the deadline for electing a new chairperson. âThe first meeting was adjourned on the technical ground of quorum. We hope the high court decides the matter on Monday,â Patil said. He also warned that any attempt by state govt to appoint expert directors with voting rights to alter the balance of power would be challenged in court. âI do not think Mahayuti will succeed. No director from our side will leave us. Mahayuti should start preparing for the next election due after five years,â Patil said. title: Arizona officials sued after 25 US citizens were wrongly flagged as possible noncitizens and blocked from voting; following court-ordered mediation, their voting access was restored days before the November 3 midterms
text: The Trump administration modified the SAVE database to identify possible noncitizens registered to vote in US elections. (AI image) With the November 3 midterm elections just days away, 25 US citizens in Arizona have regained their voting access after being wrongly identified as possible noncitizens. Their registrations were restored following a legal dispute between Maricopa County Recorder Justin Heap and Arizona Attorney General Kris Mayes. The two sides reached an agreement through court-ordered mediation on Friday, bringing the lawsuit to an end. These people had previously voted in US elections but later found their registrations restricted because officials questioned their citizenship. Investigations eventually confirmed that they were American citizens. However, that finding did not immediately resolve the problem, as Heap's office maintained that it needed documentary evidence before allowing them to vote again. Watch Trumpâs Midterm Battle: The Indian-American Voter Factor According to Arizona Mirror, the disagreement reached Maricopa County Superior Court after Mayes sought to have the affected registrations restored before the election. The matter was settled when her office provided the citizenship information requested by Heap's office. Of the 25 people covered by the lawsuit, 24 had their active voter status restored following mediation. The remaining person had already regained voting access after independently submitting proof of citizenship. The recorder's office also issued early ballots to 18 affected voters who were enrolled in the county's Active Early Voting List. Voters identified as noncitizens The dispute is related to a review of Arizona's voter registrations. Heap's office had used a federal database called the Systematic Alien Verification for Entitlements (SAVE) to identify people who might not be US citizens. The database, which had been modified under the Trump administration to help identify possible noncitizens registered to vote, has also incorrectly flagged American citizens. Using this system, Heap's office identified 207 registered voters as possible noncitizens. Their information was then forwarded to the Maricopa County Attorney's Office for further examination. Among those flagged, 60 had participated in earlier elections. Heap changed their registration status, leaving them unable to vote unless they produced the required documents establishing their citizenship. However, when the Maricopa County Attorney's Office examined those 60 cases, it found that 52 people were US citizens. Only eight were identified as noncitizens. The investigation also found that no more than three of those eight had voted in the same election. The Arizona Attorney General's Office reached similar conclusions. But even after the citizenship of the affected voters had been verified, 25 people remained without restored voting access. Watch 25 voters in Arizona get voting rights restored after legal battle Matter ended up in court The two offices disagreed over what was required to reinstate the voters. According to KJZZ 91.5 FM, Heap's lawyer told the court that although investigators had established the voters' citizenship, they had not shared the documents supporting those findings with the recorder's office. Heap maintained that the registrations could be restored once the necessary evidence was received. Meanwhile, Mayes disputed the handling of the case. Her office argued that Heap should not have restricted the registrations before confirming that the people concerned were not American citizens. Under the state law cited by the Attorney General's Office, a recorder must confirm that someone is not a US citizen before cancelling their voter registration. Mayes' office argued that suspicion alone did not meet that requirement. With the election approaching and the disagreement unresolved, Mayes filed a lawsuit seeking to restore voting access to the 25 citizens. Two sides reach an agreement At a court hearing on Friday, the Attorney General's Office indicated that it could provide the driver's licence information used to verify the voters' citizenship. Later that day, both sides met with Judge Christopher Whitten, who had been appointed to mediate the dispute. Once the documentation was provided, Heap's office reinstated the remaining affected voters. Heap defended his decision to wait for the records saying, âWe needed legally sufficient documentation of citizenship, we received it, and we immediately restored the voters. Our office fulfilled its duty to protect eligible voters while upholding Arizona law." Mayes, however, continued to question why court intervention had been necessary. âIt should not have taken litigation to make Justin Heap follow the law; that is his duty and the duty of all election officials,â she said. Maricopa County Supervisor Tom Galvin also criticised Heap for his handling of the registrations. Following the agreement, Mayes agreed to dismiss the lawsuit, while the recorder's office confirmed that the affected citizens had regained active voter status. The settlement also allowed early ballots to be issued to 18 voters on the Active Early Voting List. October 23 was the deadline for requesting an early ballot, and county officials advised voters to return mailed ballots by October 27. You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. title: 'Heightened threat environment': Avenger air defence systems deployed near Trumpâs Florida Mar-a-Lago residence - video
text: Avenger air defence systems deployed near Trumpâs Florida estate Missile defence systems have been deployed near US President Donald Trump's Mar-a-Lago residence and at Palm Beach International Airport in Florida, with viral visuals showing military equipment positioned on a barge close to the presidential estate. The deployment comes ahead of Tuesday's US midterm elections, amid what the US Secret Service has described as a "heightened threat environment". Photographs taken last week showed two Avenger Air Defence Systems positioned on a barge in the waters near Mar-a-Lago, Trump's primary residence and resort in Palm Beach. US service members in military fatigues were also seen in the vicinity, The Independent reported. An Avenger system was also installed on the southern side of Palm Beach International Airport, recently renamed Donald J. Trump International Airport, according the South Florida Sun Sentinel. The North American Aerospace Defense Command (NORAD) confirmed to WPBF that the defence systems had been installed "in and around" Mar-a-Lago. Secret Service cites heightened threat environment A Secret Service spokesperson said the agency had adjusted its protective arrangements in response to the security environment. "The US Secret Service is operating in a heightened threat environment, and we continuously adapt our protective operations to incorporate cutting-edge tools, technology, and methods to safeguard our protectees," the spokesperson told The Independent. The spokesperson added, "At the request of the US Secret Service, NORAD and US Northern Command are providing Counter-Unmanned Aircraft System capabilities in support of our protective operations." The Avenger is a mobile air defence system designed to counter aerial threats. The platform is mounted on a Humvee and uses short-range Stinger missiles and a .50-calibre machine gun to engage low-altitude aerial threats, including aircraft and unmanned aerial vehicles. Aircraft intercepted near Mar-a-Lago The deployment comes amid heightened tensions with Iran in the Middle East and follows a series of airspace security incidents near the Florida estate. Last week, while Trump was in Florida, a fighter jet intercepted a civilian aircraft that had entered restricted airspace over Mar-a-Lago. NORAD said the fighter jet carried out a standard "headbutt" manoeuvre to draw the pilot's attention, after which the civilian aircraft established communication and safely left the restricted airspace in accordance with flight instructions. NORAD, a joint US-Canadian military command, has intercepted more than 60 aircraft violating flight restrictions around Palm Beach since January last year. The Kyiv Post, citing The Telegraph, reported that federal court filings showed the Secret Service was seeking permanent flight restrictions around Mar-a-Lago. The filings cited concerns over potential terrorist threats and aerial intrusions. Secret Service Deputy Director Matthew Quinn described the threat profile in the documents as "heightened, real, and dynamic". Earlier security incidents involving Trump Trump has faced several alleged threats to his life in recent years. In 2024, an armed man was found hiding in bushes along the perimeter of the president's Florida golf club. In February this year, a 21-year-old man drove through a gate at Mar-a-Lago carrying a shotgun before he was shot and killed. On many occasions, Iran has also threatened to harm Trump. The latest deployment also comes as Trump continues his campaign appearances ahead of the midterm elections. He was at Mar-a-Lago on Saturday after holding a rally in Daytona Beach on Friday and was scheduled to travel to Kansas and Iowa for further rallies on Sunday, according to The Independent. title: MLC election results: BJP wins big, but Congress and Samajwadi Party send a message from Nagpur, Varanasi
text: BJP's big win in MLC elections comes with setbacks in Nagpur and Varanasi The MLC elections across four states brought both shock and cheer for the BJP and Congress. While the Congress suffered a humiliating defeat in Karnataka, where it is in power but failed to win a single seat, the BJP faltered in two constituencies which mattered the most. One being Nagpur, which is home to the RSS headquarters, and Varanasi, Prime Minister Narendra Modi's parliamentary constituency. The BJP nevertheless emerged as the largest party, winning 13 of the 28 seats contested, while its allies took the NDA's tally to 16. The alliance swept all four seats in Karnataka, won six of the 11 seats in Uttar Pradesh and secured four of the eight seats in Bihar. In Maharashtra, the ruling Mahayuti won two of the five seats, while the opposition Maha Vikas Aghadi secured three. The Congress's only victory came from Nagpur, a political stronghold of Maharashtra chief minister Devendra Fadnavis and Union minister Nitin Gadkari. In Uttar Pradesh, the Samajwadi Party retained the Varanasi Teachers' constituency and was heading towards victory in the Graduates' seat, both of which it had won in 2020. BJP-led NDA secured 16 of the 28 MLC seats across four states, while the SP won five seats in Uttar Pradesh and Congress retained Nagpur in Maharashtra. What began as celebrations and sharp jibes at the Congress on Wednesday turned into a war of words on Thursday, as the results in Nagpur and Varanasi gave the opposition grounds to question the BJP's claims of electoral dominance. BJP mocks Congress over 'zero' seats As the early results came in on Wednesday, BJP leaders targeted the Congress over its poor performance, particularly in Karnataka, where the party is in power but failed to win a single seat. PM Modi took a swipe at the opposition party on X, pointing out that voting in the four states had taken place using ballot papers. "Guess how many seats Congress won?" he asked. The remark came amid the Congress's repeated allegations over electronic voting machines and its demand for a return to ballot-paper voting. BJP president Nitin Nabin also targeted the Congress, saying the party had failed to win public support despite voting being conducted using ballot papers. "The people are repeatedly rejecting Congress' anarchist politics," Nabin said, adding that public trust remained with PM Modi irrespective of whether elections were conducted using EVMs or ballot papers. BJP president Nitin Nabin targeted Congress over its poor performance in the MLC elections, pointing out that voting had taken place using ballot papers. BJP spokesperson Sudhanshu Trivedi also attacked Rahul Gandhi over his allegations of vote theft "Kamchori ki aadat chhodiye. Vote chori ka shabd apke muh se khud chhoot jayega," he said, asking the Congress leader to give up what he described as a habit of avoiding hard work. Nagpur win gives Congress a chance to respond Congress candidate and sitting MLC Abhijeet Wanjari defeated BJP's Sudhakar Kohale to retain the Nagpur Division Graduates' constituency after more than 40 hours of counting. Kohale had initially taken the lead before Wanjari overtook him through preferential votes. Nagpur is important for the BJP. Besides housing the RSS headquarters, it is associated with Fadnavis and Gadkari, both of whom campaigned for Kohale. The Congress had wrested the seat from the BJP in 2020, when Wanjari defeated Sandip Joshi. By retaining it in 2026, the party prevented the BJP from reclaiming a constituency it had dominated for decades. The Maharashtra Congress also targeted Fadnavis over a social media post in which he had claimed that the party had failed to win a single seat. Congress leader Jairam Ramesh questioned the BJP's setbacks in Nagpur and Varanasi after PM Modi mocked the party's performance in the MLC elections. Sharing a screenshot of what it said was a deleted post by Fadnavis, the party accused him of celebrating before counting was complete. The post had described the Congress's performance as a "big fat zero". The Congress said Fadnavis had been forced to delete the post after the Nagpur result and warned that the outcome was only a trailer of future political battles. Congress general secretary Jairam Ramesh also responded to PM Modi's remarks, questioning the BJP's losses in Nagpur and Varanasi. "The Prime Minister needs to introspect, but instead, he's lecturing others! Before counting Congress's seats, I wish he'd also reflect on why the BJP lost both seats in his own parliamentary constituency of Varanasi, and how Congress managed to defeat the BJP in RSS's stronghold of Nagpur?" Ramesh said. "Mr. Modi, stop the trolling," he added, accusing the government of failing to address inflation, unemployment and weak private investment. Ramesh claimed that voters in Varanasi, Nagpur, Lucknow, Prayagraj and Patna had expressed dissatisfaction with the Centre's policies. Varanasi setback gives SP a boost ahead of 2027 The BJP's biggest setback in Uttar Pradesh came from Varanasi, where the Samajwadi Party retained the Teachers' seat and established an unassailable lead in the Graduates' constituency. The BJP retained six of the 11 seats contested in the state, while the SP won four and was heading towards a fifth. The SP had won both Varanasi seats in 2020 as well. Six years later, the BJP has failed to dislodge the party from either constituency despite its strong presence in the region. Although the two MLC constituencies cover a wider geographical area than PM Modi's Lok Sabha seat, the results carry political significance given Varanasi's association with the Prime Minister since 2014. They also come after PM Modi's victory margin in Varanasi declined from nearly 4.8 lakh votes in the 2019 Lok Sabha elections to around 1.5 lakh in 2024. Across Uttar Pradesh, the SP's tally is set to rise from three seats in 2020 to five, while the BJP has retained its tally of six. The SP had also emerged as the largest party in Uttar Pradesh in the 2024 Lok Sabha elections, winning 37 of the state's 80 parliamentary seats against the BJP's 33. BJP deputy chief minister Keshav Prasad Maurya acknowledged that the party had expected a better performance. "These elections are decided by highly educated and qualified voters. The BJP has repeated its previous performance, but we expected to win more seats. We will examine why we fell short," Maurya said. The SP, meanwhile, has repeatedly accused the BJP of electoral irregularities, allegations the ruling party has rejected. On polling day, Akhilesh Yadav had claimed that the BJP was attempting to influence even the MLC elections, which have a limited electorate. "If the BJP can do this in MLC polls for teachers and graduate constituencies where a limited number of people cast votes, one can imagine their preparation for the assembly polls," he had said. What do the results mean for 2027? The NDA's overall tally shows that the BJP and its allies remain ahead in these Legislative Council contests. But the results in Nagpur and Varanasi also show that the party has struggled to regain certain seats despite its strong presence in both regions. In Uttar Pradesh, the SP and Congress are preparing to contest the 2027 assembly elections together, hoping to build on their performance in the 2024 Lok Sabha polls. Join conversation View All Comments â Share your thoughts in the comments Insightful Agree Disagree Skeptical Concerning Promising Worth Reading Big Development Post Comment Be respectful Â· TOI community guidelines The alliance won 43 of the state's 80 parliamentary seats in 2024, reducing the BJP's tally from 62 in 2019 to 33. Akhilesh Yadav has said the alliance will continue in 2027, although the two parties still need to settle their seat-sharing arrangement. The MLC results, however, cannot be treated as an indication of how the state will vote in the assembly elections. These contests involve a limited electorate of registered graduates and teachers, unlike assembly polls, which are decided by a much wider voter base. For the BJP, which is seeking a third consecutive term in Uttar Pradesh, the challenge will be to counter the opposition's gains. For the SP-Congress alliance, the question is whether it can repeat its 2024 Lok Sabha performance when the state's 403 assembly seats go to the polls in 2027. title: ECI to review UP Assembly poll readiness, 18 districts to be assessed in Meerut on November 2
text: The Election Commission of India is set to convene in Meerut on Monday to evaluate the election preparations (Representative image) LUCKNOW: The Election Commission of India ( ECI ) will review preparations for the 2027 Uttar Pradesh Assembly elections across 18 districts of western UP during a meeting in Meerut on Monday. Senior Deputy Election Commissioner Manish Garg, along with other senior ECI officials, will assess election-related arrangements and the progress made by district administrations. Uttar Pradesh Chief Electoral Officer (CEO) Navdeep Rinwa and other senior officials from the CEO's office will also attend the meeting. The review is scheduled to begin at 10.30 am on Monday at Urja Bhawan, the headquarters of Paschimanchal Vidyut Vitran Nigam, on Jail Chungi Road in Saket, Meerut. The meeting will cover 18 districts falling under the Meerut, Saharanpur, Moradabad and Aligarh divisions. Divisional commissioners, police commissioners, inspectors general and deputy inspectors general of police, district election officers, senior superintendents of police and superintendents of police from the respective jurisdictions will participate. title: Centre suspends census in Manipur amid âNRC firstâ demands by Meiteis, Nagas
text: Guwahati: The Centre has now put the entire census in Manipur on hold. Until now, only the house-listing had been kept suspended by Registrar General of India (RGI) since Sept following demand by Meitei and Naga civil societies for compilation of a National Register of Citizens (NRC) first before the population count. The RGI on Friday notified the schedule for the nationwide next phase of Census 2027 starting from Jan 25, but excluded Manipur âtill further declaration,â along with Goa, Uttar Pradesh, Punjab and Uttarakhand, Ladakh and the snow-bound non-synchronous areas of Himachal Pradesh and Jammu & Kashmir. The five states â Manipur, Goa, Uttar Pradesh, Punjab and Uttarakhand â are headed for assembly elections early in 2027, while Ladakh is preparing for local-body and autonomous hill council polls. The population enumeration in the other states and UTs will be carried out till Feb 28, 2027, followed by a revisional round from March 1 to March 5. Self-enumeration will be open from Jan 10 to 24, before house-to-house enumeration begins. The reference date is 00:00 hours on March 1, 2027. Manipurâs exclusion carries particular weight in the state where the Meitei and Naga civil society organisations want NRC first, citing concerns over alleged illegal immigration, demographic changes and the need for a verified record of the indigenous population. The demand has legislative backing. The Manipur Legislative Assembly adopted a resolution in 2022 seeking the NRC before the census, and reaffirmed it in 2024. On Sept 5, the Manipur high court directed that house-listing be kept in abeyance. The Centreâs decision to defer it came at a meeting between Union home minister Amit Shah and CM Y Khemchand Singh in New Delhi on the same day. title: â200 seats haq hai hamaraâ: Congress puts its UP poll ambitions on Lucknow walls
text: State Congress leaders are said to have framed the 200-seat demand using an âA, B, C, Dâ grading model. LUCKNOW: Posters declaring â200 seat haq hai hamaraâ (200 seats are our right) have appeared outside the Uttar Pradesh Congress Committee (UPCC) headquarters in Lucknow ahead of the 2027 assembly elections. The posters feature photographs of Rahul Gandhi , Leader of the Opposition in the Lok Sabha, and Congress general secretary Priyanka Gandhi Vadra and Congress Parliamentary Party chairperson Sonia Gandhi. The assertion comes as the Congress has reportedly submitted a wishlist of 200 assembly constituencies to its INDIA alliance partner, the Samajwadi Party (SP). 'A,B,C,D' grading model State Congress leaders are said to have framed the 200-seat demand using an âA, B, C, Dâ grading model based on organisational growth under its nationwide Sangathan Srijan Abhiyan. The demand could complicate seat-sharing negotiations between the two parties, with the SP having emerged as the dominant partner in their alliance in Uttar Pradesh. The state has 403 assembly constituencies, meaning a demand for 200 seats would put Congress in contention for nearly half of them. The posters also reflect a push within the party to seek a larger role in the state rather than continue as the junior partner in the alliance. Congress has sought to build on its performance in the 2024 Lok Sabha elections, when it won six parliamentary seats in Uttar Pradesh. The SP won 37 seats, giving the INDIA bloc a strong showing against the ruling BJP. Congress also led in 38 assembly segments and finished second in another 42 during the general election. Party workers could use these figures to argue for a bigger share of constituencies in 2027. For Congress, the negotiations will involve translating its improved electoral performance into a stronger position within the alliance. For SP, led by Akhilesh Yadav , accommodating the demand could mean giving up a substantial share of constituencies in a state where it has traditionally been the principal opposition force. The display of the posters in Lucknow comes as the Congress is reportedly seeking to conclude seat-sharing talks by mid-November. With the 2027 election looming, the two allies face the challenge of reconciling their respective ambitions while maintaining a united front against the BJP. Retired US four-star General Jack Keane said Iran had not abandoned its nuclear ambitions, arguing that the regime remained committed to restoring its capabilities despite ongoing diplomatic efforts to prevent a fresh escalation. âThey certainly havenât given up on it. It defines their regime,â Keane told Fox News, describing Iran as a âdiabolical regimeâ. He said Tehran had recommitted itself to recovering its nuclear programme and accelerating its ballistic missile development after recognising the threat its weapons posed to its adversaries, according to the New York Post. Satellite images analysed by the Institute for Science and International Security showed that Tehran had constructed makeshift earth mounds around the Pickaxe Mountain and Natanz sites to complicate potential ground raids. The rebuilding efforts extend beyond nuclear infrastructure. Iran has used the pause in direct fighting to restore missile and drone facilities and replenish its arsenal, while strengthening defences against possible renewed US attacks. IAEA director general Rafael Grossi called for the longstanding disputes to be resolved through a durable, verifiable diplomatic agreement. Tehran, however, has insisted that inspections of sites damaged in military attacks must follow specially agreed procedures. Iran suspended cooperation with the agency following US and Israeli strikes on its nuclear facilities in June 2025, although it subsequently indicated that inspectors could return under agreed arrangements. title: Six Gujarat RUPPs report over â¹2,692cr in donations over five years
text: Gandhinagar : Six registered unrecognised political parties (RUPPs) in Gujarat reported total donations running into hundreds of crores of rupees over five financial years from 2020-21 to 2024-25, according to data compiled by the independent election watchdog Association for Democratic Reforms (ADR) on the partiesâ income, expenditure, donations and electoral performance. Over the past month, Gujarat Police have registered four FIRs against such parties for allegedly receiving massive funds, routing them back to donors in cash via shell entities, and charging a 2% to 10% commission to facilitate tax evasion. According to ADRâs compilation, Bharatiya Rashtriya Janata Dal reported total donations of Rs 0.36 crore in 2020-21, Rs 189 crore in 2021-22, Rs 576.5 crore in 2022-23, Rs 191.6 crore in 2023-24 and Rs 198.8 crore in 2024-25. Its reported donations over the five years totalled Rs 1,156.1 crore. New India United Party reported total donations of Rs 407.5 crore in 2022-23 and Rs 291.6 crore in 2024-25. Its total donation figures for 2020-21, 2021-22 and 2023-24 were unavailable in the compiled data. The partyâs reported cumulative total was Rs 699.1 crore. Swatantra Abhivyakti Party reported nil donations in 2020-21, Rs 75.9 crore in 2021-22 and Rs 395.4 crore in 2022-23. Its total donation figures for 2023-24 and 2024-25 were unavailable. The cumulative figure reported in the document was Rs 75.9 crore. Satyavadi Rakshak Party reported total donations of nil in 2021-22, Rs 85.7 crore in 2022-23 and Rs 330.6 crore in 2023-24. Figures for 2020-21 and 2024-25 were unavailable. Its reported cumulative total was Rs 416.2 crore. Saurashtra Janata Paksh reported zero donations in 2020-21, Rs 131.3 crore in 2021-22, Rs 53.3 crore in 2022-23, Rs 15.9 crore in 2023-24 and Rs 10.8 crore in 2024-25. Its cumulative total was reported at Rs 211.2 crore. Jan Man Party reported total donations of Rs 97.1 crore in 2021-22, Rs 35.3 crore in 2022-23 and Rs 1.2 crore in 2023-24. Its figures for 2020-21 and 2024-25 were unavailable. The document reported its cumulative total at Rs 133.6 crore. The electoral records listed alongside the financial disclosures show that the six parties did not win any seats in Lok Sabha and assembly elections of various states. Shelly Mahajan, research manager at ADR, said that it has been observed that in earlier reports too, unrecognised political parties have received a large number of donations. âThe FIRs are a welcome development, but there is still no clarity on the delisting aspect. Authorities have not specified for how long such entities will remain delisted,â she said. title: âUS will burn like Franceâ: Trump unleashes anti-immigrant tirade in bid to boost Republicans
text: Trump blames immigration for France protests US President Donald Trump invoked violent unrest in France to attack Democrats and rally support for Republican Senator Roger Marshall in Kansas, warning that similar scenes could unfold in the United States if his political opponents prevail in the November 3 midterm elections. Earlier, Trump claimed he had warned French president Emmanuel Macron to close Franceâs borders, saying Paris would otherwise become a âMuslim cityâ. Watch 'America Will Burn Like France': Trump's EXPLOSIVE WARNING In Kansas; Warns Against Dems Victory At a rally on Monday evening, Trump blamed immigration for the unrest in France, where protests over rising cost of living and declining purchasing power escalated into looting and clashes with police in several cities, according to Reuters. âIf you want to see what is at stake in this election, just look at whatâs happening in France,â Trump told the crowd. He described France as a once-great nation that had been âconquered, looted, and burned to the ground by migrants, jihadists, and communists". âWeâre not going to let that happen to this country,â he said. âWhen you see burning steeples and â raging fires in France, just remember that is what the radical Dumocrats want to do to America.â Speaking to reporters outside the White House earlier on Monday, Trump repeated his criticism of French president Emmanuel Macronâs immigration policies, claiming he had warned him years ago to tighten border controls. âEmanuel is a friend of mine. I told him a long time ago, âYouâre making a big mistake in France. Youâre letting everybody from the world come in. The whole world was coming in. Paris was going to be a Muslim city very soon, and that wasnât the deal. That wasnât the deal.â I told him he should close up his borders. Iâve known him for eight or nine years, and I told him as soon as I met him,â Trump said. âWell, France, it is a very sad situation whatâs happening in France, because whatâs happening in France has to do with immigration, not schools, not anything. Itâs immigration,â he said. Comparing Franceâs border policies with those of the United States, he said earlier, âI said youâre making a big mistake. We closed our borders; he didnât. And you know what? His borders are a problem, and he also has a little bit of a problem with energy. But they are doing better than others. Emanuel should have closed his borders a long time ago. I told him to do it,â Trump told reporters. Nationwide demonstrations in France were called over the cost of living and pressure on household purchasing power. Reports of looting, fire and clashes prompted arrests and additional security measures, although the unrestâs causes extend beyond immigration. Trumpâs remarks came as he campaigned for Marshall, who faces a competitive challenge from Democratic candidate Adam Hamilton, a Methodist megachurch pastor. Kansas, a conservative Midwestern state that Trump won by 16 percentage points in 2024, has not elected a Democrat to the US Senate in 94 years. Economic discontent and opposition to Trumpâs tariff policies have complicated the Republican incumbentâs re-election campaign, Reuters reported. Trump has also mocked Democrats by calling them âDumocratsâ. At the rally, Trump attacked Hamilton, saying, âHe wants you to repent for being born White.â Marshall, meanwhile, criticised his opponent over cultural issues, calling him âtoo wokeâ. Economic concerns remain a challenge for Republicans ahead of the midterms. A Reuters-Ipsos poll published on Monday put Trumpâs approval rating at 31 per cent, its lowest level in the survey. title: BJP plans six mega marches across UP under outreach drive
text: Lucknow: The BJP will launch six mega foot marches across its six organisational regions under the banner of âSave Democracy, Remove Anarchyâ as part of an extensive organisational and voter outreach blueprint in Nov. Presenting the partyâs election preparedness roadmap at the BJPâs state working committee meeting, state general secretary (organisation) Dharampal Singh said each march is expected to draw at least 25,000 party workers, indicating the scale of the mobilisation exercise the party intends to undertake ahead of the crucial assembly polls. The foot marches will begin on Nov 3, with the Awadh regionâs march scheduled in Lucknow in the presence of Union minister Shivraj Singh Chouhan. On the same day, the Braj region will hold its march in Bareilly, which will be attended by Union minister and former BJP national president JP Nadda. On Nov 4, Gorakhpur regionâs march will be attended by BJP national president Nitin Nabin and state president Pankaj Chaudhary. The Kashi regionâs march in Prayagraj will have deputy chief minister Keshav Prasad Maurya, while deputy CM Brajesh Pathak will participate in the Kanpur regionâs march. Chief minister Yogi Adityanath will lead the western regionâs march in Ghaziabad on Nov 5. Singh assigned a series of responsibilities to party functionaries, laying particular emphasis on maximum voter outreach, effective deployment of workers and strengthening the organisational network at the grassroots. A key component is to identify and deploy a dedicated team of active workers across the partyâs 1,918 organisational mandals. Singh said a list of 25 active workers would be prepared in every mandal from among its nearly 60-member executive committee. These workers would undertake regular visits to all booths falling within their respective mandals. Their names and mobile numbers would be compiled to facilitate accountability and coordination. Similarly, a five-member team of active workers will be constituted at every polling booth. Assembly constituency in charges and assembly-level organisational coordinators, or vistarak, will visit Shakti Kendras to assess and verify the actual state of the partyâs organisational machinery. The exercise will also involve preparing comprehensive databases of serving and former office-bearers, elected representatives, cooperative sector functionaries, workers associated with party wings and cells, and those who have joined the BJP from other parties. Responsibilities will be assigned to them according to their organisational capabilities. The emphasis on identifying active workers and mapping their deployment suggests that the BJP intends to move beyond organisational headcounts to a more targeted system of cadre utilisation and booth-level monitoring. The party has also decided to tap its pool of experienced leaders and former elected representatives to strengthen its election machinery. Social outreach meetings, or samajik chaupals, will be organised, besides assembly-level meetings of leaders who have served as office-bearers for three consecutive terms. The BJP will intensify its beneficiary outreach campaign to establish direct contact with people who have benefited from various welfare schemes of Union and state govts. The outreach will also extend to math and temple establishments, workers associated with the wider Sangh Parivar and influential religious and social leaders. A special drive will target women and young voters, particularly those in the 18-21 age group who will be among the new entrants into the electorate. The BJP will also roll out a dedicated farmer outreach programme through kisan sampark abhiyan, farmer meetings and community feasts with members of cooperative societies. A separate campaign will target small and micro entrepreneurs, with the party planning regular interactions and outreach programmes to address their concerns and keep them connected with the organisation. The election preparedness plan will also define specific responsibilities for mayors, district panchayat chairpersons, Rajya Sabha members, MLCs, MPs, MLAs, the partyâs 2022 assembly election candidates and its 2024 Lok Sabha candidates. UP BJP Plans Tour Calendar for Top Leaders UP BJP state general secretary Dharampal Singh said the party was simultaneously preparing a detailed calendar of proposed visits and public meetings by its top leadership, including Prime Minister Narendra Modi , Union home minister Amit Shah , defence minister Rajnath Singh, chief minister Yogi Adityanath, both deputy chief ministers and state party president Pankaj Chaudhary. The responsibilities for organising meetings during the proposed visits of the national president and home minister, besides programmes involving the chief minister, deputy chief ministers and state president, will be assigned to designated functionaries. Singh asked party leaders to immediately begin preparations after the working committee meeting and ensure that all programmes scheduled for Nov and Dec were completed within the stipulated timelines. title: âDespicable betrayalâ: Top Democrat slams Haley Stevens for backing Republican candidate over El-Sayed in Michigan Senate race
text: Democratic candidate for the U.S. Senate El-Sayed. A Democratic congresswoman in Michigan has endorsed Republican Senate candidate Mike Rogers over her party's nominee Abdul El-Sayed, triggering a political storm within the party just before the US midterm elections. Haley Stevens, who lost to El-Sayed in the Democratic Senate primary in August, announced her support for Rogers on Sunday after appearing alongside him at a church service in Detroit. Her endorsement came amid a rising bitter public feud with El-Sayed, who had reportedly asked her to stay away from a planned joint campaign appearance. "Our Democratic nominee for Senate said I was no longer welcome in his campaign and that I should stay away," Stevens said in a video announcing her decision. "And he's right. And that's why I am endorsing Mike Rogers for the United States Senate today." The move drew sharp criticism from Democratic leaders, with Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer calling it a "despicable betrayal". Michigan Democratic Party chair Curtis Hertel accused Stevens of abandoning the values she claimed to support. El-Sayed, however, sought to play down the development, telling reporters that he was focused on issues affecting voters, including the rising cost of living. "At the end of the day I actually don't think about Haley Stevens," he said, adding that "none of this matters". What led to Stevens' break with El-Sayed? The rift between the two Democrats has deepened since the August primary, reflecting wider divisions within the party over its political direction and US support for Israel. Stevens, a centrist Democrat and strong supporter of Israel, had called on El-Sayed to condemn an advertisement by an independent left-wing group linking US support for Israel to high grocery prices. El-Sayed criticised the advertisement and said it was not produced by his campaign. In a statement on Friday, Stevens said El-Sayed should stop blaming Israel for economic problems facing Michigan residents. "Abdul promises to get money out of politics," she wrote. "He can begin by getting Israel out of his explanation for everything Michigan cannot afford." El-Sayed responded by accusing Stevens of trying to reopen a primary contest that had ended months earlier. He also said he did not agree with the advertisement. The two were originally expected to appear together at a church event on Sunday alongside other Democratic leaders in an effort to demonstrate party unity before Election Day. However, the planned joint appearance was called off, with Stevens instead attending a service with Rogers. Democrats react as Trump praises endorsement Stevens' decision also triggered turmoil within her own office. Her longtime chief of staff resigned following the announcement, while other staff members were expected to leave, according to a person familiar with the developments. "We are shocked and heartbroken," an aide said in a statement. Hertel said the endorsement showed that Stevens had "abandoned everything she claims to care about", while Schumer publicly condemned her decision to support the Republican candidate. President Donald Trump, meanwhile, praised Stevens, describing her move as an act of bravery and highlighting her support among Black and Jewish voters in Michigan. Speaking at a campaign rally in Iowa, House Speaker Mike Johnson also said he had spoken to Stevens after the endorsement and encouraged her to keep speaking out. Rogers welcomed the congresswoman's backing, saying he was honoured by her support. Why the Michigan Senate race matters The contest between El-Sayed and Rogers is among the closely watched Senate races in Tuesday's midterm elections. The seat is currently held by retiring Democratic Senator Gary Peters, and Republicans have not won it since 1994. Michigan is a key battleground state, having backed Joe Biden in the 2020 presidential election before voting for Trump in 2024. For Democrats, holding the seat is crucial to their efforts to regain control of the Senate. The party needs a net gain of four seats to secure a majority, making Michigan one of the most consequential contests in the election. Stevens defeated El-Sayed in Wayne County, which includes Detroit, and neighbouring Oakland County during the August primary, drawing support from Black and Jewish voters. The primary was marked by bitter exchanges and heavy outside spending, including support for Stevens from a super PAC affiliated with the American Israel Public Affairs Committee. title: Indian national charged in US over false citizenship claim to vote in 2024 election; faces up to 10 years in prison
text: Mukeshkumar Somabhai Chaudhari/Image: US Department of Homeland Security An Indian national has been charged in the United States for falsely claiming to be an American citizen to vote in the 2024 general election in Minnesota, according to the US Department of Homeland Security (DHS). Mukeshkumar Somabhai Chaudhari was indicted by a federal grand jury in Minnesota on September 10 on two counts linked to the alleged offence. The indictment accuses him of knowingly claiming US citizenship to cast a ballot. According to the indictment, Chaudhari signed a voter signature certificate on November 5, 2024, as required under Minnesota law to vote in the general election. The document required him to swear or affirm that he was a US citizen. Prosecutors allege that he was not a citizen and knowingly made the false declaration to vote. US Immigration and Customs Enforcementâs Homeland Security Investigations (HSI) arrested Chaudhari, DHS said. The charges include providing false information in voting and making a false claim of citizenship to register to vote or cast a ballot. If convicted, Chaudhari faces a maximum prison sentence of five years on each count. DHS Secretary Markwayne Mullin said the administration would pursue cases involving alleged unlawful voting by noncitizens. âVoting is reserved for US citizens, and falsely claiming citizenship to cast a ballot is a serious crime,â HSI St. Paul Special Agent in Charge Travis Pickard said. He added that the agency would continue working with law enforcement partners to investigate such cases and protect election systems. You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. title: Indian-origin woman among immigrants charged in US voter fraud crackdown; citizenship bid at risk
text: immigrants targeted by federal authorities in California this week for alleged voter fraud. An Indian-origin woman is among more than two dozen legal permanent residents charged by federal authorities in California as part of a crackdown on alleged noncitizen voter registration and voting ahead of the US midterm elections. The charges could jeopardise their efforts to become American citizens, with some facing years in prison and potential deportation. According to the Associated Press, Amandeep Kaur, who has lived in the US for eight years and is in the process of becoming a US citizen, is among those charged. Her husband, Kulwinder Singh, said she obtained her driverâs licence in 2024 and may have registered to vote while applying for it. Singh said his wife took the written driving test in Hindi because she struggles with English. Singh said his wife received and returned a ballot in 2024, but both believed it was a voter registration form. He said Kaur was now distraught over the possibility that she had unknowingly broken the law. âAll she does is cry. Itâs heartbreaking,â Singh, who is a US citizen, told The Associated Press (AP). Federal authorities charged more than two dozen legal permanent residents in California on Monday over allegations of illegally registering to vote or voting as noncitizens. By Thursday morning, prosecutors had filed charging documents in 10 of the 28 cases, providing details of how investigators used voter registration records to pursue criminal charges involving immigration status. Citizenship applications at centre of several cases Most of the immigrants charged had applied for US citizenship and now face allegations of lying on naturalisation applications or during immigration interviews. Such charges could complicate or derail their attempts to become citizens. One of the accused, JosÃ© Antonio BaÃ±uelos-DÃ­az, 42, applied for citizenship in October 2025 after living in the US for 40 years as a legal permanent resident. The government alleges he improperly claimed to be a US citizen when registering to vote in 2007 and later failed to disclose it on immigration paperwork. Authorities have not accused him of casting a ballot. BaÃ±uelos-DÃ­az told AP he did not know he had registered to vote until he was arrested outside his Los Angeles home on Monday. He recalled obtaining a driverâs licence around 2007. In California, people are prompted to register to vote when applying for a driving licence. He was released after his arrest but faces up to five years in prison if convicted. Trump administration steps up scrutiny ahead of midterms The cases form part of the Trump administrationâs broader campaign against alleged noncitizen voting before the November midterm elections, despite data showing that such voting is rare and has not been demonstrated to change election outcomes. The Justice Department said six people would be charged with voting as noncitizens, a misdemeanour. The remaining 22 face a combination of felony charges, including allegedly lying on naturalisation applications, during interviews or on voter registration forms. Noncitizens convicted of illegally voting face up to one year in prison, while those convicted of lying on applications for US citizenship can face up to 10 years. The Justice Department has also sued California over its refusal to verify the citizenship status of roughly 20,000 registered voters whom the federal government suspects may be noncitizens. California, which has more than 23 million registered voters, has maintained that it complies with federal law and argued that the administration's figures are likely significantly inflated. State election officials have also pointed out that once ballots are mailed in, they are separated from individual voter identification, making it impossible to isolate ballots based on the information supplied by federal authorities. The Department of Homeland Security did not explain what initially brought the accused immigrants to investigators' attention. However, it said the agency reviewed naturalisation and other records as part of its investigation. Some court documents refer to a benefits fraud audit conducted by Homeland Security in August that may have helped identify those charged. âThe voting rights of American citizens must be protected,â First Assistant US Attorney Bill Essayli said in a statement announcing the charges. Naturalisation approvals decline sharply The crackdown comes amid wider immigration enforcement under President Donald Trump and a slowdown in the processing of citizenship applications. Government data showed that officials approved 58,000 naturalisation applications between April and June 2026, less than a quarter of the number approved during the same period in 2025. Green card holders can generally apply for US citizenship after three years if they meet the requirements applicable to spouses of US citizens, or after five years under the standard eligibility route. Applicants must undergo background checks, answer detailed questions about voting, political activities and criminal history, pass a civics test and meet English language requirements. For immigrants already seeking citizenship, allegations involving voter registration or voting can have consequences extending beyond the immediate criminal proceedings, potentially affecting their naturalisation applications and immigration status. title: 'Guilty of centralising electoral rolls': Mallikarjun Kharge lists 6 charges against CEC Gyanesh Kumar, makes 3 demands
text: Kharge accused the CEC of centralising control over electoral rolls and acting at the behest of PM Modi. NEW DELHI: Leader of the opposition in Rajya Sabha Mallikarjun Kharge on Saturday accused Chief Election Commissioner (CEC) Gyanesh Kumar of facilitating "vote theft" and listed six charges against him at a symbolic "public impeachment" organised by the opposition INDIA bloc. Kharge alleged that the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of electoral rolls was initiated to remove voters opposed to the BJP. The proceedings began at his residence on Rajaji Marg, with former Lok Sabha Speaker Meira Kumar chairing the event. Kharge accused the CEC of centralising control over electoral rolls and acting at the behest of Prime Minister Narendra Modi and Union home minister Amit Shah. Watch 'Treason': Kharge BLASTS CEC Gyanesh Kumar, Lists 6 Charges At INDIA Bloc's Mock Parliament During the proceedings, Kharge listed six allegations against Kumar: Conspired to steal elections Deleted 13.3 crore voters Rewrote Form 6 without parliamentary oversight or knowledge Seized the electoral rolls through ECINET Breached his constitutional mandate and shut out the two other election commissioners Acted at the behest of Prime Minister Narendra Modi and Amit Shah Kharge also reiterated the opposition's three demands: The removal of the CEC An end to the SIR exercise Changes to the 2023 law governing the appointment of the chief election commissioner. Kharge also accused PM Modi government of using various means to retain power since 2014, including defections, splitting parties, misuse of central agencies and alleged electoral irregularities. "The proposal we are bringing today is to safeguard the dignity of a constitutional institution. We have no personal enmity with the CEC. Our intention is that the Election Commission should function impartially in keeping with the spirit of the Constitution. The trust of the common man in it should remain intact. No one sitting in Delhi should be able to wrongly delete the voting rights of weaker sections, women, and youth using a computer," Kharge posted on X. He further alleged that the government had repeatedly tried to retain power through various means. "The Modi government has hatched every conspiracy since 2014 to cling to power: stealing MPs, breaking parties, stealing governments, Electoral Bonds, misuse of ED/CBI. And now Vote Theftâcut opposition votes and rule. There are hundreds of examples of Vote Theft," he said. Kharge also criticised the 2023 law governing the appointment of the Chief Election Commissioner (CEC), alleging that it provided the election commissioner with legal protection. "Gyanesh Kumar is able to carry out this theft because of the 2023 CEC Act. In December 2023, this bill was passed by suspending 145 opposition MPs. This law gives the CEC a lifelong protective shield that even the President and CJI do not have," he added. Questioning the results of the 2024 Maharashtra and Haryana assembly elections, Kharge alleged that the INDIA bloc's strong performance in the Lok Sabha elections was followed by a reversal in the state polls due to electoral irregularities. "In the 2024 Lok Sabha elections, we had an excellent performance in Maharashtra and Haryana, but the results flipped in the assembly elections. Reasonâvotes were illegally added before the elections and then all names were removed. This work is being done together by Modi-Shah and Gyanesh," he alleged.
