title: Boxing Federation of India mess: Ajay Singh's rival faction meets Raksha Khadse, IOA CEO; alleges support of 27 units
text: Boxing Federation of India (BFI) members discussed their way forward against current president Ajay Singh in a meeting in New Delhi. (Photo by special arrangement) NEW DELHI: Amid an ongoing political tussle, the Boxing Federation of India's (BFI) affiliaited units and executive committee (ExCo) members sat in one room on Wednesday in New Delhi to showcase their unity and strength against the current president, Ajay Singh . Claiming the support of 27 out of 35 units and 8 of 13 ExCo members, the faction met Minister of State for Youth Affairs & Sports Raksha Khadse and Indian Olympic Association (IOA) CEO Raghuram Iyer to register their concerns via a memorandum. It was originally scheduled to be a Special General Meeting (SGM) and vote of no-confidence against Singh. Those plans were shelved by the Punjab and Haryana High Court, which put the SGM in abeyance until November 13. Watch Bombay Sport Exchange: Mustafa Ghouse on ISL, India's sporting ecosystem and grassroots problem That, however, didn't dissuade the hierarchy from coming together and expressing their displeasure with the three-time BFI president and his tenure. BFI secretary general Pramod Kumar - who was suspended by Singh - treasurer Pon Baskaran, vice-president Rajesh Bhandari, Delhi Amateur Boxing Association vice-president Rohit Jain and others said they submitted a memorandum to the Sports Ministry, the IOA and World Boxing president Gennadiy Golovkin. The memorandum accused Singh of concentrating powers in his hands, sidelining elected office-bearers and undermining democratic processes within the federation. Separately, the group alleged administrative lapses, disregard for the constitution and a âHitler-ish approachâ by Singh. "We have given our memorandum to them (Sports Ministry). Whatever issued we have, whether it is related to the constitution or technical conduct, whether it is related to coaching or selection committee, and about the administration, we have told him everything. Now, it is his decision. And we have also written to the global body. Unfortunately, the meeting we wanted to hold today wasn't possible, but let's see what changes from here," said Bhandari. "Every time an official within the Boxing Federation has questioned Ajay Singh's authority, they have either been suspended or served with a show-cause notice. If we do not get any respite from this situation, it is possible that we will sit at Jantar Mantar in the coming days," said BFI Senior VP Rajesh Bhandari. Left to right: BFI Vice President Rajesh Bhandari, Secretary General Pramod Kumar and VP of Delhi Amateur Boxing Association Rohit Jain. (Photo by special arrangement) Rohit Jain, who has challenged Singh's presidency in the past and vows to do so again, claimed the biggest issue is the constitutional overreach. "This battle started in 2024. They modified the constitution as such that it suits them. They rested all the powers at the seat of the president. They suspend any state unit without giving a notice, without assigning any reasons. Have you ever heard that someone will be suspended without giving a reason and an ad-hoc committee be formed? The main reason for this, I have to say, is that I have experienced the pain. They wanted to keep me away from boxing and competition so that I could not win the elections and could not stand in front of them. They changed the constitution not once, but twice," he said. BFI claims support of 21 authorised units On the same day, 21 of BFI's 35 authorised state units participated in a two-day âMission Olympic Podiumâ meeting in Bagdogra. Representatives of 18 units attended in person, while three joined through video conferencing. The participating units included the ad hoc committees of Mizoram and Jharkhand along with the BFI Athletes committee player representative. âOur responsibility is to the boxers and their future. The participation of a majority of our authorised state units demonstrates their commitment to working together as a federation towards our Olympic ambitions, with athletes at the centre of that effort. The work begins in the states â identifying talent, supporting coaches and creating a clear pathway for boxers to progress, gain competitive exposure and represent India. The latest developments come as the administrative chaos in the BFI continues for a third year running. The current logjam was heightened after Ajay Singh suspended Pramod Kumar, who had challenged the presidentâs authority. Singh has argued that his removal will require support from three-fourths of the General Body members. But for that, SGM needs to be called as per the constitutional norms. Meanwhile, for a no-confidence vote against Singh to succeed, the rival faction needs support of 23 units, or two-thirds. Get the latest Sports News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

title: US midterms: Trump's approval stuck at 32% in latest polling
text: Trump wrapped up his midterm campaign push on Monday with a rally at the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool in Washington, DC. President Donald Trump's approval rating remained near its lowest-ever level ahead of Tuesday's US midterm elections, with a growing number of voters viewing their ballots as a chance to register opposition to the Republican leader, a Reuters/Ipsos poll found. The poll, completed on Monday, showed Democrats leading Republicans by eight percentage points on the generic congressional ballot, 46% to 38%, even as the gap narrowed from 11 points a week earlier. The findings point to mounting political challenges for Republicans, fuelled in part by soaring fuel prices following Trump's war on Iran in February. With all 435 seats in the House of Representatives at stake, Democrats are seen as having a stronger chance of reclaiming control of the chamber, while their path in the Senate remains tougher. Trump's approval rating at 32% Trump, though not on the ballot, remains a central figure in the election. Only 32% of respondents approved of his performance, unchanged from the previous week and just above his record low of 31% recorded two weeks ago. Watch Vance Grilled On Cam: âWhy Are Trumpâs Approval Ratings âUnderwaterâ? VP Abruptly Ends Gaggle Among independent voters, 50% said their vote was intended to oppose Trump, while just 13% said it was a vote in his favour. Another 33% said the president was not a factor in their decision. Who will control Congress? Cost of living emerges as key election issue The rising cost of living also emerged as a major electoral concern, with 78% saying it would be very important or the most important factor in deciding their vote. On the issue, Democrats led Republicans 43% to 32%. Democrats also appeared more motivated to vote, with 49% of their supporters describing themselves as very enthusiastic about voting, compared with 33% of Republican voters. The Reuters/Ipsos poll surveyed 1,765 US adults online and had a margin of error of two percentage points. Trump wrapped up his midterm campaign push on Monday with a rally at the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool in Washington, DC. He has no public appearances planned for Election Day, with his schedule showing a series of private meetings, including one with John Joseph Arrigo, the US ambassador to Portugal, the Associated Press reported. His schedule also includes a closed-door âsigning timeâ, during which he typically signs executive orders, proclamations and bills passed by Congress. Trump is also scheduled to host an election night reception in the White House East Room, which is listed as closed to media coverage. However, the schedule could change depending on how Republicans fare as results come in, the AP report said. You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

title: BJP organises march in city to counter INDIA blocâs rally against SIR
text: BJP members take part in the rally which began at Bapu Vatika in Morabadi and concluded at Birsa Munda Memorial Museum Ranchi: A day after the Congress-led INDIA bloc held a rally at Delhiâs Ramlila Maidan against the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of electoral rolls and demanded the removal of Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar, the Jharkhand BJP unit on Monday organised a âSave Democracy, Remove Anarchyâ march in the city. The march was part of the BJPâs nationwide campaign to counter the INDIA blocâs narrative on the revision of electoral rolls. Hundreds of BJP workers took part in the procession, which began at Bapu Vatika in Morabadi and concluded at Birsa Munda Memorial Museum near Jail More, passing through Kutchery Chowk. Union minister Jual Oram, BJP national general secretary and Jharkhand in-charge Gajendra Singh Patel, state BJP president Aditya Sahu, leader of opposition in the assembly Babulal Marandi, former chief minister Arjun Munda and JD(U) MLA Saryu Roy were among those who participated in the programme. Targeting the INDIA bloc, Oram said parties questioning the electoral process lacked faith in democratic institutions. Taking a swipe at Congress MP Rahul Gandhi , he said, âIf you want to become Prime Minister, win the election. One cannot become PM by holding a mock Parliament.â Sahu accused Congress of selectively questioning constitutional institutions. âCongress is opposing SIR on the pretext of vote theft. It raises questions about electoral institutions only where it sees no political advantage,â he said. He also criticised the JMM-led state govt over the law-and-order situation. Marandi alleged that Rahul and other INDIA bloc constituents were attempting to create an atmosphere of instability. He said the march was aimed at exposing what he described as âanti-democraticâ politics. Reacting to the BJPâs campaign, Congress state general secretary Lal Kishore Nath Shahdeo said it was an attempt to divert attention from inflation, unemployment and other public issues. âIt is ironic that a party with a history of toppling democratically elected govts and misusing central agencies is now claiming to defend democracy,â Shahdeo said. title: 72% of Telangana and Andhra Pradesh political parties fail to disclose finances: Association for Democratic Reforms
text: 72% of T, AP political parties fail to disclose finances: ADR Hyderabad : Nearly three-fourths of registered unrecognised political parties in Telangana and Andhra Pradesh failed to publicly disclose either their annual audit statements or contribution reports for 2024-25, raising fresh concerns over transparency and financial accountability in the political system, according to a report released by the Association for Democratic Reforms (ADR) on Thursday. The report also highlighted discrepancies in donation disclosures made by two Telangana-based parties. Of the 169 registered unrecognised political parties (RUPPs) in the two states, 123, or 72%, had neither annual audit statements nor contribution reports available on the websites of the respective chief electoral officers. 31 parties have both statements online Telangana accounted for 78 of the 123 parties without either disclosure, representing 75% of its 104 RUPPs. In Andhra Pradesh, 45 of the 65 such parties had not made either report available. Only 31 parties across both states had uploaded both the audit statement and contribution report. Telangana accounted for 17 of these parties, while Andhra Pradesh had 14. Another 15 parties had only one of the two disclosures available. In Telangana, six parties had uploaded only audit statements and three only contribution reports. In Andhra Pradesh, two parties had only audit statements available, while four had uploaded only contribution reports. Donation figures differ The ADR report also flagged inconsistencies in the financial disclosures of two Telangana-based parties. A Hyderabad-based political party reported zero income and zero total donations for 2024-25, but disclosed receiving â¹1.29 lakh in contributions above â¹20,000. The party reported expenditure of â¹300 during the year. It had contested seven seats in the 2023 Telangana assembly elections, polling 49,423 votes without winning any seat. Similarly, Vishwa Bharath Party, registered in Dec 2021, declared an income of â¹900, total donations of â¹200 and expenditure of â¹5,000. However, its contribution report showed donations exceeding â¹20,000 amounting to â¹30,000. The party contested one assembly constituency in the 2023 elections, securing 55 votes. The two Telangana parties were among 14 parties across the country whose reported contributions above â¹20,000 exceeded their declared total donations. ADR noted that the reasons for such discrepancies can be established only after examining the partiesâ original accounts and contribution reports. The report also noted that the Andhra Pradesh CEOâs website did not provide consolidated information on the submission status of annual reports for 2024-25. In contrast, Telanganaâs CEO website carried details on the status of audit report submissions by political parties. Available disclosures showed that Telangana-based parties reported a combined income of â¹18.9 lakh and expenditure of â¹15.8 lakh. Parties in Andhra Pradesh reported income of â¹70.8 lakh and expenditure of â¹78.2 lakh. Together, the parties declared total donations of â¹82.7 lakh, while contributions exceeding â¹20,000 amounted to nearly â¹1.9 crore. Nationally, ADR examined financial disclosures of 2,074 registered unrecognised political parties, of which only 461 had both audit statements and contribution reports available. title: From Brazil to Cuba, US turns up the heat
text: Washington gave refuge to defeated Brazilian presidential candidate Flavio Bolsonaro as he fled the country. TOI Correspondent from Washington: US President Donald Trump's campaign to assert American primacy in the western hemisphere produced fireworks on two fronts on Wednesday. First Washington gave refuge to defeated Brazilian presidential candidate Flavio Bolsonaro as he fled the country; then it expelled from the US a Cuban diplomat alleging he tried to assault an American official. The twin episodes, coming amid the US overhang on elections in Israel and Serbia, raised questions about the use of American power and influence across the world, and its international obligations. The immediate flashpoint was Brazil, Latin Americaâs largest country, where the announcement by the State Department on Tuesday that Flavio Bolsonaro and his family would receive US visas after his loss to incumbent President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva in Sundayâs presidential runoff triggered an uproar. Bolsonaro was reported to have been spirited out of Brazil even as Brazilian law-enforcement was closing in on him after a Court order requiring him to surrender his passports took effect, amid investigations into alleged financial wrongdoing that he denies. Bolsonaro, a senator and the son of former president Jair Bolsonaro, lost after campaigning on a promise to secure his fatherâs release. The elder Bolsonaro is serving a 27-year sentence under house arrest for attempting to overturn the 2022 election result, echoing the 2020 insurrection in the US Flavio too has refused to concede defeat and alleged electoral irregularities in the just concluded election without producing evidence sufficient to substantiate his claims. For Lula's government, the visa decision will be difficult to separate from Washingtonâs broader pattern of pressure on BrasÃ­lia. Trump too has questioned Brazilâs electoral process, imposed tariffs on Brazilian exports and supported the Bolsonaro familyâs political cause. Washington also revoked the visa of Brazilâs ambassador in August amid a dispute over diplomatic appointments and access for US officials. BrasÃ­lia has characterised such measures as politically motivated interference in its domestic affairs. A Brazilian judge on Tuesday ordered a police investigation into alleged ties between a donor network co-founded by Vice President JD Vance and the Bolsonaro campaign. While the distinction between granting entry and offering political protection is important -- a US visa does not confer asylum, immunity from prosecution or permanent refuge -- the political signal is unmistakable. By welcoming a defeated opposition leader facing domestic legal scrutiny, Washington risks reinforcing perceptions that its support for democratic processes is conditional on whether the winners are ideologically aligned. The precedent is not without historical parallels. In 1979, President Jimmy Carter admitted the ailing Shah of Iran, Mohammad Reza Pahlavi, for medical treatment after the Islamic Revolution had driven him into exile. Iranian revolutionaries cited the decision as justification for seizing the US Embassy in Tehran, beginning a 444-day hostage crisis that transformed relations between Washington and Tehran for generations. The episode became a potent symbol of American interference and the perceived protection of a discredited ally. The point, diplomats say, is not that sheltering a foreign political figure inevitably produces disaster. Governments, including New Delhi, often admit exiles, dissidents and former allies for humanitarian, political or strategic reasons. But decisions framed in Washington or New Delhi as individual concerns can acquire a very different meaning in the country from which the individual has fled as is happening in Brazil and Bangladesh. In a separate flare-up, US Ambassador to the UN Mike Waltz and Cuban Foreign Minister Bruno RodrÃ­guez engaged in an extraordinary slanging match during a General Assembly debate over Washingtonâs decades-old economic embargo against Cuba. Cuban delegates banged on their table and shouted objections as Waltz denounced Havana, holding up a photos of Cuban leaders, including the late Fidel Castro wearing Rolex watches. Rodriguez approached the podium and called the American ambassador a liar. âThis is America. Back up,â Waltz retorted as the fracas intensified. Observers later pointed out that while the US hosts the United Nations, it is not an American institution and Washington does not have sovereign authority over the organisation. Still, the First Secretary of Cuba's UN delegation Richard Tur de la Concepcion was sent packing back to Havana with accusations that during the altercation, he lunged at Waltz's spokesman, JP Freire, and attempted to snatch an iPhone Freire was recording with. "You lay a hand on an American here in the United States,... we're not gonna stand for it," Waltz later said, revealing that Secretary of State Marco Rubio, who is Cuban-American, has signed paperwork to expel Conception. title: Vijayawada municipal polls record 55% turnout, parties concerned
text: Vijayawada : The overall polling percentage recorded in the just-concluded Vijayawada Municipal Corporation (VMC) elections has left the two main political parties in a tizzy, with the turnout remaining significantly below expectations at just 55.35 percent. This was considerably lower than the 62.88 percent polling recorded in the 2021 municipal general elections. Political party leaders attributed the decline in voter turnout to several factors, including voters working in neighbouring states not turning up to vote and the failure to distribute voter slips to voters, which made it difficult for some to locate their polling booths following the delimitation of wards in the city. âMany had anticipated the polling percentage to cross 70 percent, but the voter turnout was just around 55 percent, which was 7.53 percentage points lower than the figure recorded in the previous municipal elections. This could result in mayoral candidates securing lower victory margins, as the total number of votes polled was only around 4.40 lakh, significantly lower than the nearly six lakh votes expected to be polled in the municipal elections,â a senior political party leader in the city said. Some leaders said that although voters enthusiastically turned up to exercise their franchise, the failure of booth-level officers (BLOs) to distribute voter slips had forced several voters to leave polling stations without casting their votes. Another reason cited by political leaders was the failure of working professionals and their families residing in neighbouring states to return to the city to cast their votes. Some voters originally from Vijayawada but currently residing in neighbouring states reportedly abstained from voting, stating that municipal elections would not have any impact on the incumbent state government. title: Hegseth fires top Pentagon military planner as Trump weighs fresh Iran strikes: Report
text: He is the second general to be ousted from the post, known in military circles as the âJ5â, under Hegseth The Pentagon's senior officer responsible for military strategy and planning has been removed from his post as the Trump administration weighs its next move in the war with Iran, adding to questions over leadership changes at the US Defence Department at a critical moment for regional security. Army Lt Gen Brett Sylvia's departure was confirmed by a US defence official on Wednesday, reported Associated Press. Sylvia headed the strategy, plans and policy directorate, known within the military as the J5, which helps coordinate military planning with the chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff and the president. The official, who spoke on condition of anonymity because the matter involved sensitive personnel issues, said no reason had been provided for Sylvia's removal and no immediate successor had been identified. Watch Iran War âLeakâ SHOCKS Pentagon; Hegseth OUSTS Top General As Trump Mulls New Military Strikes The timing is significant as President Donald Trump is reportedly considering whether to resume attacks on Iran after the November 3 US midterm elections. Washington has alerted regional partners to prepare for possible renewed military action and the risk of Iranian retaliation, according to two diplomats briefed on the warnings. Trump has not taken a final decision on further strikes. However, the warnings have prompted concerns among regional governments about attacks on energy installations and other critical infrastructure if hostilities intensify. The J5 plays a central role in translating military objectives into operational plans. The Pentagon recently sent the USS Theodore Roosevelt aircraft carrier and amphibious ships carrying Marines towards the Persian Gulf, a deployment involving about 9,000 troops. The additional forces could help expand US military options, although their presence does not establish whether or when Trump will authorise another attack. Although regional governments are said to be preparing for the possibility that a renewed US campaign could trigger retaliation extending beyond the initial period of American strikes. The diplomats said US officials had indicated that a fresh round of military action could last several days, while Iranian counterattacks and actions by allied groups could prolong the confrontation. Iran, meanwhile, has continued to signal an interest in negotiations. Foreign minister Abbas Araghchi said Wednesday that Tehran âcontinues to give diplomacy a chance to succeedâ and is working with mediators to review proposals it wants to use as a basis for restoring a ceasefire. Trump had previously rejected the proposal. The United Arab Emirates also urged the parties to avoid escalation, calling on them to âexercise wisdom and pursue political solutions to help contain tensionsâ. Trump keeps military option open Trump has alternated between suggesting the conflict could end soon and warning that further bombing remains possible. During a campaign appearance in Texas earlier this week, he said an end to the war could come âin a couple of weeks, if you donât mindâ. âSomebody asked me before, when will the war in Iran end?â Trump said. âI said, âWhenever I want it to end.â Itâll be very quick, but we have to have it end properly, with total and complete -- a total statement, they will never have a nuclear weapon. â The conflict has also created political and economic pressures for the administration ahead of the midterms. Higher gasoline prices have weighed on voters, while the Pentagon's latest estimate puts the cost of the war to American taxpayers at $47.1 billion. Jonathan Schanzer, executive director of the Foundation for Defense of Democracies, warned that Tehran might not wait for Washington's preferred timeline if it believed an attack was imminent. âWhy would they wait until after the elections here ... if they could initiate it and potentially gain the upper hand?â he said. Senior officers exit under Hegseth Sylvia's removal adds to a succession of departures among senior military leaders during Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth's tenure. He is the second general to leave the J5 director's post under Hegseth. Lt Gen Joseph McGee, his predecessor, was forced to retire last October. Before joining the Joint Staff, Sylvia commanded the 101st Airborne Division at Fort Campbell, Kentucky, until May 2025. He had previously served as vice director of the J5. The Joint Staff offered no explanation for the change but acknowledged Sylvia's service. âThe Chairman, the Joint Staff, and the Joint Force extend our deepest gratitude to Lt Gen Brett Sylvia and his family for their 32 years of distinguished service to our nation,â a spokesperson said. Nearly two dozen generals, admirals and other military leaders have been fired, pressed to retire or otherwise departed under Hegseth, with the Pentagon publicly explaining few of the cases. The departures have included civilian leaders of the Army and Navy and senior uniformed officers across the services. Hegseth has also ordered a reduction in senior officer positions. Last month, he said the military should cut the number of top officers by 20% by January 1, 2027, doubling the planned reductions. The military has roughly 800 general and flag officer positions. âI call it accountability and long overdue,â Hegseth told junior officers and enlisted leaders at Marine Corps Base Quantico on September 30. The cuts have drawn criticism from some lawmakers, who argue that removing experienced commanders could damage military leadership over the longer term. âHe's got some kind of like deep-seated grievance about leadership in the military,â Senator Mark Kelly, a former Navy combat pilot critical of Hegseth, said last month. âHe's purging a generation of great leaders of the military, and it's going to take a generation to recover from it.â Poll Vote & Share your view How do you rate the transparency of the Pentagon leadership changes under Secretary Hegseth? title: BJP can surpass 2017 tally if poll prep is completed early: Tawde

Chairing an organisational meeting at the state party office in Lucknow, Tawde emphasised that the upcoming election hinges on âmicromanagement,â requiring meticulous attention to every aspect of the action plan. The meeting was attended by UP BJP chief Pankaj Chaudhary; state general secretary (Organization) Dharampal Singh and state co-in-charges Medha Kulkarni, Jagdish Patel, Anant Ojha, and Pradeep Verma. Tawde directed that the appointment of âpravasi prabharisâ at the Assembly constituency level be expedited, and that election management committees be constituted at both the district and Assembly levels. Tawde said that members of the Mahila Morcha and Yuva Morcha will serve as the visiting in-charges at the Assembly level. He instructed all district in-charges to complete their visits to the Assembly constituencies and asked all Assembly-level in-charges to visit the Shakti Kendras. Tawdeâs observations underlines BJPâs poll urgency as it tries to scale up organisational work for the Assembly elections. His directions came a day after the UP state working committee rolled out the formal blueprint of the organisational exercise which the party would take to build on an electoral momentum. He said that âvistaraksâ (full-time party workers) must immediately begin holding meetings with active party members at the âmandal (local/zonal) level and ensure visits to the âShakti Kendrasâ. Chaudhary emphasised that the mantra for winning elections lay at the âboothâ and the voters associated with them. âWe must prioritize the verification of electoral rolls and the special revision campaign,â he said, stressing the need for having a robust team of party workers who can be engaged at all 1,918 âmandalsâ. Dharampal Singh said that as part of preparation, âDistrict Election Steering Committeesâ and âAssembly Election Steering Committeesâ were required to be formed. He noted that the most significant initiative leading up to Diwali was the series of âpadyatrasâ (foot marches) to be organised at the regional level under the âSave Democracy, Eliminate Anarchyâ. title: Trump dangles $15 billion lifeline to farmers as US midterms loom
text: Farmers have expressed mixed reactions to the assistance. While many welcome the support that could help keep their businesses afloat, some view the programmes as one-time bailouts rather than a long-term solution. The Donald Trump administration has announced more than $15 billion in payments, loans and other support for US farmers in the weeks before the midterm elections, seeking to ease the impact of soaring fuel and fertiliser costs. The measures, announced by the US Department of Agriculture (USDA), come as farmers struggle with higher expenses linked largely to Trump's tariffs and the war in Iran. The move is also aimed at supporting agricultural producers in rural states where traditionally Republican seats are becoming competitive. Trump is scheduled to visit Iowa and Kansas on Sunday, two days before the election, as he steps up his focus on rural voters. However, it remains unclear whether the financial assistance will encourage more farmers and other rural voters to turn out in support of Republican candidates. Watch 'YOU'RE FIRED, MARCO!': Trump Shocks Rubio At Kansas Rally With This 1 Liner | Watch More than half of the announced $15 billion package will go towards an $8 billion one-time payment programme for farmers facing a sharp rise in diesel prices. The USDA said it would release further details this month. However, it has not specified when farmers will receive the money. The package also includes at least $5 billion in guaranteed loans for ranchers and fishermen. Another $1.8 billion will go to producers and landowners enrolled in conservation programmes. The USDA has allocated $573 million for fertiliser manufacturing projects and $57 million to expand meat processing capacity. Specialty crop producers will receive $86.6 million in grants for innovative projects. Separately, the department plans to purchase up to $472.5 million worth of agricultural commodities to support producers and supply charitable programmes. These initiatives come in addition to $13.8 billion in safety net payments planned for eligible farmers for the 2025 crop year. The payments are intended to cover financial shortfalls for producers of key crops, including corn, soybeans, wheat and rice. The USDA has also announced measures to expand sales of diesel normally restricted to off-road use, improve transparency in cattle sale data and strengthen wolf management policies to protect livestock. Farmers face rising costs The financial assistance comes after a difficult year for US farmers, who have faced rising fuel and fertiliser costs, alongside higher expenses for agricultural equipment due to tariffs imposed last year. The trade war with China also led to a near boycott of US agricultural goods. Diesel prices have been a particular concern. On Friday, the average price stood at $6.32 per gallon, slightly below its September peak but 70% higher than a year earlier, according to motor club AAA. Filling a 100-gallon tank now costs farmers around $260 more than it did a year ago. Gregg Ibendahl, a farm management specialist at Kansas State University, said the payments could more than compensate for the increase in fuel costs and help farmers deal with expensive fertiliser. He said: âThat input side risk, I think, is the thing that really has hurt farmers this year, as well as the fact that there has been a lot more uncertainty about whatâs going to happen in the world,â Ibendahl expects the additional payments to help farmers who might otherwise fail to make a profit this year. However, he cautioned that temporary government assistance would not address the wider problems driving up production costs. âItâs hard to go to your lender in the next spring and say, âOK, well, weâre looking pretty good this year, but itâs all because of these extra temporary government payments, so how much can you make me a loan (for) next year for my crop?ââ he said. Alexandra Middlewood, an associate professor of political science at Wichita State University, said farmers have expressed mixed reactions to the assistance. While many welcome the support that could help keep their businesses afloat, some view the programmes as one-time bailouts rather than a long-term solution. Rural voters and the midterm elections The agricultural sector has traditionally been an important source of support for Trump, particularly in rural states. However, some of his policies have also affected farmers and businesses dependent on the agricultural economy. Michael Smith, a political science professor at Emporia State University, said immigration deportations have threatened the agricultural labour force. Cuts to foreign aid and food assistance programmes such as SNAP have also affected the market for agricultural products. âSome people who admire Trump really just admire the person, the man,â he said. âBut it doesnât mean they necessarily like his policies. Well, Trump himself isnât on the ballot this year. His policies are.â Middlewood said the cost of living and access to healthcare remain major concerns among rural voters. She added that there is a perception that the administration has not done enough to address these issues, despite Trump's claims at campaign rallies about a booming economy. She does not expect dissatisfied rural voters in Kansas to shift towards the Democratic Party, given the state's long-standing Republican leanings. However, some could choose not to vote or support independent candidates, potentially affecting Republican prospects. âIndependent voters make or break elections," she said. "And so thatâs really what itâs going to come down to this year is those independent voters and who theyâre breaking for.â You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

title: 'He was crying and grabbing the doctor's hands to stop him': US organ donation group faces decertification after Kentucky manâs near-fatal ordeal
text: âMy brother grabbed the doctorâs hand as he tried to harvest his organsâ¦â Donna Rhorerâs account of what happened to her brother, Anthony Thomas âTJâ Hoover II, has become central to a case raising serious questions about patient safety and oversight in the US organ donation system. Hoover, who was taken for organ donation after a drug overdose in Kentucky in October 2021, showed signs of life as preparations for organ retrieval progressed. Nearly five years later, the case has drawn renewed scrutiny after US authorities moved to decertify Network for Hope, the organisation responsible for coordinating organ donations in the region. The US Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) announced on August 5, 2026, that it had begun the process of decertifying Network for Hope following federal reviews that identified concerning patient-safety practices in multiple cases involving potential organ donors. Rhorer described her experience in testimony at the Kentucky Attorney Generalâs office, recounting how her family had been told that Hoover had no reflexes or brain activity and would not recover. They agreed to withdraw life support and honour his wishes to become an organ donor. However, she said, his behaviour during the subsequent preparations raised questions about whether he was still alive. âI was there, I saw what happened to my brother. They prepared to recover his organs while he was still alive. During that honour walk his eyes were open, he was tracking me and they told me it was just reflex,â Rhorer testified. âAnd then during the heart cath, he was thrashing, crying and grabbing the doctor's hands to stop him. Even after those signs the organ procurement continued until the physician refused to proceed.â Rhorer also alleged that a coordinator contacted the organisationâs home office after the doctor refused to continue, only to be told to find another surgeon or risk losing her job. âOne of the organisationâs own coordinators called the home office after the doctor refused, she was told, âfind another surgeon or you'll lose your job because we're finishing this case. My brother almost died that day, that should never happen to anyone. Laws and standards were clearly violated, those responsible must be held accountable,â she said. When the procedure was stopped, Rhorer said, the family was told to take Hoover home and make him comfortable because he was not expected to survive much longer. âWell, it's been five years, and he's still here. I'm grateful every day for that but he is not the same, he has nightmares, he struggles remembering things and he asked me 'sis, why do they wanna kill me?' I don't have an answer for him,â she said. Procedure stopped, but questions remained Hooverâs case came to wider public attention in October 2024, when NPR reported accounts from witnesses who said he had shown signs of life during preparations for organ recovery. The Guardian also reported on the incident, including the concerns raised by former employees of the Kentucky Organ Donor Affiliates (KODA), the organisation now known as Network for Hope. Former KODA employee Nyckoletta Martin and organ-preservationist Natasha Miller raised concerns about Hooverâs condition. Miller, whose work involved preserving organs after removal, reportedly witnessed Hoover thrashing and crying on the operating table. Other accounts described him moving his head and pulling his knees towards his chest. The organ retrieval was ultimately stopped after a physician refused to proceed. Rhorer said the family was not initially given a full explanation of what had happened. She later learned more about the incident after a former KODA employee contacted her in January 2024. Hoover survived, but his family has described lasting difficulties with memory and other aspects of his daily life. Rhorerâs account has since become part of a wider debate over the responsibilities of organ procurement organisations (OPOs), which coordinate donations between hospitals, potential donors and transplant centres. Federal investigation identifies wider concerns The controversy intensified after federal authorities examined hundreds of cases handled by Network for Hope. In its August 5, 2026 announcement, HHS said the Health Resources and Services Administration had reviewed 351 cases between 2021 and 2024 in which organ donation had been authorised but ultimately did not proceed. Of those cases, 103 had concerning features, according to the department. It said 73 patients displayed neurological signs incompatible with organ donation. The review raised concerns about neurological assessments, communication between medical teams, consent practices and the classification of causes of death, particularly in cases involving drug overdoses. The findings do not mean that organs were removed from all the patients reviewed. Instead, they point to concerns about the assessments and preparations undertaken before donation could proceed. Organ recovery must follow the applicable medical and legal requirements for determining death. US authorities move to decertify Network for Hope Following the federal review, HHS said Network for Hope had failed to demonstrate sufficient improvement despite earlier corrective measures and monitoring. Authorities therefore began the process of decertifying the organisation, which coordinates organ procurement across Kentucky and parts of Indiana, Ohio and West Virginia. The Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services issued a notice stating that its Medicare agreement with Network for Hope would be terminated on November 3, 2026, subject to the applicable process. The organisationâs donation service area is expected to be transferred through a process that depends on the outcome of any appeal or the organisationâs decision not to appeal. Network for Hope has disputed aspects of the allegations and maintained that organ procurement organisations do not provide patient care or independently declare death. The organisation has also said that organ recovery can proceed only after an independent healthcare provider has declared a patient dead. The regulatory action has placed renewed focus on how hospitals and organ procurement organisations communicate with families, assess neurological activity and respond when relatives or medical staff raise concerns about a patientâs condition. The United States has more than 100,000 people waiting for organ transplants, making public confidence in the donation system critical. Experts and transplant advocates have stressed the importance of investigating alleged failures thoroughly while ensuring that individual cases do not discourage people from donating organs that could save lives. For Rhorer, however, the issue remains deeply personal. Her brother survived the procedure that was meant to lead to organ recovery, but she says he continues to live with the consequences of what happened. His case has now become part of a wider examination of patient safety and accountability in the US organ donation system. You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

title: Dan vs Daniel: Trump administration sues to block Alaska result if GOP candidate loses race
text: Trump has repeatedly criticised Daniel J. Sullivan's presence on the ballot. The US Department of Justice has filed a lawsuit seeking to prevent Alaska from certifying its Senate election results if Republican Senator Dan Sullivan loses to Democrat Mary Peltola while another candidate with the same name remains on the ballot. The case could trigger a wider legal battle between the Trump administration and state authorities over the certification of election results, particularly in races where Republicans face a risk of losing seats. The lawsuit, filed in federal court in Alaska on Thursday, argues that the state must protect the integrity of federal elections. It asks the court to block the certification of a Peltola victory if Daniel J. Sullivan, a candidate from the small fishing community of Petersburg, remains on the ballot. âThe United States accordingly brings this lawsuit to protect the integrity of the 2026 Senate election in Alaska,â the lawsuit says. Republicans have alleged that Daniel J. Sullivan is a Democratic plant intended to draw votes away from the incumbent senator. However, he has said he entered the race independently. Two candidates with the same name on ballot The Alaska Senate race has attracted attention because its outcome could help determine which party controls the Senate. Dan Sullivan is seeking re-election against Peltola, a former congresswoman. Daniel J. Sullivan will also appear on the ballot without a party designation, while the senator will be identified as the Republican incumbent. Alaska's ranked choice voting system allows voters to rank candidates in order of preference, meaning voters confused by the two names could select both. The Alaska Supreme Court has already rejected an earlier Republican attempt to remove Daniel J. Sullivan from the ballot. Republican officials in the state also made the decisions about how the two candidates would be listed. Neither the senator's campaign nor Daniel J. Sullivan immediately responded to requests for comment. The Trump administration has increasingly used the Justice Department to pursue legal action against political opponents and Democratic-controlled states ahead of elections. Democrats and voting rights advocates have warned that the administration could try to prevent the certification of results in races lost by Trump's party, drawing comparisons with the president's unsuccessful attempts to overturn his 2020 defeat to Joe Biden. US Attorney General Todd Blanche said the department did not intend to interfere improperly in elections. âIt is not DOJâs intention to, and itâs never our intention to, improperly interfere with elections or the state certification process," he told reporters in Virginia on Thursday, before the lawsuit was filed. The lawsuit was signed by Associate US Attorney General Stanley Woodward, who represented Trump allies and defendants in cases related to the January 6 attack on the US Capitol before joining the department's senior leadership. Legal challenge faces questions over its merits Derek Muller, a law professor at the University of Notre Dame, said the case would probably become relevant only if Republicans narrowly lost the Alaska Senate race. He also questioned whether the lawsuit had a sound legal basis. âThe statute simply doesn't let the Department of Justice enjoin certification,â he said. âThe lawsuit could well be mooted by a wide Democratic victory or a narrow Republican one, and if not, the court will likely dismiss it next month.â The US Constitution gives states the authority to administer their elections, while federal elections must also follow standards set by Congress. Trump has repeatedly sought to change election procedures through executive orders, several of which have been blocked by courts. Certifying an election is the formal process through which a state confirms the winner. The Justice Department's lawsuit seeks to stop that process in a specific set of circumstances in Alaska. The state's ranked choice voting system could further complicate the race. The system allows voters to rank candidates by preference, with votes redistributed as candidates are eliminated until a winner emerges. Trump opposes the system, and a separate ballot measure will ask voters whether it should be repealed. The final result could take weeks to determine. Trump calls rival candidate's presence âcheatingâ Trump has repeatedly criticised Daniel J. Sullivan's presence on the ballot, raising the issue at a rally in Alaska this month and in social media posts. In a post on Wednesday, he wrote, âWe are looking at powerful legal options to remove the fraudulent Daniel J. Sullivan Jr. from the Ballot, and holding the Democrats accountable for their Election Interference, in the pursuit of Justice and Fairness,â In another post this week, Trump described the situation as âCHEATING.â Candidates with similar names have long been used in US elections in attempts to divert votes from a rival. Such tactics can be particularly significant in closely contested races. Republicans have also been linked to an effort to encourage Ohio voters to support a socialist candidate in that state's Senate race. title: US accuses Canada of interference in midterm elections, Carney denies charges
text: US President Donald Trump. The US Embassy in Ottawa has accused Canadian leaders of attempting to influence American politics ahead of the November midterm elections, escalating tensions between the two neighbours amid an ongoing trade dispute under President Donald Trumpâs administration. According to the BBC, the embassy released a fact sheet on Wednesday alleging that Canadian ministers and provincial premiers had openly discussed plans to influence American politics through official documents and public appearances. The document cited meetings with US Democratic leaders and calls for retaliatory tariffs targeting politically significant American states. The unsigned document singled out Canadian Industry Minister MÃ©lanie Joly, Ontario Premier Doug Ford, Liberal MP Anthony Housefather and Bernadette Jordan, a former cabinet minister who now serves as Canada's consul general in Boston. Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney and Ford rejected the allegations, arguing that Ottawa's actions were a response to Washington's trade measures rather than an attempt to interfere in US elections. Speaking at a press conference on Wednesday, Carney said the US had initiated the trade actions against Canada and that his government had responded to protect Canadian jobs and businesses. "We've responded to those to protect Canadian jobs, to protect Canadian companies and develop our economy," Carney said, adding that the measures were in the interests of Canadian workers, families and the country's economic future. Carney was announcing an aid package worth nearly C$9 billion to support businesses and workers affected by US tariffs. Joly and Ford were also present at the announcement. Ford said he had "no interest at all" in interfering in American elections, adding that his focus remained on Ontario and Canada. "I'll tell you what the American people want. They want certainty, they want stability," Ford said, adding that American voters would decide the outcome of the midterm elections. Why US has accused Canada of election interference The embassy's allegations focused partly on Canada's retaliatory tariffs against American goods. The measures were introduced in response to tariffs imposed by the Trump administration and have become a major source of friction between Washington and Ottawa. The fact sheet cited comments by Joly about targeting products from politically significant US states. In August, when Canada announced retaliatory tariffs, she said the measures were intended partly to exert political pressure on the US. The embassy also referred to Joly's response when asked what she expected from US tariff policy if Democrats won the midterm elections. "That's exactly why I'm meeting so many governors and potential presidential candidates," she said. Ontario Premier Ford had also urged Canada's federal government to consider further retaliatory tariffs on imports from states considered important to Trump's political support base. The document also highlighted Housefather's campaign activities with a Democratic candidate in Florida and alleged that Canada was the second-largest source of foreign nationals prosecuted in the US for fraudulent or illegal voting, citing figures from the US Department of Justice. It urged Canadians to refrain from attempting to participate in or influence American elections, stating that Americans should decide their own elections. Canada rejects allegations as tensions deepen Joly has repeatedly denied that Canada is interfering in US elections. Last week, she said her visits to the US were aimed at attracting investment from American companies and that she planned to continue those efforts. She also said Canadians would not accept similar interference in their own elections, according to the BBC. Earlier this month, US Ambassador to Canada Pete Hoekstra warned that American officials were closely monitoring Canadian politicians for signs of election interference. White House adviser Peter Navarro had also warned Canadians against interfering in the US midterms. "Please, if you're on K Street, get the hell out of our country," Navarro said, referring to the Washington lobbying industry. The dispute comes as relations between the two countries have deteriorated over trade, tariffs and Trump's repeated remarks about making Canada the 51st US state. Carney has also pushed for Canada to reduce its economic dependence on the US. Speaking at a rally in Calgary ahead of a referendum on Alberta's separation from Canada, he joked that Washington might interpret his remarks as election interference. "They might think that's election interference. They're a little touchy down there," Carney said. The November midterm elections will determine which party controls the US House of Representatives and Senate, potentially shaping the remainder of Trump's presidency and the administration's ability to advance its legislative agenda. Meanwhile, a petition calling for Hoekstra's removal over concerns that he has undermined Canada-US diplomatic relations has received more than 280,000 signatures. You use AI every day. title: Former Mossad officer helped FlÃ¡vio Bolsonaro flee Brazil: Report
text: File photo: After losing Brazilâs election, FlÃ¡vio Bolsonaro fled to Miami in an elaborate operation aided by a former Mossad agent, Trumpâs inner circle and Argentinaâs president A former agent of Israelâs Mossad intelligence agency reportedly accompanied Brazilian senator and defeated presidential candidate FlÃ¡vio Bolsonaro as he crossed into Argentina before flying to the United States, according to an investigation by CNN Brasil. Bolsonaro, his wife Fernanda and their two daughters crossed from Brazil into Argentina on Tuesday, October 27, through the Tancredo Neves International Bridge, which connects Foz do IguaÃ§u with Puerto IguazÃº. According to CNN Brasil, the family travelled in two vans, with Bolsonaro accompanied by the former Mossad officer in one vehicle and his family in the other. The former Israeli intelligence officer reportedly arrived in Brazil on October 19, six days before the presidential runoff. He is said to have travelled with Bolsonaro from BrasÃ­lia to the Argentine border and remained in the same van during the crossing. His identity has not been disclosed. The investigation has not established what role, if any, he played in planning or organising the departure. Security camera footage helped Brazilian investigators identify the two vans and their drivers. One was a former municipal council member from Foz do IguaÃ§u, while the other was his son. After crossing into Argentina, the family boarded a Gulfstream G400 private jet operated by Argentine charter company Baires Fly. The aircraft stopped in Guayaquil, Ecuador, to refuel before continuing to Opa-locka Executive Airport near Miami, where it landed early on Wednesday, October 28. The operation was reportedly referred to internally as âOperation Albaâ and had been planned before the election campaign ended. Brazilian investigators are examining possible logistical support from contacts linked to the governments of Argentine president Javier Milei and US president Donald Trump . However, direct involvement by either government in arranging the departure has not been established. A report by The New York Times said Trump adviser Jason Miller helped arrange the private jet. Argentine newspaper ClarÃ­n separately reported that Mileiâs adviser Santiago Caputo travelled to the border region to oversee the operation. These accounts have added to questions over the extent of assistance Bolsonaro received from political allies abroad. Bolsonaro lost the October 25 presidential runoff to incumbent Luiz InÃ¡cio Lula da Silva and had been ordered by the Brazilian Supreme Federal to surrender his personal and diplomatic passports and barred him from leaving Brazil. The order was issued amid investigations into suspected money laundering, including cases linked to gambling platforms and the funding of a film about his father, former president Jair Bolsonaro. FlÃ¡vio Bolsonaro has denied wrongdoing. Brazilâs federal police said it found no record of the senator leaving through official immigration checkpoints and is investigating how he crossed the border. Authorities are considering asking the Supreme Court to freeze his assets, including bank accounts. The allegations against him remain under investigation and have not been proven in court. The episode has also triggered diplomatic questions. Brazilâs foreign ministry summoned Argentinaâs representative to seek clarification over the senatorâs passage through the country. In the United States, 25 Democratic lawmakers reportedly asked the Trump administration whether diplomatic resources had been used to assist his departure. US secretary of state Marco Rubio has said the administration was not directly involved in the arrangements that took Bolsonaro to the United States. Trump, however, approved the familyâs entry after they reached the country. Bolsonaro entered under humanitarian parole, which is generally granted for a limited period. Trump later said Bolsonaro could remain in the United States for as long as he wished, while questioning the outcome of Brazilâs election. The US president also said he had no plans to meet the senator. Bolsonaro has meanwhile described himself as Brazilâs âleaderâ and thanked Trump and Milei for their support. title: Spain train crash: Four Americans, one Canadian among 69 killed
text: Images from the high speed train crash in Spain. Authorities in Spain have identified 66 of the 69 people killed in last week's high-speed train collision, including four Americans and one Canadian. Spanish nationals made up the majority of the victims, with 54 confirmed dead. The crash occurred last Wednesday in the province of Toledo when a high-speed train slammed into another train that had stopped on the tracks. Among the other foreign nationals identified were citizens of France, Japan, Argentina, Mexico, Portugal, Tunisia and the Czech Republic, with one victim from each country. Authorities said three bodies were yet to be identified. Three people also remain missing â two Australians and one Japanese national. The latest collision came just nine months after another train crash farther south on the same Madrid-Seville line killed 46 people. The two incidents have shaken public confidence in Spain's rail network, which has long been recognised for its high speeds and safety record. Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez has promised a full investigation and improvements to restore trust in the railway system. The network carried around 45 million passengers last year, including millions of tourists. The crash occurred a month before the November 29 general election, in which Sanchez is seeking to extend his eight-year tenure as prime minister. The incident has raised questions over railway safety and the investment made by successive governments in Spain's infrastructure. You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

title: âWhere did 300,000 children go?â: YouTuber Nick Shirley targets US NGOs over alleged trafficking network
text: âWhere did 300,000 children go?â: YouTuber Nick Shirley targets US NGOs over alleged trafficking network YouTuber Nick Shirley has accused several US non-governmental organizations (NGOs) of being involved in the trafficking of more than 300,000 children across the country. In a new investigative video, the YouTuber claimed that these groups received millions of dollars in government funding while children went missing from the system. He also questioned what happened to children who crossed the US border in recent years. Shirley called the alleged operation the "largest government-funded human trafficking ring in history." However, his claims have not been independently established. Nick Shirley Questions Where Thousands of Migrant Children Went After Entering the US In a post on X, YouTuber Shirley shared his allegations and pointed to the amount of public money he believes went to the organizations involved. "Your tax dollars trafficked over 300,000 children across the United States while NGOs enriched themselves with millions of dollars," he wrote. He also claimed that one organization received around $895 million to move children across the country, while others received more than $100 million. However, he did not establish in his post that these payments were used for human trafficking. In the video, Shirley spoke about a 17-year-old girl who reportedly crossed the US border illegally in 2023. He questioned what had happened to children who entered the country during those years and why their current whereabouts were unclear. He also interviewed a woman who was introduced as a former contract specialist at the US General Services Administration (GSA). She said the children were meant to be placed with sponsors. However, the discussion raised questions about who those sponsors were and what information was available about the children after their release. Shirley then approached several officials to ask about the children. According to the footage, the people he questioned said they did not know where the children were. One organization he named was VisionQuest, a Tucson-based group that provides services to children and families. Shirley questioned its staff about the government funding it had received and tried to get answers about its work. However, he did not receive a response from the employees he approached. Federal records do confirm that VisionQuest received government funding. According to the US government's USAspending website, the organization had a grant worth around $16.8 million for services under the Unaccompanied Alien Children Program between May 2023 and October 2026. This funding record does not establish Shirley's allegation of human trafficking. Nick Shirley Visits More NGOs After Making Claims About Missing Children VisionQuest was not the only organization Shirley approached. He also visited the Jewish Family & Children's Service of Southern Arizona and asked its staff about children who had crossed the border between 2021 and 2024. One employee did not provide the information he was seeking and said someone would contact him later. Shirley then visited another organization and asked similar questions. The footage showed staff members unable to give him details about the children's whereabouts. The video has brought attention to the way the US government tracks and places unaccompanied migrant children with sponsors. However, questions about record-keeping and the movement of children do not by themselves prove that NGOs were involved in trafficking. This is not the first time Shirley has faced attention over claims involving government-funded organizations. In December 2025, he released a video accusing several Somali-run childcare centers in Minnesota of receiving public money without providing proper daycare services. According to NPR, his video led to fresh scrutiny of the centers and prompted state and federal officials to look into the allegations. However, the Minnesota Department of Children, Youth, and Families said in January 2026 that nine centers it checked were operating as expected. CBS News also reported that its review found no recorded evidence of fraud at the centers it examined. President Donald Trump later praised Shirley for his Minnesota daycare video, according to CBS News. His latest investigation now raises a different set of questions about federal funding and the care of migrant children. The allegations against the NGOs, however, still need independent evidence and official findings. You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

title: EC can't monopolise voter awareness campaigns: SC; sets aside order denying permission to civil society
text: Voter awareness not EC's monopoly, says SC; sets aside SEC order BEW DELHI: The Supreme Court on Monday said Election Commission did not have a monopoly over conducting âvoter awareness campaignsâ while disapproving ECâs refusal to permit a civil society group led by Aruna Roy from running a campaign to educate voters to choose representatives carefully and not barter their votes for bribes. Setting aside Rajasthan State Election Commissionâs Oct 9 refusing permission for the civil society in this regard, a bench of Chief Justice Surya Kant, and Justices Joymalya Bagchi and V Mohana gave 48 hours to the SEC to consider their representation to run voter awareness campaigns for the final phase of Zila Parishad and Panchayat Samiti elections scheduled for Nov 14. SEC, through advocate Amit Kuri, said permission was refused keeping in mind the imposition of prohibitory orders for maintenance of law and order situation before the elections to keep at bay unwanted and anti-social elements. Royâs counsel Prashant Bhushan said it is a voter awareness campaign and not political activity and questioned the legitimacy of blanket imposition of prohibitory orders under Section 163 of BNSS to prohibit congregation for any political purpose. title: âNo Iran attack planned before voteâ: Israel defence minister rejects Netanyahu-army chief rift reports
text: Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and Defence Minister Israel Katz attend a graduation ceremony of new Israeli army officers at a base near Mitzpe Ramon, Israel, October 21, 2026. REUTERS/Amir Cohen Israeli defence minister Israel Katz on Monday denied reports of a major confrontation between Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and military chief lieutenant general Eyal Zamir over possible military action against Iran, saying Israel had no plans to launch an attack before the countryâs election. âThe reports of disagreements between the political leadership and the IDF on Iran are completely baseless and false,â Katz said in a statement reported by the Times of Israel. Katz said Israel had no intention of initiating an attack on Iran before the election but warned that any Iranian attack would prompt a forceful response. âI state unequivocally that Israel had no intention of initiating an attack on Iran before the elections in Israel, while making clear that if Iran attacks Israel, we will respond with great force,â Katz said, adding that âall reports on this matter are completely falseâ. Watch Back-To-Back Explosions Rock Iranâs Radar Site Near Tabriz As Trump Mulls Fresh Strikes The denial followed reports by Channel 12 on Saturday that Netanyahu and Zamir had clashed over an instruction from the prime minister for unspecified military action. Defence officials reportedly believed the move could trigger a rapid confrontation with Iran shortly before the election. State-owned Army Radio published similar details on Sunday, citing two senior security officials, the Times of Israel reported. Netanyahu also rejected the reports during an interview with Channel 14, calling them ânonsenseâ and saying âthere was no fightâ with Zamir. Earlier in the interview, he said he had recently âinstructed the IDF and Mossad to topple the [Iranian] regimeâ, although it was unclear whether the remark was connected to the reported instruction. The reports came as US President Donald Trump renewed his endorsement of Netanyahu on Sunday, urging Israelis to vote for the prime minister in Tuesdayâs election. In a post on Truth Social, Trump praised their relationship and called Netanyahu an âoutstanding Warrior Prime Ministerâ. He also urged voters to back Netanyahu, writing: âVote for Bibi Netanyahu for Prime Minister, we have to finish the job that we started.â Netanyahu also posted an AI-generated image depicting a nuclear explosion in Tel Aviv on Sunday. Two days before the election, he warned that voting for anyone other than him could expose Israelis to the danger of a âsecond Holocaustâ. title: CAG Flags NMCâs Rs1,646cr Pending Utilisation Certificates, Negative Balance In Smart City Account
text: CAG Audit Nagpur: A Comptroller and Auditor General (CAG) inspection audit of Nagpur Municipal Corporation (NMC) has flagged several financial and accounting lapses, including pending utilisation certificates (UCs) worth Rs1,646 crore, unadjusted advances of Rs4.2 crore and a negative balance of Rs52.44 crore in the Nagpur Smart and Sustainable City Development Corporation Ltd account (NSSCDCL). The audit observations raise questions about the civic bodyâs financial management, monitoring of govt grants and internal accounting controls. The findings are part of the inspection report on the accounts of NMCâs chief accounts and finance officer for the period covered by the audit. One of the major concerns is the non-submission of utilisation certificates worth Rs1,646 crore. The pending certificates relate to grants received from govt agencies and are required to establish that funds were spent for their sanctioned purposes. The delay could complicate financial accountability and affect the processing of future grants. The audit also highlights a negative balance of Rs52.44 crore in the account of NSSCDCL. The provisional balance sheet for 2024-25 showed the deficit under grants and contributions for specific purposes. The report also recorded a reduction in the grant balance for special city development projects. Another observation concerns advances of Rs4.20 crore paid to various officials and department heads that remain unadjusted. The audit sought details of pending advances, indicating shortcomings in monitoring and reconciliation of expenditure. The report also raised concerns over statutory accounting procedures. While NMCâs annual accounts for 2023-24 were examined and approved by the chief auditor, the accounts for 2024-25 had been prepared but further action was still underway. The audit sought an update on compliance with statutory requirements. Among other outstanding observations are a loan liability of Rs94.41 crore pending for over 16 years and avoidable interest payments linked to delays in loan-related procedures. Former NCP corporator Vedprakash Arya submitted a memorandum to municipal commissioner Vipin Itankar, demanding a high-level inquiry into the financial irregularities and accountability of officials concerned. title: After Ashoka Hotel's snub, oppn to hold âpublic impeachmentâ of CEC at Khargeâs residence

title: SP to showcase âAyodhya-Kashiâ wins to spice up its 2027 poll narrative
text: Akhilesh Yadav Lucknow: The Samajwadi Party is all set to showcase its â Ayodhya â (part of Faizabad Lok Sabha seat) victory in the 2024 polls and recently concluded Varanasi win in MLC elections (Teachers and Graduate Constituencies) to spice up its election campaign for the 2027 UP Assembly polls. Of the 11 MLC seats that went to polls, the SP bagged five â an addition of two seats as compared to its previous tally. The catchline not only focused on the partyâs win in temple towns of Ayodhya and Kashi but also the fact that candidates from the PDA spectrum emerged victorious in the two elections. Ayodhya MP Awadhesh Pasi happens to be a Dalit while Lalbihari Yadav (of Other Backward Classes) and Ashutosh Sinha (Upper Caste) complete the caste bouquet of the SPâs PDA plank. Originally comprising Pichde (Backward classes), Dalits and Alpsankhyaks (Minorities), the SPâs PDA plank went on to include Agde (upper castes) also in the PDAâs caste matrix. The SP retaining the graduate and teacher seats in Varanasi â represented in the Lok Sabha by Prime Minister Narendra Modi â makes the achievement important for the SP strategists. The SP also bagged the Agra teacher seat, the Allahabad-Jhansi graduate seat and the Lucknow graduate seat. In a post on X, SP chief Akhilesh Yadav described the partyâs win in Varanasi as a âdouble defeatâ for the BJP . He said the BJP lost the two seats both in the initial counting and the subsequent recounting as well.
