title: As Trump mulls fresh strikes after midterms, Vance writes to Iran, Tehran says 'won't surrender'
text: US-Iran war tensions escalate as midterms approach: Vance writes to Iran; Tehran pushes for 7-day ceasefire NEW DELHI: Iran is pursuing a seven-day plan to secure a ceasefire and reopen the Strait of Hormuz as diplomatic efforts intensify amid the possibility of renewed US military strikes after the November 3 midterm elections. US Vice President JD Vance has reportedly reached out to Iranâs security leadership to explore a framework for negotiations, even as Washington warns Gulf allies to prepare for a potential escalation. Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said on Wednesday that Tehran was working with regional mediators to advance the proposal, which Iran had previously conveyed to the United States through Qatar. He said the plan could be implemented in less than a week if the necessary conditions were met. Watch JD Vance-Linked Group In Bolsonaro Poll Probe! Brazil Investigates Alleged Plot Against Lula "While our Brave Armed Forces are fully prepared to defend the Homeland, Iran continues to give diplomacy a chance to succeed," Araghchi said in a post on X. "We remain in close and ongoing contact with intermediaries to review ideas that can ensure implementation of our 7-Day Plan in even less than a week." The proposal dates back to September, when the Iranian delegation was in New York for the United Nations General Assembly. It has resurfaced following recent diplomatic engagements in the region, particularly Qatar's involvement, according to Al Jazeera's reporting from Tehran. An Iranian security source told Al Jazeera that the plan was not fundamentally new. Tehran has also indicated that the seven-day period could be shortened, suggesting that the central question is whether Iran's demands and conditions can be met. Under the proposal, the Strait of Hormuz would reopen within seven days if conditions, including a ceasefire across the Middle East, were fulfilled. Iran has also demanded the unfreezing of its assets held abroad, the lifting of sanctions on its oil sector and an end to the US naval blockade. Vance contacts Iran's security chief as Washington explores talks The diplomatic push comes as The Wall Street Journal reported that Vance had sent a letter to Mohsen Rezaei, secretary of Iran's Supreme National Security Council and a former commander of the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC), in an effort to revive negotiations and avert renewed American attacks. The report said the contact was made at the direction of US President Donald Trump. The letter and subsequent discussions between US and Iranian officials focused on exploring a framework for negotiations rather than the details of a comprehensive peace proposal. Separately, US news website Axios reported that regional mediators led by Qatar were pushing for an agreement to restart US-Iran talks and prevent a resumption of hostilities after the November 3 US midterm elections. Trump has not made a final decision on whether to launch fresh strikes against Iran, according to diplomats briefed on the matter and cited by The Associated Press (AP). Washington has warned several Gulf Arab countries to prepare for a possible "short, intense military campaign" against Iran after the elections, The Wall Street Journal reported. US officials have also urged regional allies to prepare for potential Iranian retaliation against energy facilities and other critical infrastructure. Iran warns of economic fallout from renewed attacks Tehran has warned that renewed military action could have far-reaching consequences for global energy markets, particularly if fighting disrupts shipping through the Strait of Hormuz. âDevastating impact on intâl markets of any Israel-instigated military misadventure in Arabian Gulf region remains major concern for both gas suppliers and consumers,â Araghchi said in a post on X, referring to discussions at the Gas Exporting Countries Forum summit in Moscow. The Strait of Hormuz is a critical shipping route through which around a fifth of global oil and liquefied natural gas supplies previously passed. Iran has restricted maritime traffic through the waterway since the war began in late February and has attacked vessels attempting to cross without its authorisation. The United States, meanwhile, has maintained a naval blockade of Iranian ports to put pressure on Tehran's economy. Iran has warned that any renewed attack would trigger a broader response. Rezaei has threatened strikes against US-linked infrastructure, including data centres and facilities associated with artificial intelligence. Concerns over the safety of American personnel have also intensified. In a memo dated October 23 and reviewed by Reuters, US Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton warned that Iran had stepped up efforts to target American personnel and that alleged plots against US citizens had reached advanced stages. "Specifically, through various channels, we have received intelligence that Iran has substantially increased efforts to target US personnel," Clayton wrote to US Secretary of State Marco Rubio. "The lethal plotting efforts by the Iranians against US citizens have reached advanced stages in both the Middle East and certain other countries," he added. Trump keeps military option open ahead of midterms Trump has repeatedly suggested that the conflict could end soon while keeping open the possibility of renewed bombing after the November 3 elections. During a campaign stop in Lubbock, Texas, on Tuesday, Trump said a conclusive end to the conflict could come âin a couple of weeks, if you donât mind.â âSomebody asked me before, when will the war in Iran end?â Trump said earlier in the same address. âI said, âWhenever I want it to end.â Itâll be very quick, but we have to have it end properly, with total and complete -- a total statement, they will never have a nuclear weapon.â The conflict has become a political challenge for Republicans ahead of the midterms, with rising petrol prices adding to voter concerns about its economic consequences. The Pentagon's latest estimate to Congress put the cost of the war to American taxpayers at $47.1 billion. The military situation has also become more complicated as the conflict has spread across the region. Iran-backed Houthi rebels have attacked Saudi oil infrastructure and airports, while a Saudi-led coalition has carried out strikes against Houthi-held territory in Yemen. The United Arab Emirates foreign ministry has urged the parties to âexercise wisdom and pursue political solutions to help contain tensionsâ and prevent a return to full-scale military operations. Mojtaba Khamenei calls for end to 'neither war nor peace' situation Iran's Supreme Leader Ayatollah Sayyid Mojtaba Khamenei has called for an end to the region's state of 'neither war nor peace', as Tehran prepares for the possibility of renewed military confrontation with the United States and Israel. Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian told the country's cabinet on Wednesday that the government would pursue the implementation of the supreme leader's directive with full commitment and resources, according to Iran's state news agency IRNA. The Iranian cabinet discussed the country's prevailing conditions, strengthening national resilience and countering external threats. Pezeshkian stressed the need for continuous preparedness to deal with different possible scenarios. "All ministers, heads and deputies of the executive branches are obliged to maintain full readiness based on requirements, and use the existing capacities to increase productivity and strengthen the national power," he said. Pezeshkian also called for greater resilience against threats, sanctions and external pressure. "Enemies should not think they can weaken the will of the Iranian nation and force the country to surrender," he stressed. During the meeting, Araghchi briefed the cabinet on diplomatic developments and regional consultations, particularly those involving a visiting Qatari delegation and Pakistan's army chief. The remarks come as Tehran pursues diplomatic efforts to revive negotiations while preparing for a possible confrontation. Vance's reported outreach to Rezaei and the proposed seven-day plan indicate that diplomatic channels remain active, even as Washington keeps the military option open. Whether the proposal can meet Iran's demands, secure a ceasefire and restore normal shipping through the Strait of Hormuz remains uncertain as the November 3 US midterm elections approach. title: US midterms 2026: Who is Ami Bera, Indian-American Democrat seeking re-election from California's newly redrawn district
text: Bera was first elected to the US House in 2012 and took office in January 2013. Indian-American Democratic Congressman Ami Bera is seeking re-election to the US House of Representatives in the November 3, 2026, general election, but will contest from California's newly redrawn 3rd Congressional District instead of the 6th District he currently represents. Bera will face Republican candidate Robb Tucker, a member of the Nevada County Board of Supervisors, in the race. The 3rd District covers large parts of Placer, El Dorado and Nevada counties and extends into the city of Sacramento. Bera, who lives in Elk Grove, California, has represented the state in Congress since 2013. He is the longest-serving Indian-American member of the US Congress and serves on the House Foreign Affairs Committee and the House Permanent Select Committee on Intelligence. Who is Ami Bera? Born in Los Angeles to Indian immigrant parents with roots in Gujarat, Bera is a physician by training and a lifelong Californian. He earned his bachelor's degree and medical degree from the University of California, Irvine. After graduating from medical school in 1991, he completed his residency in internal medicine at California Pacific Medical Center, where he eventually became chief resident. He then practised medicine in the Sacramento area and held leadership positions in healthcare management. Bera later served as medical director of care management at Mercy Healthcare, where he developed strategies to improve care across its seven-hospital system. He also served as chief medical officer for Sacramento County, focusing on healthcare access, affordability and job creation. He subsequently joined the University of California, Davis, as a clinical professor of medicine and associate dean for admissions and outreach, helping train future doctors and support community healthcare initiatives. Bera's political career and priorities Bera was first elected to the US House in 2012 and took office in January 2013. He has since won re-election six times, building a political career centred on healthcare, economic opportunity and public service. In Congress, he serves on the House Foreign Affairs Committee as ranking member of its Subcommittee on East Asia and the Pacific. He is also a member of the House Permanent Select Committee on Intelligence and the New Democrat Coalition, a group of Democrats that advocates economic growth, innovation and fiscal responsibility. Bera has said his experience as a doctor shapes his approach to public service, with an emphasis on listening to constituents and working across party lines. His congressional office says it has helped return more than $23 million to local taxpayers through assistance with issues such as delayed veterans' benefits and Social Security payments. It has also helped more than 36,000 Sacramento County residents since 2013. Bera currently represents California's 6th Congressional District, which lies entirely within Sacramento County. Following changes to California's congressional district boundaries, he decided to run in the 3rd District in the 2026 election. The contest will pit Bera against Tucker, a Republican who serves on the Nevada County Board of Supervisors. The outcome will determine who represents the district in the US House for the next term. Bera has lived in Sacramento County for more than three decades with his wife, Janine, who is also a physician. They have a daughter, Sydra. You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. title: An Indiana doctor cut her hours to care for her newborn and reported earning $6,677 a week, but her divorce court calculated her earning capacity at $8,811 a week; an appeals court has upheld the ruling
text: Ashraf reduced her workload to three-quarters of a full-time schedule to look after their daughter (AI image) An Indiana doctor who reduced her working hours to care for her newborn daughter has lost her appeal against a divorce court's decision to calculate her weekly earning capacity at $8,811, despite her reporting an income of $6,677 a week. The Indiana Court of Appeals ruled on Thursday siad that the lower court had sufficient evidence to conclude that Aiza Ashraf, a radiologist, was capable of working full-time. The judges also upheld an order allowing her former husband, Mohsin Mukhtar, to spend three nights a week with their young daughter. Ashraf and Mukhtar, both radiologists employed by Indiana University, married in 2018 and welcomed their daughter in August 2024, according to the case details available on Justia . Ashraf filed for divorce the following month. The couple's separation led to disagreements over their daughter's care, parenting time, and the income that should be considered when calculating child support. Both doctors received payments from Indiana University for teaching and from IU Health for providing medical services. They also had opportunities to earn additional money by taking extra shifts, commonly referred to as "moonlighting". Before taking maternity leave, Ashraf earned the same base salary as her husband. However, in January 2025, Ashraf reduced her workload to three-quarters of a full-time schedule to look after their daughter. She told the court that her gross weekly income was $6,677. Mukhtar argued that she could still earn the same base salary as him if she returned to full-time work. Why court calculated income higher During the divorce proceedings, Ashraf explained that she specialised in breast imaging radiology and planned to maintain her credentials in that field rather than general diagnostic radiology. She said opportunities for additional shifts were limited because breast imaging was generally performed during regular working hours. Mukhtar disagreed. He told the court that both had the same employment contract and that Ashraf retained the training, qualifications and licence needed to perform general radiology work. He asked the court to calculate both parents' weekly income at $8,811, excluding earnings from additional shifts. On October 13, last year, the Hamilton Circuit Court accepted that Ashraf could work full-time and assessed her earning capacity at $8,811 per week. Ashraf challenged the decision, arguing that she had reduced her hours to care for her daughter rather than to avoid financial responsibilities. The appeals court examined whether the lower court had acted improperly by using her potential earnings instead of her reported income. Under Indiana's child support rules, courts can consider what a parent is capable of earning when that parent is voluntarily unemployed or working fewer hours than their qualifications and opportunities would allow. The appeals judges noted that Ashraf had acknowledged she could work additional hours if she wanted. They also considered evidence that she previously earned the same base salary as Mukhtar. The court rejected her argument that the $8,811 figure improperly included her husband's additional earnings. Both parents' financial documents identified that amount as his base weekly pay, excluding extra shifts. Dispute over overnight stays with father The case also involved a disagreement over how much time Mukhtar should spend with their daughter. According to the judgment, both parents initially helped care for the baby after her birth. However, in September 2024, Ashraf began sleeping in the nursery and prevented Mukhtar from entering the room. A preliminary court order issued in December 2024 did not allow overnight stays with the father. It provided that he could request them when the child turned six months old or began eating solid food. Mukhtar subsequently requested more time with his daughter, but Ashraf refused. On one occasion, she left the child with her maternal grandmother in Texas for two nights rather than arrange overnight care with Mukhtar. At the final divorce hearing in March 2025, Ashraf proposed gradually increasing the father's parenting time, with overnight stays beginning when their daughter turned two. She explained that she intended to continue breastfeeding until that age and wanted to be available to comfort the child at night. Mukhtar sought equal parenting time, including overnight stays. He told the court that he had participated in the baby's early care, regularly exercised his permitted parenting time and completed parenting courses. The lower court eventually awarded him three days of parenting time each week, including overnight stays. Appeals court upholds both decisions Ashraf challenged the overnight arrangement, arguing that the immediate increase from no overnight stays to three per week was not in their daughter's best interests. The appeals court acknowledged that the arrangement went beyond the usual recommendations under Indiana's parenting time guidelines for young children. However, it found that the lower court had considered the circumstances of the family, including Mukhtar's involvement in childcare, his completion of parenting courses and his ability to provide suitable accommodation. The judges also considered the lower court's concern that a gradual increase in parenting time might not happen because Ashraf had previously refused additional visits. The appeals court therefore concluded that the lower court had sufficient grounds to approve the arrangement. You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

title: Netanyahu pushes Donald Trump for fresh Iran strikes after US midterms: Report
text: File photo: US President Donald Trump and Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu US President Donald Trump and Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu held a telephone conversation on Saturday to discuss Washington's negotiations with Iran and the possibility of resuming military operations, with Netanyahu pressing for fresh strikes after Tuesday's US midterm elections, according to a report by Axios. The call came amid differences over the approach towards Tehran, with the Israeli prime minister urging immediate military action after the elections, while Trump wants to allow diplomatic efforts to continue for now, Axios reported, citing one Israeli and one US source. An Israeli source described the conversation as "tough", while a US source called it "direct". Watch WATCH: James Talarico Wages War On Musk, Ken Paxton & âCorruptâ Texas Billionaires | MIDTERMS 2026 However, Trump told reporters in Iowa on Sunday that he had a "very good talk" with Netanyahu and confirmed that Iran was among the subjects discussed, without giving further details. The White House and the Israeli prime minister's office declined to comment on the call. Also Read: 'They'll become garbage': Trump says he'll become 'Mr. Veto'if Democrats win midterms Trump keeps diplomatic and military options open Trump is pursuing parallel diplomatic and military approaches, seeking an agreement that could restart peace talks with Iran while keeping preparations underway for a possible return to major combat operations after the midterm elections. Speaking to reporters on Saturday, Trump said negotiations with Iran were "going fine" and that he was not "in much of a hurry". He also said Tehran wanted a deal but questioned its reliability. "They make a deal and then they back out," Trump said. At the same time, the US president indicated that Washington still needed to address one or two nuclear sites in Iran. Referring to the suspected underground facility at Pickaxe Mountain, he said, "We can do that in 10 minutes. We have that planned. You can look at Pickaxe Mountain. We need to take care of that. We can do that very quickly." The US was keeping the possibility of renewed military action open even as it pursued negotiations. LIVE BLOG: Follow for latest updates Vance's outreach and Qatar's mediation The diplomatic engagement has included a letter sent last week by US Vice President JD Vance to Iran's national security chief, Mohsen Rezaei, concerning the possibility of restarting negotiations. It was the highest-level US outreach to Tehran in several months. Meanwhile, Qatari mediators met Iranian officials on Sunday for the third consecutive day in an effort to reach an agreement that would allow direct negotiations between Washington and Tehran to resume. Iranian foreign minister Abbas Araghchi said no agreement had been reached so far and that progress depended on the US responding to questions raised by Tehran. "We are making every effort in this regard and hope that the other side will demonstrate enough rationality to choose diplomacy over other paths," Araghchi said. In an interview shared on his Telegram channel, Araghchi said consultations with mediators were continuing and that the final outcome depended on the answers provided by Washington to Iran's questions. He said Iran remained prepared for both defence and diplomacy, depending on the US response. Araghchi had also said on Saturday that Iranian negotiators were in Qatar discussing a proposal that could reopen the Strait of Hormuz within two days if Washington met several conditions. He stressed that no direct talks were taking place between Iran and the US, AP reported. The latest diplomatic efforts come as the two sides explore the possibility of restarting negotiations while the prospect of renewed military operations remains under discussion. title: LA LA land goes Lal? After NYC, an Indian-origin socialist takes aim at Los Angeles
text: TOI Correspondent from Washington: For all the attention that the 2026 midterm elections in the US are attracting over control of the House, Senate, and governorships, a municipal contest in California with strong political and electoral ties to India is challenging the Golden State -- and Americaâs -- reputation as a bastion of capitalism. The Mayoral election in Los Angeles, whose $ 15 billion budget matches that of Costa Rica or Chhattisgarh, pits incumbent Karen Bass, 73, against Nithya Raman, 45, an India-born socialist councilwoman whose challenge has turned into one of the more intriguing political contests of the election season. Polls show the race currently tied, with Bass, a Democrat backed by the establishment, including California Governor Gavin Newsom, Kamala Harris, and Nancy Pelosi, clawing back from a ten-point deficit in September. If however Raman wins on Nov 3, LA will join New York City, now led by Zohran Mamdani, in having a mayor of Indian ancestry identified with democratic socialism. It would underscore the irony of two of America's most economically powerful, globally influential and famously expensive cities being governed by politicians from a movement that Trump and his political allies routinely portray as an existential threat to American capitalism. Raman's story has a typical Indian middle class template. Born in Kerala, she moved to the U.S at the age of six and grew up in Louisiana and Massachusetts, going to become an accomplished urban planner after graduating from Harvard and MIT. She moved back to India in 2009, establishing Transparent Chennai, an urban research and advocacy initiative, and worked on sanitation and water access in the city. Returning to LA in 2013, she became involved in neighborhood activism, particularly around homelessness and affordability. She is married to Vali Chandrasekaran, a Hollywood tv screenwriter, whose credits include episodes for hit sitcoms 30 Rock and Modern Family. In 2020, Raman defeated an incumbent to become the first Indian elected to the LA City Council and went on to build a reputation for activism on affordable housing, tenant protections, and climate policy, eventually identifying herself as a Democratic Socialist. Her Mayoral campaign centers around a simple proposition: LA is a spectacularly wealthy city that is somehow lousy at providing basic services to its residents. She promises more affordable housing, better public infrastructure and a more accountable homelessness program, pointing to a nearly 50% reduction in street homelessness in her council district, even as the city's overall numbers have increased -- a jab at Bass whose term is dogged by rising living costs, infrastructure gridlock and persistent homelessness in the City of Angels. There is, incidentally, an interesting Indian historical footnote to LAâs -- and for that matter Californiaâs and Americaâs -- flirtation with socialism. Long before Mamdani and Raman began making their mark in American municipal politics, several prominent Indian nationalists and intellectuals had encountered the country's radical political traditions first hand. Lala Lajpat Rai spent five years in the U.S between 1914 and 1919, establishing the India Home Rule League and publishing the journal Young India in New York. The radical humanist MN Roy arrived in the US in 1916 as a global itinerant, encountered American radicals and began studying socialism, subsequently moving to Mexico City, where he founded the Communist Party of Mexico in 1919. He later played a foundational role in establishing the Communist Party of India in 1920. B.R. Ambedkar, meanwhile, studied at Columbia University in NYC, encountering some of America's leading liberal and progressive intellectuals, including philosopher John Dewey. And Jayaprakash Narayan spent seven years in America (1922-1929), studying at Berkeley, Iowa, and Wisconsin, where he encountered Marxism and returned to India a committed socialist. All this was at a time socialism was enjoying considerable electoral popularity. In 1912, Socialist Party presidential candidate Eugene Debs won nearly a million votes, then about 6% of the national total. Socialists also held hundreds of municipal offices, including mayoralties. In fact, in the early 1950s Donald Trumpâs father Fred Trump clashed with the folk singer Woody Guthrie, an avowed socialist, over racial segregation and housing discrimination in Brooklyn, causing him to write a song -- a scalding takedown of a predatory landlord -- titled âOld Man Trump" who stirred up racial hatred "in the bloodsport of the human heart. " The subsequent âRed Scareâ and the association of socialism with communism marginalized the movement, but almost a century later âthe times they are a-changing.â Of course, Mamdani and Raman represent a different generation and a more modern version of democratic socialism. Neither is proposing to abolish private property or install a Soviet-style command economy; their politics revolve around housing affordability, public services, redistribution, workers' rights and making the wealthy contribute more towards the common good. For Trump, who has made fighting socialism a defining feature of his political identity, the prospect of New York and Los Angeles being governed by two such politicians, that too of âforeignâ origin, might be particularly galling. For India, meanwhile, there is something deliciously ironic about the possibility that two of America's most influential cities could be led by activists with Indian roots, carrying forward a political tradition that some of India's own intellectual giants first encountered on American soil. title: Congress leaders confident of record Haryana turnout at November 1 rally
text: Congress functionaries Rao Narender Singh, Sanjay Dutt and Randeep Singh Surjewala Chandigarh: Haryana Congress leaders are expecting a massive turnout from the state at the partyâs November 1 âSave Vote, Save Nationâ rally at Ramlila Maidan in New Delhi, claiming that participation could surpass the attendance at all previous Congress rallies in the national capital. Reiterating the partyâs resolve to continue its nationwide campaign, the leaders said the Congress would fight to protect every citizenâs right to vote, uphold the Constitution and safeguard democratic institutions. title: US midterms 2026: Indian-American Democrat Aruna Miller seeks re-election as Maryland Lt Governor alongside Wes Moore
text: Aruna Miller Indian-origin politician Aruna Miller is seeking another term as Marylandâs lieutenant governor, running alongside Democratic Governor Wes Moore in the November 3 US midterm elections. Born in Hyderabad, Miller made history in 2023 as Marylandâs first Asian American lieutenant governor and the first woman of colour to hold the office. Miller and Moore are seeking re-election after taking office in January 2023. The Democratic ticket advanced through the partyâs primary on June 23, setting up a general election contest against Republican gubernatorial candidate Dan Cox and his running mate. Miller has made education, childhood poverty and affordability key themes of her campaign. In a statement announcing the re-election bid, she said she wanted to continue improving public schools and help more families afford to live in Maryland. âI am thrilled to stand alongside Governor Wes Moore as we launch our campaign to continue the work to make our public schools the best in America, to end childhood poverty once and for all, and to make sure more Marylanders can afford to live here, buy a home, create wealth for their families, and live a secure middle-class life,â Miller said. From Hyderabad to Maryland politics Millerâs journey into public service began long before she entered elected office. She studied civil engineering at the University of Missouri and earned a bachelorâs degree in Technology in 1989, before entering public service in Maryland. She has been elected to public office twice: first to the Maryland House of Delegates, where she represented District 15 from 2011 to 2019, and later as lieutenant governor in 2022. Her election to the stateâs second-highest office marked a milestone in Maryland politics. Miller joined Moore, who became the stateâs first Black governor, on a ticket that won the 2022 general election with 64.5% of the vote, defeating Republican Dan Cox, who received 32.1%. The pair assumed office in January 2023, becoming Marylandâs executive leadership team. Millerâs role has placed her among Indian-origin politicians serving in senior elected positions in the United States. Miller pushes back against Trump over ballot error Earlier this year, Miller defended Marylandâs election officials after President Donald Trump called for a Justice Department investigation into incorrect mail-in ballots sent to some voters ahead of the stateâs primary elections. Trump accused Governor Moore of allowing the error to benefit Democrats, but Miller told Fox News Digital that the state election board operated independently of the governorâs administration. âI think it was just an error by the vendor,â Miller said, rejecting claims of deliberate wrongdoing. Maryland election officials attributed the mistake to their mail-ballot printing vendor and said safeguards were in place to prevent duplicate voting. Trump said he had asked the Justice Department to investigate, but the department had not publicly announced an investigation. A joint campaign focused on families and affordability Moore has highlighted reducing costs, lowering crime and addressing unemployment as priorities in his re-election campaign. He has also criticised President Donald Trumpâs administration over federal job cuts, Medicaid and rising prices for household essentials. Millerâs campaign statement points to public education, childhood poverty and the cost of living as key areas for the next term. She has called for policies that help families remain in Maryland, purchase homes and build financial security. â You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

title: Debates before PUTA poll bring teachersâ concerns to fore
text: Patna University Patna : The Patna University Teachersâ Association (PUTA) election has generated unusual interest this year, with candidates for president and general secretary posts participating in the associationâs first-ever debates ahead of the Nov 4 polls. The debates have revived discussion about PUTAâs role in safeguarding university autonomy, protecting teachersâ financial interests and representing the academic community of Bihar . Elections are being held after a gap of more than three years for seven key posts, including president, two vice-presidents, general secretary, two joint secretaries and treasurer. Results are likely to be announced on the polling day. For an organisation that has long played a leading role in Biharâs teachersâ movement, the election is about more than choosing office-bearers. The next leadership will inherit a body closely associated with struggles over salaries, promotions, pensions and teachersâ rights. PUTA emerged after the 1952 reorganisation of Patna University as a teaching-cum-residential institution and the creation of Bihar University for colleges outside Patna. It soon became one of the most influential teachersâ associations in the state. One of its early leaders was Vina Mazumdar, who joined Patna University as a political science lecturer in 1951 and later became the associationâs first secretary. Teacher activist Nawal Kishor Chaudhary said Mazumdar represented a generation that combined academic work with public engagement. Among PUTAâs earliest campaigns was the successful effort to protect Patna Universityâs teaching-cum-residential character. title: Manhattan friar claimed to run two Beirut medical clinics and posed as a surgeon injured in the 2020 explosion before investigators exposed the charity fraud
text: Image: Britannica A Manhattan-based Franciscan friar was sentenced to five years in prison after raising more than $560,000 through a fake medical charity supposedly operating two clinics in Beirut, Lebanon. Paul Bielecki falsely claimed to be a physician and surgeon with multiple PhD degrees and told donors he had been badly injured in the August 2020 Beirut explosion, which had also damaged his clinics. The US Department of Justice (DOJ) said he collected donations from more than 350 victims over nearly a decade, claiming the money would fund medicines, medical equipment, baby incubators, food and an ambulance. Instead, he used the funds for personal expenses. The fraud came to light after investigators found that the charity's claimed medical operations and professional credentials were fabricated, leaving donors with no evidence that their contributions had supported patients in need. Manhattan friar falsely claimed to be a surgeon running two medical clinics in Beirut Paul Bielecki, a Manhattan-based friar belonging to the Capuchin Order, spent nearly a decade soliciting donations for two medical clinics he claimed to operate in Lebanon. According to the DOJ, he falsely presented himself as a physician, vascular surgeon, cardiac surgeon and general surgeon, while also claiming to hold multiple PhD degrees. He told potential donors that the clinics needed money for medicines, medical equipment, baby incubators, food and an ambulance. Bielecki used his position within the Catholic religious community to reach donors through church Masses, other religious events, radio programmes, online podcasts and crowdfunding campaigns. The DOJ established that neither of the claimed medical clinics existed. He claimed the 2020 Beirut explosion injured him and damaged his clinics Bielecki also used the August 2020 Beirut explosion as part of his fundraising appeals, falsely telling donors that he had been badly injured in the disaster and that his medical clinics had suffered extensive damage. The explosion, which devastated parts of the Lebanese capital, became part of his account of why the supposed facilities needed financial assistance. His claims about being a surgeon and operating medical facilities were also false, according to the DOJ. The fraudulent representations helped him obtain donations from people who believed they were supporting medical services and humanitarian assistance in Lebanon. Investigators established that the fundraising operation was based on fictitious medical facilities rather than an actual charitable healthcare programme. More than 350 victims donated over $560,000 to the fake medical charity Through the scheme, Bielecki obtained more than $560,000 from over 350 victims, according to the DOJ. He solicited contributions through religious gatherings, media appearances and online fundraising campaigns, presenting the money as support for his purported clinics. Despite taking a vow of poverty as a member of the Capuchin Order, he used the donations to finance personal spending. The DOJ identified first-class travel, multiple trips to the Hamptons, meals at high-end restaurants and a luxury gym membership costing $334.40 per month among his expenses. He also spent thousands of dollars on aesthetic plastic surgery. The donations intended for medical supplies and humanitarian assistance were therefore diverted towards his personal lifestyle. Paul Bielecki sentenced to five years in prison for wire fraud Bielecki pleaded guilty to one count of wire fraud on November 11, 2024, before US District Judge Vincent Briccetti. On March 27, 2025, he was sentenced to five years in prison by the US District Court for the Southern District of New York. In addition to the prison sentence, the 48-year-old was ordered to serve three years of supervised release, forfeit $563,448 and pay restitution. Acting US Attorney Matthew Podolsky said Bielecki had exploited his position as a friar to defraud hundreds of people and use the money for personal luxury. The investigation involved special agents from the US Attorneyâs Office for the Southern District of New York and the Internal Revenue Service's Criminal Investigation division, with assistance from US Customs and Border Protection. title: A charity founder stole millions meant for struggling families and spent $320,000 on restaurants; he also put a bartender and his housekeeper on a fake board of directors
text: Image Credit: AI Generated The founder of a New York charity established to help low-income families has been sentenced to 8 years in prison after stealing more than $2.5 million in donations to fund an expensive personal lifestyle. Keith Taylor, who led the Modest Needs Foundation, used money intended for people struggling with unexpected bills to pay for luxury accommodation, costly restaurant meals, food deliveries and other personal expenses. He also created a fake board of directors, listing people including a bartender and his housekeeper without their knowledge, to make his spending appear authorised. How did the charity founder steal millions meant for struggling families According to the US Department of Justice, Taylor founded Modest Needs in 2002 with the aim of helping low-income individuals and families facing unexpected financial difficulties. The charity operated through a crowdfunding model, allowing donors to contribute towards essential expenses that people living from one pay cheque to the next could not afford. Its support was intended for situations such as unexpected medical bills and repairs to broken household appliances. The organisation focused on people who were working but had little financial security when an emergency arose. However, prosecutors said Taylor gradually turned the charity's finances towards his own needs. The Department of Justice's October 28, 2026 sentencing announcement stated that he had embezzled more than $2.5 million from the organisation and its donors since at least 2015. The earlier criminal complaint, announced by the US Attorney's Office on June 11, 2024, placed the alleged period of theft between 2016 and May 2024. It described how donations intended to provide short-term financial assistance were instead used to maintain Taylor's lifestyle. The Associated Press reported that the charity had attracted attention for its small-scale approach to philanthropy, allowing donors to see how their contributions could directly help individuals facing financial problems. Where did the stolen charity money go The money was spent on a range of personal luxuries, with expensive restaurant visits accounting for a substantial portion of the stolen funds. According to the Department of Justice, Taylor spent more than $320,000 of charity money at some of New York City's most expensive restaurants and steakhouses. These included Per Se, Jean-Georges, Masa and Marea. He reportedly visited these establishments regularly, sometimes dining out twice in a single day. AP highlighted the prices associated with some of the restaurants. Marea's menu included a dry-aged ribeye costing $240, while Per Se offered a nine-course tasting menu priced at $390. Restaurant bills were only part of the spending. More than $300,000 of the charity's money went towards rent for Taylor's luxury apartment on the 30th floor of a Manhattan skyscraper. He also spent over $100,000 on food delivery services and used charitable funds to purchase expensive electronic devices. The money was also used to cover his personal medical expenses, including cosmetic surgery. The Justice Department further revealed that Taylor transferred more than $270,000 directly into his personal brokerage account. He also routinely paid other personal bills using the charity's bank accounts. Taylor used a fake board to hide the spending Prosecutors said Taylor attempted to conceal the misuse of donations by creating a fake board of directors. He claimed that the board had approved his personal expenses and provided oversight of the organisation's finances. However, the people named as board members had no knowledge of their supposed positions. According to the Justice Department, Taylor used the names of acquaintances and listed them on the charity's website and tax documents as members of its governing board. Those individuals included a bartender at Jean-Georges, a friend and his housekeeper. None of them had attended a board meeting or even knew that their names were being used in this way. The arrangement allowed Taylor to create the appearance that his financial decisions had been reviewed and authorised by others, even though the people named had no involvement in the charity's management. What happened after the investigation began Taylor's activities came under federal investigation, leading to his arrest on June 11, 2024. The initial complaint accused him of embezzling approximately $2.5 million, committing tax offences and using other people's identities as part of the scheme. The criminal case also involved allegations of tax evasion. According to the original Justice Department announcement, Taylor had failed to file personal income tax returns or pay taxes on money received from the charity for at least the calendar years 2017 through 2022. Prosecutors said this resulted in more than $1 million in unpaid federal income taxes. Taylor continued using the charity's money even after his arrest in June 2024. The Justice Department said he had purportedly resigned from his position and was no longer supposed to have access to the organisation's bank accounts under the conditions of his pretrial release. Despite those restrictions, he continued using the funds for personal expenses, including meals, medical bills and rent. The department said these actions also violated the conditions of his release. What punishment did the charity founder receive Taylor eventually pleaded guilty to the charges on August 18, 2025. On October 28, 2026, US District Judge Jennifer L Rochon sentenced the 59-year-old to 8 years in prison. The sentence also included three years of supervised release after his imprisonment. He was ordered to pay $3,118,237 in forfeiture and $4,144,645 in restitution. The case was investigated by the Internal Revenue Service's Criminal Investigation division and special agents from the US Attorney's Office for the Southern District of New York. title: CINTAA-FWICE row: October 20 poll by Poonam & Padmini-led faction draws High Court contempt notice
text: Upasana Singh and Poonam Dhillonâs rival CINTAA factions remain embroiled in an election dispute, with Padmini Kolhapure backing Dhillonâs faction. The dispute between the Cine and Television Artistes Association (CINTAA) and the Federation of Western India Cine Employees (FWICE) has taken another turn. On October 21, the City Civil Court rejected CINTAAâs plea for interim relief, and a day later, the Bombay High Court issued a contempt show-cause notice to the Poonam Dhillon and Padmini Kolhapure-led CINTAA faction over an election it conducted on October 20. FWICE had filed the contempt petition, alleging that the faction had violated the High Courtâs orders dated September 11 and October 19. The High Court found a prima facie case of wilful disobedience and breach of undertaking, issued a show-cause notice to the faction, and directed it not to act on the election or its results. Watch Arjan Bajwa, Poonam Dhillon & Stars Celebrate Eid & Riwaj Success Upasana Singh , who resigned as CINTAAâs general secretary in August and topped the election conducted by FWICE on September 12, says, âThe other faction claimed that the federation could not conduct the elections and that its executive committee had never been dissolved. However, the court observed that the committee had dissolved on August 7, after which they disaffiliated from FWICE. It also questioned the validity of that decision. The court had asked us not to take any further steps until the matter was decided. However, they went ahead with the election on October 20. We approached the High Court on October 19 over the contempt of court, and on October 22, it issued a show-cause notice. The orders have given us relief, and we will consider our next steps. I have always had faith in the High Court and the Indian judiciary. I believed justice would prevail.â CINTAAâs lawyer Suvigya Vidyarthi, representing Poonam Dhillonâs faction, says, âNo court has so far ruled that CINTAA cannot conduct its own elections or that FWICE had the authority to conduct elections on its behalf. The matter is still pending before the City Civil Court, which has only decided on the plea seeking a stay on the elections conducted by FWICE. Since the elections had already been held by the time the order was passed on October 21, the plea was no longer relevant. Whether FWICE had the authority to conduct elections on behalf of CINTAA can be determined only after a full trial, as the court also observed in its October 21 order.â On the contempt proceedings, he says, âIt is yet to be decided whether we have committed contempt of court. We have been asked to submit our response. The courtâs October 19 order did not direct CINTAA to stay the elections scheduled for October 20.â The latest orders are a relief: FWICE chief BN Tiwari, president, FWICE, says, âThey had challenged FWICEâs authority to conduct the election before the civil court, but CINTAAâs application for interim relief was rejected. The court observed that the executive committee had dissolved on August 7 and questioned whether CINTAAâs subsequent disaffiliation from FWICE complied with our constitution. The federation conducted the election on September 12 under its scrutiny committee after the courts declined to stop the process. The latest orders are a relief for us. This is not just our victory, but a victory for the 38 associations. We are grateful to the court.â Get the latest TV News, TV Shows and more. Download the TOI app.

title: Iran war bill hits $47.1 billion for US taxpayers as Trump weighs fresh strikes
text: The growing financial burden, coupled with the war's impact on energy prices, could hurt Republicans as voters decide which party will control Congress for the final two years of Trump's presidency. According to a recent AP-NORC poll, most Americans want Congress to prioritise ending the conflict. The cost of the Iran war to American taxpayers has risen to an estimated $47.1 billion, according to the latest Pentagon figures provided to Congress, as the eight-month conflict threatens to become a key issue in next week's US midterm elections. The estimate, compiled by US central command (Centcom) as of October 16, marks a $3.5 billion increase since early September. It comes as President Donald Trump leaves open the possibility of renewed strikes against Iran and sends additional military resources to the Middle East. The growing financial burden, coupled with the war's impact on energy prices, could hurt Republicans as voters decide which party will control Congress for the final two years of Trump's presidency. According to a recent AP-NORC poll, most Americans want Congress to prioritise ending the conflict. The latest estimate, obtained by The Associated Press this week, puts the cost of replacing munitions at about $29 billion, making it the largest component of the war's expenses. Defensive missile interceptors, including those used by the Army's Patriot and Terminal High Altitude Area Defence (THAAD) systems, account for a significant share of the demand. A single Patriot interceptor can cost millions of dollars. The Pentagon estimates that operational costs account for about $11.9 billion, while equipment losses have added another $6 billion. The Air Force's costs stand at $7.6 billion, while the Army's have exceeded $2 billion. The Navy's reported costs, however, have fallen to $1.45 billion from $2.2 billion in early September. The Navy and Centcom referred questions about the decline in the Navy's cost estimate to the Pentagon. The department did not immediately respond to emails seeking comment. The latest figures do not include damage to US military bases across the Middle East. Iran has targeted American installations with ballistic missiles and drones. A Pentagon inspector general's report released last month said Iranian strikes had damaged or destroyed hundreds of buildings and other structures at US bases in Kuwait, Bahrain, Qatar, the United Arab Emirates, Saudi Arabia, Iraq, Oman and Jordan. The Pentagon's official tally lists 21 US service members killed and 865 wounded in the conflict. The figures include deaths from medical events and other circumstances not directly linked to the fighting. Eighteen service members were killed in Iranian strikes, combat aircraft crashes or during the disposal of Iranian drones. War costs become political flashpoint The financial toll has intensified the debate in Congress over military spending. The Trump administration is seeking approval for a proposed $1.5 trillion military budget, which would be a historic level of spending. The White House has also asked lawmakers to approve a $95 billion package to help fund the Iran war and other priorities. Wednesday marks eight months since the conflict began. Democrats have repeatedly tried to end the war through legislation, but their efforts have failed in the Republican-controlled Congress. Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer criticised the administration's handling of the conflict and called for an end to the fighting. âTrump and his ego led us into this war with no plan, no authority, and no exit strategy," Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer of New York said in a news release. "Senate Democrats will continue to do everything in our power to end this disaster of a war and stop the costs, chaos, and corruption seeping from the White House.â Trump initially promised a military campaign lasting only a matter of weeks. He has since repeatedly weighed the possibility of reaching a deal with Iran against the option of escalating the conflict. The president has said further strikes remain an option after the midterm elections. Meanwhile, a third aircraft carrier and thousands of additional troops are heading to the region. The administration has also reduced staffing at some US embassies after receiving intelligence that Iran had stepped up efforts to target American personnel. With the cost of the war rising in lives, public funds and economic disruption, the prospect of renewed hostilities could add to pressure on the administration as voters prepare to decide control of Congress. title: Barmer poll row: State election chief orders probe, says result can be challenged only in court
text: Jaipur: Rajasthan State Election Commissioner Rajeshwar Singh said Thursday that the commission would investigate how a candidate whose nomination papers were rejected was allotted a symbol, allowed to contest and declared the winner of Gadra Road gram panchayat sarpanch election in Barmer. Singh, who was on a Barmer visit, made it clear that the commission cannot overturn the result. Any challenge to Pooraramâs election, he said, will have to be filed before a competent court through an election petition. Speaking to TOI, Singh said the matter was brought to his notice Thursday, and the commission would look into the facts. âIf any official is found guilty, action will be taken in accordance with the rules,â he said, adding that the commission would investigate whether the election symbol was allotted deliberately or by mistake. In conversation with TOI a day earlier, while Pooraram defended his victory and dismissed the rejection of his nomination as a rumour, his closest rival, Kuldeep Singh , who finished second, alleged through his brother and representative that Pooraramâs nomination was rejected through a public notice issued by the election officials. âThe affected party can approach the court and file an election petition within a month,â Singh Box âCourt can invalidate Barmer sarpanch poll result' SEC canât overturn result after winner is declared: PDT Achary Jaipur: State Election Commission (SEC) cannot overturn an election result once a candidate has been declared the winner, and only a competent court can invalidate it on the basis of an election petition, former Lok Sabha secretary general and constitutional expert PDT Achary said. He was commenting on the Barmer case in which a candidate whose nomination was rejected was allegedly allotted an election symbol and declared sarpanch. Achary said the âOnce a candidate is declared winner, the election is complete and the result canât be overturned by SEC. The SEC can investigate the matter and take appropriate action against the official concerned if found guilty. Since the official is a govt employee, departmental proceedings may also be initiated against him,â Achary said. He added that the court, while delivering its verdict, could also issue directions for action against the official concerned. The matter relates to the sarpanch election held earlier this week in Barmerâs Gadra Road gram panchayat where the returning officer allegedly allotted an election symbol to Pooraram even though his nomination papers were rejected. Pooraram subsequently won the election, raising questions over the poll process. title: CDC deputy director Jennifer Shuford to exit role after midterms amid vaccine policy changes: Report
text: Jennifer A. Shuford, MD, MPH, is deputy director and chief medical officer of the CDC Jennifer Shuford, deputy director and chief medical officer of the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC), is set to leave the Trump administration after next week's midterm elections, the Washington Post reported on Monday, citing sources. The reason behind Shuford's exit remains unclear. title: Oil prices today: Crude falls over 1% as Iran-Qatar talks raise hopes of diplomatic progress
text: Representative image Oil prices fell more than 1% on Monday as Iranian and Qatari officials held talks for a third consecutive day aimed at securing an agreement to end the US-Israeli war on Iran, easing some immediate concerns over supply disruptions. Brent crude futures declined $1.59, or 1.40%, to $111.84 a barrel by 0011 GMT. US West Texas Intermediate (WTI) crude fell $1.56, or 1.50%, to $102.56 a barrel, according to Reuters. The decline followed a strong rise last week, with Brent ending October at its highest level in six months amid concerns that the conflict between the US, Israel and Iran could escalate again after Tuesday's US midterm elections. Tim Waterer, chief market analyst at KCM Trade, said the fall reflected a technical correction after last week's gains, alongside hopes of progress in diplomatic efforts. "Oil is seeing a technical pullback this morning after last weekâs strong gains," Waterer said, as quoted by Reuters. "Lingering hopes of some form of diplomatic progress, combined with the absence of any meaningful military escalation over the weekend, have taken some of the immediate heat out of prices for now." However, he cautioned that the market remained alert to the possibility of stronger rhetoric over Iran, which could push Brent crude towards $120 a barrel after the midterm elections. Iran-Qatar talks and Strait of Hormuz disruptions The latest price movement came as Iranian and Qatari officials continued consultations aimed at facilitating an agreement to restart direct negotiations between Washington and Tehran. Iranian foreign minister Abbas Araqchi said on Sunday that the purpose of the "ongoing and progressing" discussions was to continue consultations with Qatari mediators. He added that Tehran was prepared for "both defence and diplomacy". The diplomatic efforts are taking place against the backdrop of attacks on oil tankers travelling through the Strait of Hormuz, which have pushed up global energy and shipping costs. The waterway is a key route for global oil shipments, and disruptions to tanker movements have remained a concern for energy markets during the conflict. Opec+ keeps December output targets unchanged Meanwhile, the Organisation of the Petroleum Exporting Countries and its allies, a grouping known as Opec+, kept their December production targets unchanged on Sunday. The decision was in line with market expectations and indicated that the group would not make further policy adjustments until next year, as it continues to face export disruptions linked to the Iran war. Separately, Saudi Arabia increased its crude oil exports in October compared with September, despite attacks by Iran-aligned Yemeni Houthi forces on its energy infrastructure, Reuters reported, citing two of three ship-tracking companies. The developments in the Gulf, the outcome of diplomatic efforts involving Iran and Qatar, and the possibility of renewed military escalation after the US midterm elections remain key factors for oil markets. title: US midterms 2026: Meet Sandeep Srivastava, Indian-American candidate contesting Texas House District 66
text: Texas has traditionally been a Republican stronghold in federal elections Indian-American candidate Sandeep Srivastava is seeking a seat in the Texas House of Representatives, contesting District 66 in the November 3 US midterm elections. A Plano-based small business owner with a background in technology and real estate, Srivastava is pitching his candidacy as an alternative to special-interest politics as he seeks to represent the district in the state legislature. His campaign comes at a time when Texas, a Republican stronghold, is seeing a more competitive slate of legislative and congressional races than in recent years. Democrats are targeting Republican-held seats, while concerns over the cost of living and President Donald Trump's policies have emerged as key issues in several contests. All about Sandeep Srivastava Srivastava lives in Plano, Texas, and has longstanding ties to the surrounding community. According to his campaign profile, he is married, has two children and runs a small business. He has positioned his candidacy around the promise of representing constituents rather than special interests. Srivastava graduated from Lucknow University in 1986, as per BallotPedia. His professional experience includes working as a broker and real estate consultant with RE/MAX, as well as serving as a data architect at Xerox Corporation and a principal architect at Fidelity Investments. His career spans real estate and technology, experience that he brings to his bid for public office. His campaign describes him as a candidate seeking to offer a different approach to leadership in Austin, the Texas state capital. The Texas House of Representatives has 150 seats, with Republicans holding an 88-62 majority. Democrats would need to flip 14 seats to take control of the chamber, although gains short of a majority could still alter the legislative balance. The competitiveness of individual races varies across the state, with several closely contested districts in and around major metropolitan areas, including Dallas-Fort Worth. All about the Texas race Texas has traditionally been a Republican stronghold in federal elections, but its expanding number of competitive races has made it an important state to watch as the party seeks to retain control of Congress. Republicans control both chambers of the Texas legislature and have redrawn congressional boundaries in an effort to gain additional US House seats. The revised map was designed to give the party an opportunity to secure as many as five additional seats. However, polling published by The Washington Post and George Mason University's Schar School of Policy and Government on October 23 found closely contested races in two South Texas congressional districts that Trump carried by about 10 percentage points in 2024. The poll, conducted among likely voters from October 14 to 19, showed Democrat Vicente Gonzalez leading Republican Eric Flores by 50% to 43% in the 34th Congressional District. In the 35th District, Republican Carlos De La Cruz and Democrat Johnny Garcia were closely matched. The findings point to the challenges Republicans face in translating their 2024 presidential gains into congressional victories. The cost of living was the leading concern among voters surveyed in both districts, while immigration ranked second. Trump has been campaigning across the country to support Republican candidates, including in traditionally conservative states. His rallies have focused on defending his economic record, while voters have continued to raise concerns about everyday expenses. For candidates across Texas, including those contesting state legislative seats, the midterms will take place against this broader political backdrop. The outcome will help determine the balance of power in Austin and Washington, while testing whether Trump's appeal among voters can translate into sustained Republican support across the state. title: Amit Shah to join T BJPâs padayatra on Nov 2
text: Hyderabad: Union home minister Amit Shah will participate in a BJP Telangana padayatra in Hyderabad on Nov 2, marking his first visit to the state since May 2024, after several proposed trips were deferred or cancelled. BJP plans to step up its campaign against Congress over the special intensive revision (SIR) of electoral rolls. The Telangana programme, announced by BJP Telangana president N Ramchander Rao on Monday, would be held under the slogan âLoktantra Bachao, Arajakta Hatao (Save Democracy, Remove Anarchy)â. It comes a day after Congress and other Opposition leaders are scheduled to hold a rally at Delhiâs Ramlila Maidan on Nov 1, alleging irregularities in electoral roll revision and demanding the removal of chief election commissioner Gyanesh Kumar. The back-to-back programmes are part of BJPâs effort to counter the Oppositionâs allegations over SIR and mobilise party workers through public outreach. Shahâs participation in both Telangana and Haryana is expected to give the campaign a national profile. Shahâs proposed visits to Telangana have faced repeated disruptions. His last visit was in May 2024 for Lok Sabha election campaigning. Several subsequent programmes were postponed or cancelled, including a visit scheduled for Oct 3 and 4 this year. That trip, which was to include events in Toopran and Karimnagar and meetings with party leaders, was cancelled at the last minute. Rao has accused Congress of spreading misinformation about SIR and challenged chief minister A Revanth Reddy to identify eligible voters whose names were wrongly deleted. He also criticised Congress leaders for planning to attend the Delhi rally while Telangana faces rainfall deficits and water shortages. After Hyderabad, Shah is scheduled to participate in a padayatra in Karnal (Haryana) on Nov 5. The consecutive programmes underline BJPâs plan to counter the Congress campaign through coordinated public mobilisation. title: Powering fourth: Karnataka moves up in Indiaâs TOEFL league, leapfrogs Gujarat
text: Karnataka overtakes Gujarat, with 9.3% share of Indiaâs test-takers in FY 2025-26 Bengaluru: Karnataka has overtaken Gujarat to become the fourth-largest state in terms of TOEFL-takers, according to data shared by Educational Testing Service (ETS), which administers the English-language test. The stateâs share of test-takers has seen a consistent increase, up from 8.1% in FY 2023-24 to 8.7% in FY 2024-25 and 9.3% in FY 2025-26. Telangana leads overall with a share of 18.1%, followed by Maharashtra and Andhra Pradesh (15.1% each). Karnataka is marginally ahead of Gujarat at 9%. âBengaluru continues to be a significant centre for TOEFL participation. The city ranked fourth among Indiaâs leading TOEFL iBT test-taking cities in 2021 before moving to third place in 2022 and 2023. Mysuru also featured among the countryâs top 10 test-taking cities in 2023,â said Karan Lalit, executive director â South Asia, TOEFL & GRE, ETS. According to ETS, it currently has more than 60 active institutional partners across Karnataka, including Bengaluru, Mangaluru, Mysuru, Hubballi and Dharwad. These partnerships support student outreach, awareness initiatives and access to TOEFL preparation resources. However, access to testing infrastructure remains concentrated in Bengaluru, which has four TOEFL test centres. ETS said it is in discussions with several universities and colleges across Karnataka to strengthen student support, particularly in test preparation and registration. While the US, UK, Canada and Australia continue to be popular choices among Indian students, interest in destinations such as Germany, France, Ireland and countries in the Middle East is also growing. âAt a global level, TOEFL score reports sent to universities in Japan increased by 10% in FY 2025-26, while reports sent to universities in Hong Kong increased by 24% in 2025. These figures reflect global ETS data and should not be interpreted as trends specific to Karnataka,â Lalit said. ETS said students are increasingly evaluating multiple countries before making study-abroad decisions, taking into account visa regulations, affordability, admission requirements, and post-study work opportunities. âGermany enrolled approximately 59,000 Indian students in the 2024-25 winter semester, representing a year-on-year growth of around 20%. France recorded approximately 9,100 Indian students in 2025. Ireland recorded 9,175 Indian students in 2024-25. The Niti Aayog report on internationalisation of higher education also identifies the UAE as a destination for Indian students. These figures illustrate the range of international education markets attracting Indian students,â he said. TOEFL iBT is accepted by more than 13,500 institutions across over 160 countries as a common English-language proficiency assessment when applying to universities in different destinations. title: NOAA awards $8.5 million to restore Hawaiiâs Tern Island, where rising seas, storms and wildlife threaten vital seabird nesting grounds
text: Representative Image of coastal habitat restoration on Tern Island, with seabirds thriving amid conservation efforts and rising sea levels (AI-generated image) A remote island in the Northwestern Hawaiian Islands is set to receive federal funding for coastal habitat restoration as conservation managers confront rising seas, storms and deteriorating infrastructure. On September 10, 2026, the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) announced an $8.5 million award to the PapahÄnaumokuÄkea Marine Debris Project for work at Tern Island, part of Lalo, also known as French Frigate Shoals. Tern Island has the largest area of available land at the atoll and is identified as a priority landmass for species diversity and population size. Its habitat supports seabirds and other wildlife but is vulnerable to flooding, erosion and damage from animals moving inland. A 2024 report outlines possible restoration measures, including addressing contaminants and derelict structures and improving habitat conditions. Why Tern Island is important for seabird nesting and wildlife conservation in Hawaii Tern Island lies within Lalo, the largest atoll in the Northwestern Hawaiian Islands. Tern Island is part of the PapahÄnaumokuÄkea Marine National Monument and the Hawaiian Islands National Wildlife Refuge, according to the US Environmental Protection Agency. Tern Island has the largest amount of available land at Lalo. An earlier state-of-knowledge paper cited in the 2024 Lalo (French Frigate Shoals) Resilience Implementation Options Report identifies it as the priority landmass for species diversity and population size. The island also retains infrastructure from earlier military and US Fish and Wildlife Service occupation, including former barracks, a boat ramp, a runway and a seawall. Some structures have deteriorated, creating potential hazards for wildlife. The island supports black-footed albatrosses, Laysan albatrosses, Bonin petrels and Tristramâs storm petrels. The report notes that a high proportion of the global populations of these four species breed at a small number of sites, many only a few metres above sea level. Tern Island also has a history of long-term wildlife research. The report describes Lalo as having hosted âthe most comprehensive and long-termâ breeding seabird monitoring programme in the US tropical Pacific. The US Fish and Wildlife Service maintained more than 30 years of data on breeding pairs, breeding seasons and reproductive performance for most of the 21 monument species in its database. Annual monitoring ended after severe weather damaged field research facilities in 2012. What NOAAâs $8.5 million Tern Island habitat restoration grant is intended to support NOAA announced the award as part of a wider allocation of $103 million for 16 habitat restoration projects intended to benefit fisheries. The September 10, 2026, announcement names the PapahÄnaumokuÄkea Marine Debris Project as the recipient of $8.5 million for coastal habitat restoration at Tern Island. The funding comes from the federal government, not the state of Hawaii. NOAA describes the project broadly as restoring coastal habitat but does not provide a detailed breakdown of the work or confirm that every measure proposed in the 2024 report will be funded through the award. The PapahÄnaumokuÄkea Marine Debris Project, a Hawaii-based nonprofit, carries out marine debris removal work across the monument, including efforts to remove discarded fishing gear and other materials that threaten marine wildlife. The 2024 report was prepared for the monumentâs management board following a March 2023 workshop involving specialists in climate science, wildlife biology, Native Hawaiian cultural practice and coastal engineering. Its recommendations provide context for the restoration challenges but are not a confirmed list of grant-funded activities. Contaminant cleanup, abandoned buildings and proposed habitat improvements on Tern Island The report identifies contaminant removal as a high-urgency action that should precede longer-term habitat improvements. It discusses options including removing contaminated sediment for disposal in the main Hawaiian Islands, containing remaining contaminants in concrete and considering bioremediation. The work is linked to a separate cleanup effort overseen by the EPA. Its Tern Island Removal Action profile says waste from the former Coast Guard LORAN station was placed in a large dump, while a legacy burn pit contributed high concentrations of polychlorinated biphenyls (PCBs) to the soil. A Coast Guard cleanup in 2001 was not completed, leaving high PCB concentrations that affected surrounding water and wildlife. The EPA is working with the US Fish and Wildlife Service on the removal action, but its public profile does not establish whether field cleanup has since been completed. Infrastructure modification is another high-urgency priority. The report recommends removing derelict barracks and outbuildings, improving the boat ramp and davit, and establishing a more permanent research shelter. It also proposes breaking up the Tern Island runway to create nesting habitat for burrowing seabirds. The report recommends planning for seawall removal or replacement, subject to further engineering and hydrodynamic studies. Coastal engineering experts at the workshop believed the seawalls could not be removed entirely because currents in the dredged channel on the islandâs north side would cause rapid erosion. For habitat stabilisation, the report recommends identifying suitable indigenous plant species to improve nesting and resting areas, provide shade and retain sand. It does not prescribe naupaka for future planting. Instead, it notes that US Fish and Wildlife Service teams have sown naupaka seeds on the island several times since Hurricane Walaka in 2018. The report also recommends coordinating planting with invasive-plant removal and considering a shade house and water catchment system. How rising seas, Hurricane Walaka and wildlife threaten Tern Island seabird habitat Hurricane Walaka caused severe damage to East Island, another important nesting site at Lalo, in 2018. Following the loss of vegetation and a black-pipe barrier on Tern Island, Hawaiian green sea turtles moved farther inland to lay their eggs. The report says this movement has increased the destruction of seabird nests and incubating eggs. It also records that monk seals and green sea turtles have wandered inland from beaches into vegetated areas where seabirds nest, contributing to the destruction of nests and eggs. Separately, the report says more frequent use of Tern Island by displaced monk seals has increased disturbance to more sensitive seals, including mothers with pups and moulting individuals, caused by nesting turtles. The report stresses that restoration decisions should account for ecological conditions, engineering constraints and Native Hawaiian cultural perspectives. It also calls for cultural consultation in considering seawall replacement. NOAAâs new award provides funding for coastal habitat restoration, while the specific measures to be implemented at Tern Island remain to be established. You use AI every day. title: 'Utilizing Iran for politics': IDF chief, Netanyahu clash over military action ahead of Israel elections - report
text: Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and IDF chief of staff general Eyal Zamir are reportedly at odds over a possible military operation. The reported disagreement comes just a day before Israel heads to polls, with speculation that the operation could involve a new strike on Iran. According to Israel's Channel 12, citing anonymous sources, Zamir sought further discussions and written legal authorisation from Netanyahu before proceeding with the operation. The report did not specify the nature of the proposed action. A military source told Channel 12, âThis relates to an action that could lead to a flare-up with Iran, at a sensitive and dramatic moment, creating this potential miscalculation.â Other unnamed sources expressed concern that Israel's political leadership could be trying to use the Iran issue for political gain. Watch âWill Make Israel Uninhabitable In An Hourâ: Iran's Dire Warning To Netanyahu; 'Don't Miscalculate' However, Netanyahu dismissed the allegations as ânonsenseâ in an interview with Israel's Channel 14, according to the Times of Israel. In an earlier television appearance, he said he had instructed the IDF and Mossad to work towards toppling the Iranian regime. The reported disagreement comes amid heightened political tensions ahead of the election, with pollsters projecting a close contest between Netanyahu and his main rival, Gadi Eisenkot. The reported face-off comes as US President Donald Trump again endorsed Netanyahu on Sunday, reiterating his support for the Israeli prime minister and urging voters to back him in Tuesday's election. "To the people of Israel, to those who havenât seen it, I am attaching the Endorsement I gave one week ago to your Prime Minister, Bibi Netanyahu. As everyone is aware, including the enemy, Bibi and I have had a great relationship in winning together ... When you go to the Polls, please remember that Bibi has been an outstanding Warrior Prime Minister!â The US President further wrote on Truth Social, âIsrael was called The Little Satan, with the United States being called The Big Satan, by some very evil people. There can no longer be the chant heard around the World of âDeath to America, Death to Israel,â and there wonât be. Vote for Bibi Netanyahu for Prime Minister, we have to finish the job that we started." Israeli PM Netanyahu also posted an AI-generated image on social media on Sunday depicting a nuclear explosion in Tel Aviv. Two days before the election, he warned that voting for anyone other than him could expose Israelis to the danger of a âsecond Holocaust.â Quoting right-wing activist Yuval Blumberg's statements, Netanyahu's post read,"The State of Israel is in real and tangible existential danger. If the Iranians acquire nuclear weapons, nothing will ever be the same again. Everything is so trivial compared to the existential threat of Iran and the Shiite axis." The post further argued that the remaining period of Trump's presidency presented a window to address the Iranian threat, while questioning whether a future US administration would offer the same opportunity. The final projections for Tuesday's election, published on October 23, indicated continued political gridlock. Neither the ruling coalition nor the opposition bloc was projected to secure enough support to form a government following the vote. title: EC orders officialsâ transfers ahead of 2027 UP polls
text: TNN Lucknow : The Election Commission of India has issued transfer and posting guidelines for officials directly associated with election duties ahead of the UP Assembly elections, directing the state govt to ensure compliance by Nov 30. UP CEO Navdeep Rinwa said on Tuesday that officials completing three years of service in the same district during the preceding four years, as of May 31, 2027, must be transferred. The guidelines cover district election officers, returning officers, assistant returning officers, ADMs, SDMs, tehsildars, block development officers, divisional commissioners, municipal commissioners and officials of development authorities. Police, excise and transport department officials of sub-inspector rank and above will also come under the transfer policy. The commission has prohibited postings in officersâ home districts. Officials who served in a particular constituency or district during the previous Assembly election or subsequent byelections cannot be retained or reposted there in specified election-related positions. Officials posted at state headquarters, technical personnel unrelated to election work and those serving as sector officers or zonal magistrates are generally exempt. Officials retiring by May 31, 2027, are also exempt but cannot hold key election-related positions. The chief secretary and DGP must submit a consolidated compliance report to the commission by Nov 30.
